topics.ch: Part I: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation
topics.t: Harappan civilisation: names, culture and sites
topics.h: Over 4,500 years ago, people from the Indus plains to Gujarat were using the same kind of bricks, seals and weights. How do we even name a world that left no readable writing?
p: The Indus valley civilisation is also called the Harappan civilisation, after Harappa, the first site where it was discovered.

In archaeology, a 'culture' means a group of objects of a distinctive style, usually found together within a specific geographical area and period of time. Harappan seals, beads, weights and stone blades form such a group.
The Mature Harappan phase is dated c. 2600–1900 BCE. Cultures before it in the same area are called Early Harappan; those after it are called Late Harappan.

Early Harappan settlements were generally small, had distinctive pottery, agriculture and pastoralism, and some crafts. A break between early and mature phases is shown by large-scale burning at some sites and abandonment of certain settlements.

Key sites: Harappa and Mohenjodaro (now in Pakistan), Dholavira and Lothal (Gujarat), Kalibangan (Rajasthan), Rakhigarhi and Banawali (Haryana), Chanhudaro (Sindh), Nageshwar (Gujarat coast), Balakot (Baluchistan coast) and Shortughai (Afghanistan).

ex.q: A student finds burnt layers at a site lying between Early Harappan pottery below and Mature Harappan seals above. What does this suggest?
st: Lower layers are older; upper layers are younger.
Early Harappan material lies below, so it came first.
Burnt layers between them point to destruction or a break.
This matches the break seen at some sites before the mature phase.
ex.a: There was a break, possibly with burning and abandonment, between the Early Harappan and Mature Harappan phases at that site.

topics.rl: Dholavira in Kutch, Gujarat, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021, so a Harappan city is now as much a part of India's heritage list as the Taj Mahal.

topics.ch: Part I: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation
topics.t: Subsistence: what the Harappans ate
topics.h: A burnt grain of barley, smaller than a grain of rice, can tell us what was cooked in a Mohenjodaro kitchen 4,500 years ago.
p: Harappans ate a wide range of plant and animal products, including fish. Archaeologists reconstruct diet from charred grains and seeds studied by archaeo-botanists.
Grains found include wheat, barley, lentil, chickpea and sesame. Millets are found at sites in Gujarat. Finds of rice are relatively rare.
Animal bones include cattle, sheep, goat, buffalo and pig; studies by archaeo-zoologists show these were domesticated.
Bones of wild species such as boar, deer and gharial are also found. We do not know if Harappans hunted these themselves or got the meat from other hunting communities.
Bones of fish and fowl are found as well, so food came from farmers, herders, fisherfolk and possibly hunter-gatherers.

ex.q: List the groups that may have supplied food to a Harappan city.
st: Grains and pulses: farmers.
Milk and meat of cattle, sheep, goat: herders/pastoralists.
Fish: fisherfolk.
Wild animals: hunters, maybe other communities.
ex.a: Peasants, pastoralists, fisherfolk and hunter-gatherers (or communities trading meat).

topics.rl: Just as Gujarat today grows bajra and jowar while Punjab grows wheat, Harappan millet finds come mainly from Gujarat sites.

topics.ch: Part I: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation
topics.t: Farming technology and irrigation
topics.h: At Kalibangan, archaeologists found a field ploughed nearly 5,000 years ago, with furrows still visible. A farmer in Rajasthan today might recognise the pattern!
p: Seals and terracotta sculptures show the bull was known, so oxen were probably used for ploughing.
Terracotta models of the plough have been found at sites in Cholistan and at Banawali (Haryana).

At Kalibangan (Rajasthan), a ploughed field was found, associated with Early Harappan levels. It had two sets of furrows at right angles to each other, suggesting two different crops were grown together.

Irrigation was probably needed as most Harappan sites lie in semi-arid lands. Traces of canals were found at Shortughai (Afghanistan), but not in Punjab or Sindh. Water from wells and water reservoirs at Dholavira (Gujarat) was also used.
For harvesting, Harappans may have used stone blades set in wooden handles, or metal tools; archaeologists are still not sure.

ex.q: Why do furrows at right angles in the Kalibangan field suggest two crops were grown together?
st: One set of furrows can be used for one crop.
A second set at right angles creates a grid.
Two crops sown in different directions in one field is a known practice.
So the pattern hints at mixed cropping.
ex.a: Criss-crossing furrows suggest that two different crops were grown in the same field at the same time.

topics.rl: Rajasthan farmers still grow mustard and gram together in one field; the Kalibangan furrows hint that mixed cropping is a very old Indian practice.

topics.ch: Part I: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation
topics.t: Mohenjodaro: a planned city and its drains
topics.h: Many Indian cities still struggle with waterlogged streets in the monsoon. Mohenjodaro had covered street drains about 4,500 years ago!
p: Mohenjodaro was divided into two parts: a smaller but higher Citadel (to the west) and a much larger but lower Lower Town (to the east). The Citadel was walled, and so was the Lower Town.
Buildings were built on platforms, which served as foundations. This means the settlement was planned first and then built. Platforms needed an enormous amount of labour.
Bricks, sun-dried or baked, were of a standardised ratio: length four times the height and breadth twice the height (4:2:1). This ratio was used across Harappan settlements.
Streets were laid out in an approximately grid pattern, intersecting at right angles. Drains seem to have been laid out first, and houses built along them.
House drains, carrying waste water, were connected to street drains. Long drainage channels had sumps at intervals for cleaning. Drainage systems are found in smaller settlements too, such as Lothal.

ex.q: A Harappan brick is 10 cm high. Using the standard ratio, what are its breadth and length?
st: Ratio length : breadth : height = 4 : 2 : 1.
Breadth = 2 × 10 = 20 cm.
Length = 4 × 10 = 40 cm.
ex.a: Breadth 20 cm, length 40 cm.

topics.rl: Smart City projects in India stress planned drainage first. Mohenjodaro's planners seem to have done that long ago: drains first, houses next.

topics.ch: Part I: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation
topics.t: Houses, the Citadel and the Great Bath
topics.h: Imagine a house in Mohenjodaro: you walk in from a lane but cannot see the courtyard from the doorway. Privacy mattered even 4,500 years ago!
p: Many Lower Town houses were centred on a courtyard with rooms on all sides. The courtyard was probably used for cooking and weaving, especially in hot and dry weather.
There were no windows in walls along the ground level, and the main entrance did not give a direct view of the interior or the courtyard, which suggests concern for privacy.

Every house had its own bathroom paved with bricks, with drains connected through the wall to the street drains. Some houses had staircases to a second storey or roof. Many houses had wells; Mohenjodaro had about 700 wells.
The Citadel had structures probably used for special public purposes, like the warehouse (only lower brick portions survive; upper wooden parts decayed) and the Great Bath.

The Great Bath was a large rectangular tank in a courtyard with a corridor on all four sides, two flights of steps on the north and south, bricks set on edge with gypsum mortar to make it watertight. Its uniqueness and location suggest a special ritual bath.

ex.q: Give two reasons why scholars think the Great Bath had a special, perhaps ritual, purpose.
st: It is a unique structure, not found elsewhere in that form.
It stands in the Citadel, among public buildings.
It had careful watertight construction and side rooms, one with a large well.
ex.a: Its unique design and its location in the Citadel with other special buildings suggest a ritual bath.

topics.rl: The idea of a sacred tank survives across India, from temple tanks (kalyani or pushkarini) in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu to ghats on the Ganga.

topics.ch: Part I: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation
topics.t: Tracking social differences: burials and 'luxuries'
topics.h: In Egypt, pharaohs were buried with mountains of gold. What did Harappans place in their graves, and what does that tell us?
p: Archaeologists study burials and artefacts to find social or economic differences.

At Harappan burial sites the dead were generally laid in pits. Some pits were lined with bricks. Some graves contain pottery and ornaments, perhaps showing a belief that these could be used in the afterlife.

Jewellery is found in burials of both men and women. In one Harappa burial (excavated in the 1980s), a man had an ornament of three shell rings, a jasper bead and hundreds of micro beads. Some burials had copper mirrors.
Overall, Harappans do not seem to have believed in burying precious things with the dead, so burial differences are not very sharp.

Artefacts are classified as utilitarian (daily-use objects like querns, pottery, needles, flesh-rubbers, made of stone or clay, found everywhere) or luxuries (rare objects of costly non-local materials or complicated technology, such as little faience pots). Faience vessels are found in large cities like Mohenjodaro and Harappa but not in small ones like Kalibangan. Gold was rare and found in hoards.

ex.q: A grave has a brick-lined pit with pottery, while another has a plain pit with nothing. What can a historian infer, and what caution is needed?
st: Brick lining and goods mean more effort and resources.
This hints at differences in status.
But Harappan graves rarely have precious items.
So differences existed but were not extreme.
ex.a: There were some social differences, but the evidence does not show sharp inequality like that in Egyptian royal burials.

topics.rl: Today, archaeologists at Rakhigarhi in Haryana study skeletons and grave goods with DNA and dating methods to learn about the people buried there.

topics.ch: Part I: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation
topics.t: Craft production: Chanhudaro and bead-making
topics.h: A red carnelian bead from the Indus could end up in a royal grave in Mesopotamia. Its journey began at a tiny town called Chanhudaro.
p: Chanhudaro was a tiny settlement (less than 7 hectares) almost exclusively devoted to craft production: bead-making, shell-cutting, metal-working, seal-making and weight-making.
Bead materials: stones like carnelian (beautiful red), jasper, crystal, quartz and steatite; metals like copper, bronze and gold; and shell, faience and terracotta (burnt clay).
Beads were made in many shapes: disc, cylindrical, spherical, barrel and segmented. Some were decorated by incising or painting, some had etched designs.

Techniques: nodules were chipped into rough shapes, then flaked into final form; grinding, polishing and drilling completed the process. The red colour of carnelian came from firing the yellowish raw material and beads at various stages. Specialised drills have been found at Chanhudaro, Lothal and Dholavira.

To identify a production centre, archaeologists look for raw material (stone nodules, whole shells, copper ore), tools, unfinished objects, rejects and waste material. Waste is one of the best indicators.

ex.q: An excavator finds shell pieces with cut marks, broken bangles and whole shells in one area. Is it a craft workshop?
st: Whole shells = raw material.
Pieces with cut marks = waste.
Broken bangles = rejects/unfinished objects.
All three together point to production on the spot.
ex.a: Yes, it was probably a shell-working centre, because raw material, waste and unfinished objects are found together.

topics.rl: Khambhat (Cambay) in Gujarat is still famous for agate and carnelian bead-making, a craft with roots going back to Harappan times.

topics.ch: Part I: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation
topics.t: Procuring materials within the subcontinent
topics.h: Copper from Rajasthan, gold from the south, blue lapis lazuli from Afghanistan: Harappan craftspeople ran a supply chain long before trucks and railways.
p: Harappans got raw materials in many ways. Bullock carts carried goods over land; riverine routes along the Indus and its tributaries and coastal routes were probably also used. Terracotta toy models of bullock carts have been found.

One strategy was to set up settlements near sources: Nageshwar and Balakot near shell sources; Shortughai in far Afghanistan near lapis lazuli (a blue stone); Lothal near carnelian (from Bharuch, Gujarat), steatite (south Rajasthan and north Gujarat) and metal (Rajasthan).
Nageshwar and Balakot specialised in making shell objects such as bangles, ladles and inlay, which were sent to other settlements.
Another strategy was sending expeditions: to the Khetri region of Rajasthan for copper and to South India for gold.

In the Khetri area, archaeologists found evidence of the Ganeshwar-Jodhpura culture, with distinctive non-Harappan pottery and an unusual wealth of copper objects. Its people may have supplied copper to the Harappans.

ex.q: Why would the Harappans set up Shortughai so far away in Afghanistan?
st: Shortughai lies near sources of lapis lazuli.
Lapis lazuli was a highly valued blue stone.
A settlement near the source made regular supply easier.
ex.a: To secure a steady supply of lapis lazuli from close to its source.

topics.rl: Today, India's Khetri Copper Complex in Rajasthan (Hindustan Copper Ltd) works the same copper belt that Harappans may have obtained copper from.

topics.ch: Part I: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation
topics.t: Contact with distant lands
topics.h: Clay tablets from Mesopotamia speak of a far-off land called Meluhha that sent carnelian and timber. Many scholars think that land was the Harappan region!
p: Copper was probably brought from Oman, on the southeastern tip of the Arabian peninsula. Chemical analyses show both Omani copper and Harappan artefacts have traces of nickel, suggesting a common origin.
A large Harappan jar coated with a thick layer of black clay has been found at Omani sites, and Harappan objects have been found there too.
Mesopotamian texts from about the mid-third millennium BCE mention contact with Dilmun (probably the island of Bahrain), Magan (perhaps Oman) and Meluhha (possibly the Harappan region).

Products from Meluhha mentioned include carnelian, lapis lazuli, copper, gold and varieties of wood. A Mesopotamian myth says of Meluhha: 'May your bird be the haja-bird' — some scholars think the haja-bird was the peacock.
Meluhha is described as a land of seafarers. Mesopotamian seals show ships and boats, and Persian Gulf seals have been found, suggesting sea trade.

ex.q: A Mesopotamian text lists carnelian and timber coming from 'Meluhha'. Why do scholars identify Meluhha with the Harappan region?
st: The goods listed (carnelian, lapis lazuli, copper, gold, wood) match Harappan resources.
Harappan objects and seals are found in the Gulf region.
Meluhha is called a land of seafarers, fitting coastal Harappan sites.
ex.a: Because the goods and the evidence of sea links match the Harappan region, though the identification is still 'possible', not certain.

topics.rl: Gujarat's Lothal is being developed as a National Maritime Heritage Complex, recalling India's earliest sea trade with the Gulf.

topics.ch: Part I: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation
topics.t: Seals, script and weights
topics.h: Your online parcel has a barcode; a Harappan sack of goods had a clay sealing. Both said: 'Untouched, from the right sender!'
p: Seals and sealings were used to facilitate long-distance communication. A sack of goods was tied with rope, the knot covered with wet clay, and seals pressed on it. The impression is called a sealing; an intact sealing showed the goods were not tampered with and identified the sender.
The Harappan seal is typically made of steatite (a stone). It often has an animal motif and signs from a script that remains undeciphered.
The script was probably not alphabetic, because it has too many signs: somewhere between 375 and 400. It was written from right to left (wider spacing on the right, cramped on the left).
Inscriptions are short; the longest has about 26 signs. Writing appears on seals, copper tools, rims of jars, copper and terracotta tablets, jewellery, bone rods and even an ancient signboard.

Weights were usually cubical, made of chert, with no markings. Lower denominations were binary (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, … up to 12,800), while higher denominations followed the decimal system. Smaller weights were probably for jewellery and beads; metal scale-pans have been found.

ex.q: In the binary series 1, 2, 4, 8, …, what are the next three weights after 8?
st: Each weight is double the previous one.

topics.rl: Courier companies and India Post use tamper-proof seals and tracking codes; Harappan sealings did the same job of proving goods were untouched.

topics.ch: Part I: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation
topics.t: Ancient authority: who ruled the Harappans?
topics.h: Same brick ratio from Punjab to Gujarat, same weights, planned cities. Who made all these decisions? Historians still argue!
p: Signs of complex decisions: extraordinary uniformity of Harappan artefacts (pottery, seals, weights, bricks); bricks of standard ratio even though not produced in a single centre; planned settlements; craft production organised in places near raw materials.
Palace and king? A large building at Mohenjodaro was labelled a palace by archaeologists, but no spectacular finds were associated with it.

A stone statue was labelled 'priest-king' because archaeologists were familiar with Mesopotamian history and its 'priest-kings'. Harappan ritual practices are not yet understood, so we cannot know if those who performed them held political power.

Theories: (1) there were no rulers and everybody enjoyed equal status; (2) there was no single ruler but several, such as one each for Mohenjodaro and Harappa; (3) these were part of a single state, given the similarity in artefacts, planned settlements, standard bricks and settlements near raw material sources.
As things stand, the last theory seems the most plausible, as it is unlikely entire communities could have collectively made and implemented such complex decisions.

ex.q: Which theory of Harappan political organisation does the uniformity of bricks across distant sites support most strongly, and why?
st: Bricks were made in many places, not in one factory.
Yet they share the same 4:2:1 ratio.
Such uniformity suggests decisions taken and enforced over a large area.
This fits best with a single state.
ex.a: It supports the single-state theory, since a common authority could enforce such standards.

topics.rl: The Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) sets uniform standards for bricks, cement and more across India today; Harappan standardisation suggests some authority did a similar job.

topics.ch: Part I: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation
topics.t: The end of the civilisation
topics.h: Imagine a city where people stopped using writing, seals and standard weights within a few generations. That is roughly what happened after c. 1900 BCE.
p: By c. 1800 BCE most Mature Harappan sites in regions such as Cholistan had been abandoned.
At the same time, population expanded into new settlements in Gujarat, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh.

In the few Harappan sites that continued to be occupied after 1900 BCE, material culture changed: distinctive artefacts such as weights, seals and special beads disappeared; writing, long-distance trade and craft specialisation also disappeared. House construction techniques deteriorated and large public structures were no longer built. These are called Late Harappan or 'successor' cultures, and show a rural way of life.
Suggested causes include climatic change, deforestation, excessive floods, the shifting and/or drying up of rivers, and overuse of the landscape.

These causes may explain the end of some settlements but not the collapse of a whole civilisation. One explanation is the disappearance of a strong unifying element, perhaps the Harappan state, shown by the vanishing of seals, the script, distinctive beads and pottery.

ex.q: Why is 'floods' alone not a convincing explanation for the end of the entire Harappan civilisation?
st: Floods could ruin settlements near rivers.
But Harappan sites were spread over a vast area with different conditions.
A local cause cannot explain the simultaneous disappearance of seals, script and weights everywhere.
So a wider explanation, like the collapse of a unifying state, is suggested.
ex.a: Floods may explain the abandonment of some sites but not the civilisation-wide loss of seals, script and standard weights.

topics.rl: Ghaggar-Hakra channels and drying rivers are studied by Indian scientists today using satellite images from ISRO to understand how river shifts affected ancient settlements.

topics.ch: Part I: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation
topics.t: Discovering Harappa: Cunningham to Wheeler
topics.h: Alexander Cunningham held a Harappan seal in his hands in the 1870s but could not tell how old it was. The discovery waited another 50 years!
p: Alexander Cunningham, the first Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI), began excavations in the mid-nineteenth century. He used accounts of Chinese Buddhist pilgrims (4th–7th centuries CE) to locate early settlements; his main interest was the Early Historic period.
Harappa did not fit his framework. An Englishman gave him a Harappan seal; he tried to place it in a familiar time-frame and failed to realise how old Harappa was (Report on Harappan seal, 1875).

In the early twentieth century, Daya Ram Sahni found seals at Harappa in layers much older than Early Historic levels; R.D. Banerji found similar seals at Mohenjodaro. In 1924 John Marshall, Director-General of the ASI, announced the discovery of a new civilisation in the Indus valley.

Marshall excavated along regular horizontal units measured uniformly throughout the mound, ignoring the site's stratigraphy. So artefacts from different layers were grouped together and their context was lost.

R.E.M. Wheeler, Director-General of the ASI from 1944, corrected this by following the stratigraphy of the mound. Later landmarks: Wheeler at Harappa (1946), S.R. Rao at Lothal (1955), B.B. Lal and B.K. Thapar at Kalibangan (1960), R.S. Bisht at Dholavira (1990).

ex.q: Why was Marshall's method a problem?
st: A mound has layers formed at different times (stratigraphy).
Marshall dug in uniform horizontal units regardless of layers.
Objects from different layers got mixed in one unit.
So their date and context were lost.
ex.a: Ignoring stratigraphy mixed up artefacts of different periods, destroying valuable information about context.

topics.rl: The ASI, founded in Cunningham's time, still protects over 3,600 monuments across India, from Dholavira to the Red Fort.

topics.ch: Part I: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation
topics.t: New sites and the problems of interpretation
topics.h: A small clay figure of a woman with heavy jewellery: is she a goddess, a toy or a household charm? Archaeologists must decide with no label attached!
p: After Partition (1947) the major sites Harappa and Mohenjodaro were in Pakistan. Indian archaeologists explored new areas: surveys in Kutch, Punjab and Haryana added many sites, with Kalibangan, Lothal, Rakhigarhi and Dholavira excavated in India. Explorations continued in Pakistan too.

New techniques and questions: scientific analysis of materials, and studies of plant and animal remains, are used to understand diet, trade and environment; since the 1980s there has been growing international interest.

Classifying finds is a basic step: by material (stone, clay, metal, bone, ivory) and by function. Function is hard to know; archaeologists often compare with present-day objects (e.g. querns) or study the context of the find.

Religion is inferred from objects: terracotta female figurines, heavily jewelled with elaborate head-dresses, were called 'mother goddesses'; rare stone statues of men seated in a standard posture were labelled 'priest-king'; fire altars are reported from Kalibangan and Lothal; seals show a 'unicorn' and a figure seated cross-legged in a 'yogic' posture surrounded by animals, regarded as 'proto-Shiva'; conical stones have been classified as lingas.

Such interpretations often use later traditions. For example, Rudra appears in the Rigveda, but he is not depicted there as Pashupati or as a yogi. So using later texts to explain Harappan objects has limits.

ex.q: Why is the 'proto-Shiva' identification of the yogic figure on a seal debated?
st: The identification relies on later Hindu ideas of Shiva as Pashupati and yogi.
The Rigveda, an earlier text, mentions Rudra.
But Rudra in the Rigveda is not shown as Pashupati or as a yogi.
So the link between the seal and later Shiva is uncertain.
ex.a: Because it projects later religious ideas backwards; even the Rigveda's Rudra does not match the image.

topics.rl: Archaeologists at Rakhigarhi (Haryana) have used ancient DNA analysis, an example of new scientific techniques changing what we know about Harappans.

topics.ch: Part I: Kings, Farmers and Towns: Early States and Economies
topics.t: Prinsep, Piyadassi and the power of inscriptions
topics.h: For centuries people walked past pillars covered in strange letters. In 1838 a mint officer cracked the code, and a forgotten emperor stepped back into history.
p: An inscription is writing engraved on a hard surface such as stone, metal or pottery. It usually records the achievements, activities or ideas of those who commissioned it, and serves as a permanent record.

James Prinsep, an officer in the mint of the East India Company, deciphered Brahmi and Kharosthi, two scripts used in the earliest inscriptions and coins. He achieved the decipherment of Asokan Brahmi in 1838.

Most Asokan inscriptions call the king Piyadassi, meaning 'pleasant to behold'. He is also called Devanampiya, 'beloved of the gods'. A few inscriptions name him Asoka, which helped scholars identify Piyadassi with the Asoka of Buddhist texts.

Reading inscriptions gave a new direction to early Indian political history: scholars could link rulers named in inscriptions and coins with dynasties in texts and build an outline of political history.

ex.q: A pillar inscription mentions 'Devanampiya Piyadassi'. How did historians conclude this was Asoka?
st: Buddhist texts describe a great Mauryan king called Asoka.
Most edicts use the titles Devanampiya and Piyadassi.
Some inscriptions also mention the name Asoka with these titles.
So Piyadassi and Asoka were identified as the same king.
ex.a: By matching the titles in inscriptions with the name Asoka found in some inscriptions and in Buddhist texts.

topics.rl: The Lion Capital of Asoka's pillar at Sarnath is India's national emblem, printed on every rupee note and passport.

topics.ch: Part I: Kings, Farmers and Towns: Early States and Economies
topics.t: The earliest states: sixteen mahajanapadas
topics.h: Sixteen big kingdoms and republics jostled for power in north India around 2,500 years ago. Think of it as an ancient IPL with sixteen teams!
p: The sixth century BCE is often seen as a major turning point: early states, cities, growing use of iron, the development of coinage, and new systems of thought including Buddhism and Jainism.

Early Buddhist and Jaina texts mention sixteen states known as mahajanapadas. The lists vary, but names such as Vajji, Magadha, Koshala, Kuru, Panchala, Gandhara and Avanti occur often, showing they were among the most important.

Most mahajanapadas were ruled by kings. Some, known as ganas or sanghas, were oligarchies where power was shared by a number of men, often collectively called rajas. Mahavira and the Buddha both belonged to such ganas. In some, like the Vajji sangha, the rajas probably controlled resources such as land collectively.
Each mahajanapada had a capital city, often fortified. Maintaining these cities, early armies and bureaucracies needed resources.

From c. the sixth century BCE, Brahmanas began composing Sanskrit texts called Dharmasutras, which laid down norms for rulers and other social categories. Rulers were ideally Kshatriyas, advised to collect taxes and tribute from cultivators, traders and artisans. Raids on neighbouring states were seen as a legitimate way to gain wealth.

ex.q: How did a gana or sangha differ from a kingdom?
st: In a kingdom, one king held power.
In a gana/sangha, power was shared by many men called rajas.
Resources like land may have been controlled collectively.
So a gana was an oligarchy, not a monarchy.
ex.a: A gana or sangha was ruled by a group of rajas sharing power, unlike a kingdom ruled by one king.

topics.rl: Vaishali in Bihar, capital of the Vajji sangha, is often called one of the world's earliest republics; a pillar of Asoka still stands at Kolhua near Vaishali.

topics.ch: Part I: Kings, Farmers and Towns: Early States and Economies
topics.t: Magadha: first amongst sixteen
topics.h: From Rajgir in the hills to Patna on the Ganga, Magadha's rise is a story of iron, elephants, fertile soil and ambitious kings.
p: Between the sixth and fourth centuries BCE, Magadha (in present-day Bihar) became the most powerful mahajanapada.

Modern historians explain this through several factors: agriculture was especially productive; iron mines (in present-day Jharkhand) were accessible and gave resources for tools and weapons; elephants, an important part of the army, were found in forests in the region; and the Ganga and its tributaries provided a cheap and convenient means of communication.
Early Buddhist and Jaina writers explained Magadha's power through the policies of ambitious, ruthless rulers such as Bimbisara, Ajatasattu and Mahapadma Nanda, and their ministers.

The early capital was Rajagaha (the Prakrit name for present-day Rajgir), a fortified settlement among hills. In the fourth century BCE the capital shifted to Pataliputra (present-day Patna), which commanded routes of communication along the Ganga.

ex.q: Why would shifting the capital from Rajagaha to Pataliputra make sense?
st: Rajagaha was protected by hills, good for defence.
Pataliputra stood on the Ganga.
River routes allowed easier movement of goods and armies.
So Pataliputra suited a growing kingdom that needed communication.
ex.a: Pataliputra commanded routes along the Ganga, better for an expanding state than hill-girt Rajagaha.

topics.rl: Patna remains Bihar's capital, and Rajgir is now a pilgrimage and tourist town with the Nalanda University campus nearby, linking modern Bihar to ancient Magadha.

topics.ch: Part I: Kings, Farmers and Towns: Early States and Economies
topics.t: An early empire: Chandragupta Maurya and the sources
topics.h: A Greek ambassador, a political manual, rock edicts and Buddhist legends: historians use all of these to piece together the Mauryan empire.
p: The growth of Magadha culminated in the Mauryan empire. Chandragupta Maurya founded it around 321 BCE; it extended as far north-west as Afghanistan and Baluchistan.
His grandson Asoka, arguably the most famous ruler of early India, conquered Kalinga (present-day coastal Odisha).

Sources include archaeological finds, especially sculpture; contemporary works such as the account of Megasthenes, a Greek ambassador to Chandragupta's court, which survives in fragments; and the Arthashastra, parts of which were probably composed by Kautilya or Chanakya, traditionally believed to be Chandragupta's minister.

Later Buddhist, Jaina and Puranic literature, and Sanskrit literary works, also mention the Mauryas. The inscriptions of Asoka on rocks and pillars are often regarded as among the most valuable sources.

ex.q: Why is the account of Megasthenes useful but limited as a source?
st: He was a Greek ambassador who saw Chandragupta's court.
So he gives a contemporary, eyewitness view.
But his work survives only in fragments.
And as a foreigner he might misunderstand things.
ex.a: It is a valuable contemporary account, but it survives only in fragments and reflects an outsider's view.

topics.rl: The Arthashastra's ideas on taxation and administration are still discussed in Indian management and policy courses, often under the name 'Kautilyan economics'.

topics.ch: Part I: Kings, Farmers and Towns: Early States and Economies
topics.t: Administering the Mauryan empire
topics.h: How do you run an empire from Taxila to Karnataka without phones or trains? The Mauryas used five power centres and a military committee.
p: There were five major political centres: the capital Pataliputra and the provincial centres of Taxila, Ujjayini, Tosali and Suvarnagiri, all mentioned in Asokan inscriptions.
Taxila and Ujjayini lay on important long-distance trade routes. Suvarnagiri (literally 'the golden mountain') was possibly important for tapping the gold mines of Karnataka.
Administrative control was strongest in areas around the capital and the provincial centres. Communication along both land and riverine routes was vital for the empire's existence.
Megasthenes mentions a committee with six subcommittees for coordinating military activity: navy; transport and provisions; foot-soldiers; horses; chariots; elephants.
The transport subcommittee arranged bullock carts to carry equipment, procured food for soldiers and fodder for animals, and recruited servants and artisans to look after the soldiers.

ex.q: List the six subcommittees mentioned by Megasthenes.
st: Navy.
Transport and provisions.
Foot-soldiers.
Horses.
Chariots.
Elephants.
ex.a: Navy; transport and provisions; foot-soldiers; horses; chariots; elephants.

topics.rl: Indian Railways is divided into zones with headquarters, like Mauryan provinces, to manage a vast network from different centres.

topics.ch: Part I: Kings, Farmers and Towns: Early States and Economies
topics.t: Asoka's dhamma and the Mauryan legacy
topics.h: After a war in which a hundred thousand were killed, an emperor carved his regret in stone. Asoka's Kalinga edict is one of history's rarest confessions.
p: Asoka's Rock Edict XIII records that in the eighth year of his reign he conquered Kalinga: about 1,50,000 people were deported, 1,00,000 killed, and many more died. He expressed deep remorse.

Asoka tried to hold his empire together by propagating dhamma. Its principles were simple and universal: respect towards elders; generosity towards Brahmanas and those who renounced worldly life; treating slaves and servants kindly; respect for religions and traditions other than one's own.
He appointed special officers, the dhamma mahamatta, to spread dhamma. Asoka believed dhamma would ensure the well-being of people in this world and the next.

Nineteenth-century historians found the Mauryan empire an exciting discovery; the stone sculpture and the inscriptions seemed to mark a high point. Twentieth-century Indian nationalists found Asoka an inspiring figure.

Yet its limits matter: the empire lasted about 150 years, which is not very long, and it did not cover the whole subcontinent. Control was strongest near the capital and provincial centres and much weaker elsewhere.

ex.q: How does Rock Edict XIII show a change in Asoka's thinking?
st: It records the Kalinga conquest and the huge loss of life.
Asoka says he felt deep remorse.
He then turned to spreading dhamma through officials and edicts.
ex.a: It shows a shift from conquest by war to spreading dhamma, prompted by remorse for the suffering in Kalinga.

topics.rl: The Ashoka Chakra on India's national flag comes from the dhamma chakra on Asokan pillars, a reminder of the ideals of righteousness and tolerance.

topics.ch: Part I: Kings, Farmers and Towns: Early States and Economies
topics.t: New notions of kingship: chiefs, Satavahanas and Kushanas
topics.h: In the south, chiefs were praised in Tamil poems for giving away wealth. In the north-west, Kushana kings called themselves 'son of god'. Two very different ideas of power!
p: In the far south (Tamilakam), new chiefdoms and kingdoms emerged, including the Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas. They were prosperous and stable. We know about them from Tamil Sangam texts, poems that describe chiefs and how they acquired and distributed resources.

A chief is a powerful man whose position may or may not be hereditary. He derives support from his kinsfolk. His functions include performing special rituals, leading in warfare and arbitrating disputes. He receives gifts from subordinates (rather than collecting taxes) and redistributes them. Generally, chiefs had no regular officials or army.

Several kings, including the Satavahanas who ruled over parts of western and central India and the Shakas, a people of Central Asian origin who set up kingdoms in the north-west and west, derived revenues from long-distance trade.

Rulers also claimed high status by identifying with deities. The Kushanas (c. first century BCE–first century CE) ruled from Central Asia to north-west India. Colossal statues of Kushana rulers were installed in a shrine at Mat near Mathura (UP), and similar statues in a shrine in Afghanistan.
Many Kushana rulers adopted the title devaputra, or 'son of god', possibly inspired by Chinese rulers who called themselves sons of heaven.

ex.q: Compare a chief with a king.
st: A chief relied on kinsfolk and gifts from subordinates.
A chief usually had no regular officials or army.
A king collected regular taxes and had a bureaucracy and army.
So a king's power was more institutionalised.
ex.a: Chiefs depended on gifts and kin and lacked officials and armies; kings collected taxes and kept officials and standing armies.

topics.rl: The Government Museum in Mathura displays a headless statue of the Kushana king Kanishka, a famous example of how rulers projected power through colossal images.

topics.ch: Part I: Kings, Farmers and Towns: Early States and Economies
topics.t: The Guptas, samantas and the Prayaga Prashasti
topics.h: Harishena wrote that Samudragupta's body was 'most charming, covered with the plenty of the beauty of the marks of hundreds of scars'. Was it history or poetry?
p: By the fourth century there is evidence of several large states, including the Gupta empire. Many depended on samantas: men who maintained themselves through local resources, including control over land, and offered homage and military support to rulers.
Powerful samantas could become kings; conversely, weak rulers might find themselves reduced to subordination.
Histories of the Guptas are reconstructed from literature, coins and inscriptions, including prashastis composed in praise of kings by poets.

The Prayaga Prashasti (also called the Allahabad Pillar Inscription) was composed in Sanskrit by Harishena, the court poet of Samudragupta, arguably the most powerful Gupta ruler, nearly 1,700 years ago.
Prashastis give useful information, but historians read them carefully: they are poetic praise meant to glorify the king, and may not be literally true.

ex.q: A prashasti says the king defeated every rival and was kinder than any god. How should a historian use it?
st: Note what it claims: victories, virtues.
Remember the author was a court poet paid to praise.
Check claims against coins, other inscriptions and texts.
Accept what is confirmed; treat the rest as royal ideals.
ex.a: Use it for the king's claims and ideals, but cross-check facts with other sources before accepting them.

topics.rl: The Allahabad (Prayagraj) Pillar stands inside the Allahabad Fort and carries an Asokan inscription as well as Harishena's prashasti and later inscriptions, a stone 'notebook' of many centuries.

topics.ch: Part I: Kings, Farmers and Towns: Early States and Economies
topics.t: A changing countryside: kings, subjects and production
topics.h: In a Jataka story, a wicked king's subjects all complain: an old woman, cowherds, villagers, even a frog! What did ordinary people think of kings?
p: Ordinary people rarely left accounts, but stories in the Jatakas (written in Pali around the middle of the first millennium CE) and the Panchatantra give clues about how they saw kings.

The Gandatindu Jataka describes the plight of subjects of a wicked king: elderly women, men, cultivators, herders, village boys and even animals suffer. Another story shows people fleeing to the forest to escape heavy taxes. Kings often tried to fill their coffers by demanding high taxes, which peasants found oppressive.

To meet growing demands for taxes, people adopted new ways to increase production. One was the shift to plough agriculture, which spread in fertile alluvial river valleys such as those of the Ganga and the Kaveri from c. the sixth century BCE. The iron-tipped ploughshare turned the soil better.
In the Ganga valley, paddy transplantation (raising saplings and then planting them in waterlogged fields) greatly increased yields, though it was very hard work.

Irrigation through wells and tanks, and less commonly canals, was another strategy. Communities as well as individuals organised irrigation works; powerful men, including kings, often recorded such works in inscriptions. Iron ploughs were not used everywhere: in semi-arid parts of Punjab and Rajasthan they came only in the twentieth century, and hilly tracts used the hoe.

ex.q: Compare what a king wanted from subjects with what the subjects wanted, using Jataka stories.
st: The king wanted higher taxes and tribute.
Subjects wanted protection and fair treatment.
When kings were oppressive, subjects suffered and sometimes fled to forests.
ex.a: Kings sought revenue; subjects wanted relief from heavy demands and fair rule, which created tension.

topics.rl: Paddy transplantation is still how most rice is grown in Bihar and West Bengal during the monsoon, back-breaking work that boosts yields, just as it did 2,500 years ago.

topics.ch: Part I: Kings, Farmers and Towns: Early States and Economies
topics.t: Rural society and land grants
topics.h: A copper plate gifting a whole village to a Brahmana: thousands of such grants survive. What do they tell us about kings, women and peasants?
p: New technologies did not benefit everyone equally. Early Buddhist texts refer to landless agricultural labourers, small peasants and large landholders. The term gahapati was often used for small peasants and large landholders. The gahapati was the owner, master or head of a household, controlling women, children, slaves and workers.
Tamil Sangam texts mention vellalar (large landowners), uzhavar (ploughmen) and adimai (slaves).

From c. the first century CE, land grants were recorded in inscriptions, some on stone but most on copper plates, often given to religious institutions or to Brahmanas. Land granted to Brahmanas was called agrahara; it was usually exempt from land revenue and other dues to the king, and Brahmanas often got the right to collect these dues locally.

Prabhavati Gupta, daughter of Chandragupta II (c. 375–415 CE), married into the Vakataka family of the Deccan. Sanskrit legal texts said women had no independent access to land, but her grant shows she had land which she granted, perhaps because she was a queen and her situation exceptional.

Historians debate land grants: some see them as a strategy by ruling lineages to extend agriculture to new areas; others see them as a sign of weakening political power, as kings tried to win allies by granting land. Grants also give a glimpse of relations between cultivators and the state.

ex.q: Why is Prabhavati Gupta's land grant significant for the history of women?
st: Sanskrit legal texts denied women independent access to land.
Yet her inscription shows she held land and granted it.
This was perhaps because she was a queen.
So texts' norms and actual practice could differ, at least for elite women.
ex.a: It shows an elite woman controlling and granting land, unlike the norms of Sanskrit legal texts.

topics.rl: Copper-plate land grants are still being found by farmers in Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka and handed to epigraphists of the ASI at Mysuru for reading.

topics.ch: Part I: Kings, Farmers and Towns: Early States and Economies
topics.t: Towns, guilds and trade
topics.h: Black pepper from Kerala was so prized in Rome that historians call it 'black gold'. The towns of early India were busy hubs on the routes that carried it.
p: Many major towns grew along routes of communication: Pataliputra on a riverine route, Ujjayini along land routes, and Puhar near the coast, from where sea routes began. Cities like Mathura were bustling centres of commercial, cultural and political activity.

Most cities were fortified. Rulers and urban elites lived in them. Archaeologists have found fine pottery bowls and dishes with a glossy finish called Northern Black Polished Ware (NBPW), probably used by rich people, plus ornaments, tools, weapons and figurines of gold, silver, copper, bronze, ivory, glass, shell and terracotta.

By the second century BCE, short votive (donative) inscriptions in many cities record gifts to religious institutions by washing folk, weavers, scribes, carpenters, potters, goldsmiths, blacksmiths, officials, religious teachers, merchants and kings.
Guilds or shrenis were organisations of craft producers and merchants. They probably procured raw materials, regulated production and marketed the finished products.

From the sixth century BCE, land and river routes criss-crossed the subcontinent and reached Central Asia and beyond; sea routes went across the Arabian Sea to East and North Africa and West Asia, and through the Bay of Bengal to Southeast Asia and China. Goods included salt, grain, cloth, metal ores and products, stone, timber and medicinal plants. Spices, especially pepper, and textiles were in great demand in the Roman Empire.

ex.q: Compare craft production evidence in Harappan cities with that in early historic cities.
st: Harappa: craft centres identified by raw material, tools, waste and unfinished objects (e.g. Chanhudaro).
Early historic cities: similar finds plus NBPW and many materials.
Early historic cities also have donative inscriptions naming crafts and guilds (shrenis).
So early historic evidence combines archaeology with written records.
ex.a: Both have archaeological evidence of crafts, but early historic cities also have inscriptions naming craftspeople and guilds.

topics.rl: Kerala still exports black pepper worldwide; the ancient port of Muziris is being explored through the Muziris Heritage Project near Kochi.

topics.ch: Part I: Kings, Farmers and Towns: Early States and Economies
topics.t: Coins and kings
topics.h: Roman gold coins buried in Tamil Nadu, Kushana coins matching Roman weights: coins are like ancient receipts of global trade.
p: Exchanges were facilitated by coinage. Punch-marked coins of silver and copper (c. sixth century BCE onwards) were among the earliest to be minted and used. Their symbols have been identified with royal families, including the Mauryas, though some may have been issued by merchants, bankers and townspeople.
The first coins to bear the names and images of rulers were issued by the Indo-Greeks, who established control over the north-western part of the subcontinent around the second century BCE.

The first gold coins were issued c. the first century CE by the Kushanas. They were virtually identical in weight to those of contemporary Roman emperors and the Parthian rulers of Iran. Hoards of Roman coins have been found in south India, showing networks of trade.
Tribal republics such as the Yaudheyas of Punjab and Haryana (c. first century CE) issued several thousand copper coins, showing their interest and participation in economic exchange.

The Gupta rulers issued some of the most spectacular gold coins; the earliest are remarkable for their purity. From the sixth century CE, finds of gold coins taper off. Some historians link this to a decline in long-distance trade after the collapse of the Western Roman Empire; others note new towns and networks were emerging, and that coins may simply not have been hoarded.

ex.q: Arrange the coin 'firsts' in order and give one feature of each.
st: Punch-marked coins (c. 6th century BCE): silver and copper with symbols.
Indo-Greek coins (c. 2nd century BCE): first with names and images of rulers.
Kushana gold coins (c. 1st century CE): first gold coins, Roman weight standard.
Gupta gold coins (from 4th century CE): spectacular, pure gold.
ex.a: Punch-marked → Indo-Greek → Kushana gold → Gupta gold.

topics.rl: The Reserve Bank of India's Monetary Museum in Mumbai displays punch-marked and Kushana coins, showing the long story of Indian money from silver bits to the UPI era.

topics.ch: Part I: Kings, Farmers and Towns: Early States and Economies
topics.t: How are inscriptions deciphered?
topics.h: Imagine solving a puzzle by working backwards from today's Bengali letters to 2,000-year-old Brahmi. That is how the code was cracked!
p: Brahmi was used in most Asokan inscriptions. From the late eighteenth century, European scholars, aided by Indian pandits, worked backwards from contemporary Bengali and Devanagari manuscripts, comparing their letters with older specimens.
Scholars sometimes assumed early inscriptions were in Sanskrit, but the earliest were actually in Prakrit. After decades of painstaking work, James Prinsep deciphered Asokan Brahmi in 1838.

Kharosthi, used in inscriptions of the north-west, was read differently. Indo-Greek coins carried kings' names in both Greek and Kharosthi. European scholars who could read Greek compared the letters, e.g. matching the symbol for 'a' in names like Apollodotus.

Reading an edict, epigraphists identify titles (Devanampiya Piyadassi), place names and key phrases, add words in brackets to clarify meaning, and then draw inferences, for instance about Asoka's remorse after Kalinga or the officials he appointed.

Landmarks in epigraphy: 1784 founding of the Asiatic Society (Bengal); 1838 Prinsep's decipherment of Brahmi; 1877 Cunningham publishes a set of Asokan inscriptions; 1888 first issue of Epigraphia Indica; 1965–66 D.C. Sircar publishes Indian Epigraphy and Indian Epigraphical Glossary.

ex.q: A coin shows a Greek legend 'BASILEOS APOLLODOTOU' on one side and Kharosthi letters on the other. How does this help decipherment?
st: Scholars could read the Greek name.
The same name was assumed to be written in Kharosthi on the other side.
Matching sounds to symbols revealed Kharosthi letters.
These letters could then be used to read other inscriptions.
ex.a: The bilingual coin acted as a key: the known Greek name revealed the values of Kharosthi signs.

topics.rl: The ASI's Epigraphy Branch in Mysuru still reads and publishes newly found inscriptions in Brahmi, Tamil-Brahmi and other scripts.

topics.ch: Part I: Kings, Farmers and Towns: Early States and Economies
topics.t: Limits of inscriptions and reconstructing ordinary lives
topics.h: Inscriptions shout about kings' victories but whisper almost nothing about a farmer's daily meal. How do historians fill the silence?
p: Technical limits: letters may be very faintly engraved, so reconstructions are uncertain; inscriptions may be damaged or have missing letters; and it is not always easy to be sure of the exact meaning of words, some of which were specific to a place or time.
Several thousand inscriptions have been discovered, but not all have been deciphered, published or translated. Many more must have existed but have not survived.

Not everything we consider politically or economically significant was recorded: routine agricultural practices and the joys and sorrows of daily life are rarely mentioned. Inscriptions project the perspective of those who commissioned them.
To reconstruct ordinary lives, historians combine inscriptions with texts (Jatakas, Panchatantra, Sangam poems), coins, and archaeology (houses, pottery, tools, crops).

Timeline: c. 600–500 BCE mahajanapadas, paddy transplantation, punch-marked coins; c. 327–325 BCE Alexander's invasion; c. 321 BCE accession of Chandragupta Maurya; c. 272/268–231 BCE Asoka's reign; c. 185 BCE end of the Mauryas; c. 200 BCE–200 CE Shakas, Satavahanas, Kushanas and Sangam literature; c. 320 CE beginning of Gupta rule; c. 606–647 CE Harshavardhana.

ex.q: A historian wants to know what peasants in the Ganga valley ate around 300 CE. Which sources should she use?
st: Inscriptions rarely mention food, so use them carefully.
Use texts like Jatakas or Sanskrit literature for references to food.
Use archaeology: charred grains, pottery, storage jars.
Combine all and note gaps.
ex.a: She should combine texts and archaeological evidence (grains, pottery) because inscriptions alone say little about daily life.

topics.rl: Many Indian village histories are now being recorded through oral history projects, because, like ancient inscriptions, official records leave out everyday experience.

topics.ch: Part I: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
topics.t: The Mahabharata as a source and its Critical Edition
topics.h: Imagine collecting handwritten copies of an epic from Kashmir to Kerala, in a dozen scripts, and comparing them verse by verse. Scholars did it for 47 years!
p: Historians use the Mahabharata, among other texts, to study social history c. 600 BCE–600 CE, especially families, marriage, varna and gender.
In 1919, under the leadership of the Sanskritist V.S. Sukthankar, a team of scholars began preparing a Critical Edition of the Mahabharata. It took 47 years to complete.

They collected Sanskrit manuscripts, written in a variety of scripts, from different parts of the country and selected verses that appeared common to most versions. The result was published in several volumes running into over 13,000 pages.

Two things emerged: there were common elements in the Sanskrit versions across the subcontinent, and there were also enormous regional variations, recorded in footnotes and appendices. These showed the complex processes of transmission of the text over centuries.

Many social history sources were Sanskrit texts written by and for Brahmanas, such as the Dharmasutras and Dharmashastras. They were normative: they laid down how society ought to be, which is not always how it actually was.

ex.q: Why did the Critical Edition project record regional variations in footnotes instead of deleting them?
st: The aim was to find verses common to most manuscripts.
But differences also tell us how the text changed in different regions.
Recording them preserves evidence of transmission and local traditions.
ex.a: Because the variations themselves are historical evidence of how the epic was transmitted and reshaped across regions.

topics.rl: The Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute in Pune, where the Critical Edition was prepared, is still a major centre for manuscript research in India.

topics.ch: Part I: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
topics.t: Families, lineages and the ideal of patriliny
topics.h: The world's longest epic is, at its heart, a family fight over property and power between cousins. Sound familiar?
p: Families were usually part of larger networks of people called relatives or kinfolk. Sanskrit texts use kula for family, jnati for the larger network of kinfolk, and vamsha for lineage.

The Mahabharata is a story of a feud over land and power between two groups of cousins, the Kauravas and the Pandavas, who belonged to the Kuru lineage that ruled the Kuru janapada. The Pandavas finally won.

After that, patrilineal succession was proclaimed. Patriliny means tracing descent from father to son, grandson and so on (matriliny traces descent through the mother). The epic reinforced the idea that patriliny was valuable.

Under patriliny, sons could claim the resources of their fathers (including the throne, in the case of kings) after their death. Most ruling dynasties from c. the sixth century BCE claimed to follow this system.
There were variations: sometimes there were no sons, and brothers or other kinsmen succeeded; in very exceptional cases, women such as Prabhavati Gupta exercised power.

ex.q: Why might patriliny have been especially important to elite families?
st: Elite families controlled land, wealth and sometimes the throne.
Patriliny ensured these passed from father to son within the lineage.
Keeping resources within the male line preserved the family's power over generations.
ex.a: Patriliny kept property and political power within the male line, preserving elite families' wealth and status.

topics.rl: Indian property law changed in 2005, when the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act gave daughters equal coparcenary rights in ancestral property, a big shift from strict patriliny.

topics.ch: Part I: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
topics.t: Rules of marriage and the eight forms
topics.h: Who could marry whom? Ancient lawgivers wrote long lists of rules, and listed eight ways of getting married, only some of which they approved.
p: Under patriliny, daughters had no claim to the household's resources; they were married into families outside the kin. This system of marrying outside a unit is called exogamy.
Endogamy means marriage within a unit: a kin group, caste or a group living in the same locality. Polygyny is the practice of a man having several wives; polyandry is a woman having several husbands.
Kanyadana, the gift of a daughter in marriage, was considered an important religious duty of the father.
The Manusmriti, compiled between c. 200 BCE and 200 CE, recognises eight forms of marriage. The first four were considered 'good', while the remaining were condemned.
Historians suggest the condemned forms may have been practised by those who did not accept Brahmanical norms, showing that texts' rules and actual practice differed.

ex.q: Classify: (a) a man marrying within his own caste; (b) a woman married into a family outside her kin group; (c) a man with three wives.
st: Marriage within a unit = endogamy.
Marriage outside the kin group = exogamy.
A man with several wives = polygyny.
ex.a: (a) endogamy, (b) exogamy, (c) polygyny.

topics.rl: Many Indian communities still follow gotra exogamy rules, avoiding marriage within the same gotra, which shows how old norms continue to shape practice.

topics.ch: Part I: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
topics.t: Gotras, mothers and Gandhari's advice
topics.h: A powerful king named himself 'son of Gotami' after his mother. Does that mean mothers were in charge? Not so fast!
p: From c. 1000 BCE onwards, Brahmanas classified people (especially Brahmanas) into gotras. Each gotra was named after a Vedic seer, and all its members were regarded as his descendants.
Two Brahmanical rules: women were expected to give up their father's gotra and adopt their husband's on marriage; and members of the same gotra could not marry.

Satavahana inscriptions show that some wives of rulers had names derived from their father's gotra (such as Gotami and Vasithi), so they retained their father's gotra instead of adopting the husband's. Some wives belonged to the same gotra as their husbands, suggesting endogamy, contrary to the Brahmanical ideal; this may reflect kinship practices in parts of the south.

Satavahana rulers were identified through metronymics (names derived from the mother), e.g. Gotami-puta Siri-Satakani, 'son of Gotami'. Though this suggests mothers were important, succession to the Satavahana throne was generally patrilineal.

In the Mahabharata, Gandhari urged her eldest son Duryodhana to make peace with the Pandavas, warning that greed and anger would ruin him. Duryodhana did not listen, fought and lost: the episode shows a mother's voice, and its limits.

ex.q: A Satavahana inscription names a king 'Gotami-puta' and his queen 'Vasithi'. What two conclusions can be drawn?
st: 'Gotami-puta' means son of Gotami: a metronymic.
So mothers were socially significant in naming.
'Vasithi' comes from her father's gotra: she kept it after marriage.
This differs from the Brahmanical rule of adopting the husband's gotra.
ex.a: Mothers mattered in identity, and queens retained their fathers' gotra, unlike the Brahmanical norm; yet succession stayed patrilineal.

topics.rl: Many Indian surnames and gotra names, such as Bharadwaj, Kashyap and Vashisht, are still traced to Vedic seers, keeping this old classification alive.

topics.ch: Part I: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
topics.t: The varna order and the 'right' occupation
topics.h: Ancient lawbooks tried to fix every person's job by birth. Did society actually follow? Historians check the rulebook against real life.
p: The Dharmasutras and Dharmashastras set out an ideal social order of four categories, or varnas: Brahmanas at the top, followed by Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras.

Prescribed occupations: Brahmanas were to study and teach the Vedas, perform sacrifices and get them performed, and give and receive gifts. Kshatriyas were to engage in warfare, protect people, administer justice, study the Vedas, get sacrifices performed and make gifts. Vaishyas were also to study the Vedas, get sacrifices performed and make gifts, and to engage in agriculture, pastoralism and trade. Shudras were assigned only one occupation: serving the three higher varnas.

Brahmanas used three strategies to enforce these norms. First, they asserted the varna order had a divine origin, citing the Purusha Sukta of the Rigveda, in which the four varnas emerge from the body of the primeval man, Purusha.

Second, they advised kings to ensure that these norms were followed within their kingdoms. Third, they tried to persuade people that their status was determined by birth, reinforced by stories in the Mahabharata and other texts.
These were norms. Historians compare them with other evidence to see how far they were followed in practice.

ex.q: How did the Purusha Sukta help support the varna order?
st: It describes the four varnas arising from Purusha's body.
This presents the order as divinely created.
Something divine appears natural and unchangeable.
So it gave religious authority to the hierarchy.
ex.a: By presenting varna as divinely ordained, it made the hierarchy seem natural and beyond question.

topics.rl: The Constitution of India, through Articles 15 and 17, prohibits discrimination based on caste and abolishes untouchability, rejecting birth-based hierarchy.

topics.ch: Part I: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
topics.t: Were kings always Kshatriyas?
topics.h: The rulebook said kings should be Kshatriyas. Yet Brahmanas, Shakas from Central Asia and families of uncertain origin all ruled. Rules and reality clashed!
p: According to the Shastras, only Kshatriyas could be kings. But many important ruling lineages had different origins.

The Mauryas: later Buddhist texts suggested they were Kshatriyas, but Brahmanical texts described them as being of 'low' origin. The Shungas and Kanvas, the immediate successors of the Mauryas, were Brahmanas.
In fact, political power was effectively open to anyone who could muster support and resources, and rarely depended on birth as a Kshatriya.

The Shakas came from Central Asia and were regarded as mlechchhas (barbarians, outsiders) by the Brahmanas. Yet one of the earliest inscriptions in Sanskrit describes how Rudradaman, the best-known Shaka ruler (c. second century CE), rebuilt the Sudarshana lake.

The Satavahana ruler Gotami-puta Siri-Satakani claimed to be a unique Brahmana (eka bamhana) and a destroyer of the pride of Kshatriyas. He also claimed to have prevented intermarriage among the four varnas, yet entered into a marriage alliance with the kin of Rudradaman, a Shaka.

ex.q: Use Gotami-puta Siri-Satakani to show the gap between norms and practice.
st: He claimed to uphold the varna order and prevent intermarriage.
He called himself a unique Brahmana.
Yet he made a marriage alliance with the Shakas, considered outsiders.
So political needs overrode the norms he claimed to defend.
ex.a: He claimed to protect the varna order, yet married into a Shaka family, showing practice often departed from norms.

topics.rl: The Junagadh rock in Gujarat carries inscriptions of Asoka, Rudradaman and Skandagupta on the same boulder, a single stone recording three very different rulers.

topics.ch: Part I: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
topics.t: Jatis, guilds and social mobility
topics.h: Silk weavers from Gujarat migrated to Madhya Pradesh, built a sun temple and some even changed jobs. A 1,500-year-old inscription tells their story!
p: In Brahmanical theory, jati, like varna, was based on birth. But while there were only four varnas, there was no fixed number of jatis.

Whenever Brahmanical authorities encountered new groups (for example, people living in forests such as the nishadas) or wanted to assign a social status to an occupation (such as the goldsmith, suvarnakara), they classified them as a jati. So the jati system was open to new groups.
Jatis that shared a common occupation or profession were sometimes organised into shrenis or guilds.

The Mandasor inscription (Madhya Pradesh, c. fifth century CE) records the history of a guild of silk weavers who originally lived in Lata (Gujarat) and migrated to Mandasor, then known as Dashapura, with their children and kinfolk, having heard of the greatness of the local king.

The inscription says they built a temple to the sun god. It also records that some members took up other occupations, which shows that guild members shared an identity beyond their craft and that occupations were not always fixed.

ex.q: What does the Mandasor inscription suggest about the rigidity of occupations?
st: The guild was defined by silk weaving.
After migrating, some members took up other occupations.
They still shared a common identity as a guild.
So occupation was not strictly fixed by birth for everyone.
ex.a: It suggests occupations could change and that guild identity went beyond a single craft, so the system was more flexible than the norms claim.

topics.rl: Mandsaur in Madhya Pradesh is today known for its Pashupatinath temple and opium-poppy farming, while Gujarat's silk weaving lives on in Patan's famous patola saris.

topics.ch: Part I: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
topics.t: Beyond the four varnas: integration, exclusion and Ekalavya
topics.h: A forest boy taught himself archery by practising before a clay image of his teacher, and was asked to cut off his thumb. Why does this story still trouble readers?
p: Integration: some communities, such as forest dwellers who hunted, gathered or practised shifting cultivation (like the nishadas, to whom Ekalavya belonged), and nomadic pastoralists, were not easily fitted into the varna order. People who spoke non-Sanskritic languages were labelled mlechchhas. Ideas and beliefs were exchanged between these groups and others.

Subordination: Brahmanas classified certain social categories as 'untouchable', declaring activities like handling corpses and dead animals 'polluting'. Those classified as chandalas were placed at the very bottom; the Manusmriti laid down that they live outside the village, use discarded utensils, wear clothes of the dead, dispose of bodies with no relatives, and serve as executioners.

The Chinese pilgrim Fa Xian (c. fifth century CE) wrote that 'untouchables' had to sound a clapper in the streets so that people could avoid seeing them. Xuan Zang (c. seventh century) observed that executioners and scavengers were forced to live outside the city.

In the Ekalavya story, Drona refused to teach Ekalavya, a forest-dwelling nishada. Ekalavya made a clay image of Drona, practised and became an expert archer. Drona then demanded his right thumb as his fee; Ekalavya cut it off and lost his speed. Drona thus kept his word to Arjuna that no one would be better than him.

Another episode: in the forest, Bhima married Hidimba, a rakshasa woman, and they had a son, Ghatotkacha. Stories like these show contact with communities outside the Brahmanical order, though described in Brahmanical terms.

ex.q: What message about social hierarchy might the Ekalavya story convey to readers in Brahmanical tradition, and how can a modern historian read it?
st: Drona refuses an outsider and demands his thumb.
Ekalavya obeys without protest.
The story seems to uphold the idea that skills belong to certain groups.
A historian reads it as evidence of exclusion, and also of how texts justified it.
ex.a: It reflects and reinforces the exclusion of forest groups from elite learning; historians read it critically as evidence of social exclusion.

topics.rl: Many schools and sports academies in tribal areas of India today, such as Eklavya Model Residential Schools, are named after Ekalavya, reclaiming him as a symbol of talent and determination.

topics.ch: Part I: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
topics.t: Gender and property: stridhana and the Manusmriti
topics.h: Draupadi was staked in a game of dice as if she were property. Could women in early India own property themselves?
p: In the Mahabharata's game of dice, Yudhishthira lost his wealth and then staked and lost Draupadi, which raises questions about whether women were treated as property. Gender was a key factor in access to property.

According to the Manusmriti, the paternal estate was to be divided equally among sons after the death of both parents, with a special share for the eldest. Women could not claim a share of these resources.

Women were allowed to keep the gifts they received at marriage as stridhana (literally, a woman's wealth). This could be inherited by their children, and the husband had no claim on it. However, the Manusmriti warned women against hoarding family property, or even their own valuables, without the husband's permission.

The Manusmriti lists seven means of acquiring wealth for men: inheritance, finding, purchase, conquest, investment, work, and acceptance of gifts from good people. For women it lists six: what was given before the nuptial fire, in the bridal procession, as a token of love, and by her brother, mother and father; plus subsequent gifts and what an 'affectionate' husband gave.
Elite women such as Prabhavati Gupta had access to land, but in general, land, cattle and money were controlled by men, so social differences between men and women were sharpened.

ex.q: Using the Manusmriti, compare how men and women could acquire wealth.
st: Men had seven means including inheritance, purchase, conquest, investment and work.
Women had six means, all essentially gifts from family or husband.
Women could not inherit the paternal estate.
So women's economic independence was limited.
ex.a: Men could inherit, earn and conquer; women mainly received gifts (stridhana), so women had far less control over resources.

topics.rl: Today, the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 gives daughters equal rights in ancestral property, a sharp contrast with the Manusmriti's rules.

topics.ch: Part I: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
topics.t: Varna, wealth, Buddhist critiques and the social contract
topics.h: What if kings were not chosen by gods, but by people tired of quarrelling over rice? A Buddhist story suggested exactly that!
p: According to Brahmanical texts, access to wealth was linked to varna: Shudras could only serve, while Brahmanas and Kshatriyas were, in theory, the wealthiest. Yet texts also mention poor Brahmanas and wealthy members of other groups.

Buddhists recognised social differences but did not regard them as natural or inflexible. They rejected the idea of claims to status on the basis of birth. In a story from the Majjhima Nikaya, a disciple of the Buddha, Kachchana, tells King Avantiputra that a rich Shudra could have Brahmanas, Kshatriyas and Vaishyas as his servants, and that wrongdoers of any varna would suffer the same fate, so birth does not decide worth.

In the Tamil Sangam anthologies, chiefs were patrons of bards and poets, and their generosity in distributing wealth was praised. This shows an alternative ideal where sharing wealth, not hoarding it, brought status.

The Sutta Pitaka has a myth explaining kingship: as greed, vindictiveness and deceit grew, people decided to select a being who would censure and punish wrongdoers, and to give him a share of rice in return. He was chosen by the whole people and called mahasammata, the great elect.
This suggests kingship was based on human choice, with taxes as payment for services: a 'social contract'. It contrasts with the Brahmanical idea that the social order was divinely ordained.

ex.q: How did the Buddhist explanation of kingship differ from the Brahmanical view?
st: Brahmanical view: social order, including kings and varnas, is divinely ordained.
Buddhist myth: people chose a ruler (mahasammata) to settle disputes.
The ruler was paid with a share of rice.
So authority rests on human choice and can be questioned.
ex.a: Buddhists saw kingship as a human institution based on choice and exchange (a social contract), not as a divine order.

topics.rl: In a democracy like India, rulers are chosen through elections and paid through taxes, an idea that echoes the Buddhist mahasammata story.

topics.ch: Part I: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
topics.t: Handling texts: language, content, authors and dates
topics.h: The Mahabharata grew from a war story of perhaps 10,000 verses to about 1,00,000 verses. How does a story grow ten times bigger?
p: Language: the Mahabharata's Sanskrit is far simpler than that of the Vedas or the prashastis, so it was probably widely understood.

Content: historians classify it into narrative sections containing stories and didactic sections containing prescriptions about social norms. The Mahabharata is often described as itihasa, meaning 'thus it was', a history.

Authors: it is traditionally attributed to the sage Vyasa. Historians think the original story was probably composed by charioteer-bards called sutas, who accompanied Kshatriya warriors to the battlefield and composed poems celebrating their victories. These circulated orally.

From the fifth century BCE, Brahmanas took over the story and began to write it down. Between c. 200 BCE and 200 CE, the worship of Vishnu grew and Krishna came to be identified with Vishnu. Between c. 200 and 400 CE, large didactic sections resembling the Manusmriti were added.

Composition spread over a long period (c. 500 BCE onwards, up to c. 400 CE). The text grew from perhaps less than 10,000 verses to about 1,00,000 verses. Textual timeline: Rigveda (c. 1500–1000 BCE) → later Vedic texts (c. 1000–500 BCE) → Dharmasutras and early Buddhist and Jaina texts (c. 500–200 BCE) → Manusmriti (c. 200 BCE–200 CE) → Puranas (compiled from c. 200 CE onwards).

ex.q: Why do historians call the Mahabharata a text 'composed over centuries'?
st: The story began as oral poems of sutas.
Brahmanas began writing it down from the fifth century BCE.
Krishna's identification with Vishnu was added c. 200 BCE–200 CE.
Didactic sections were added c. 200–400 CE.
So different layers come from different times.
ex.a: Because it has layers added by different composers at different times, growing from under 10,000 to about 1,00,000 verses.

topics.rl: Doordarshan's Mahabharat (1988–90) and many later TV and web adaptations show how the epic keeps growing and being retold for new audiences.

topics.ch: Part I: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
topics.t: Hastinapura and Draupadi's marriage: searching for convergence
topics.h: Was the Hastinapura of the epic a real city? An archaeologist dug in a village with that very name in the 1950s to find out.
p: Historians search for convergence between texts and archaeology. Between 1951 and 1952, the archaeologist B.B. Lal excavated at a village named Hastinapura in Meerut (Uttar Pradesh).

He found evidence of five occupational levels. The second phase (c. twelfth to seventh centuries BCE) had houses with mud walls and mud-brick; the third phase (c. sixth to third centuries BCE) had houses of mud-brick and burnt bricks, soakage jars and brick drains, and terracotta ring wells.
Whether this was the Hastinapura of the epic remains uncertain; the similarity of names may be a coincidence. The descriptions in the epic may have been added later when cities flourished.
Draupadi's marriage to the five Pandavas (polyandry) is a central episode. The epic itself offers explanations, but historians suggest others.

Some suggest polyandry may have been prevalent among ruling elites at some point, and fell out of favour among Brahmanas who reworked the text. Some note that polyandry existed in the Himalayan region. Others suggest that a shortage of women during times of warfare may have led to it.

ex.q: Why can't historians simply say B.B. Lal found the Hastinapura of the Mahabharata?
st: The village has the same name.
Its remains date to the right broad period.
But no inscription links it to the Kauravas.
Epic descriptions may come from a later time.
So the identification remains uncertain.
ex.a: Because a shared name and broad date are not proof; the match between text and site is uncertain.

topics.rl: Hastinapur in Meerut district is now home to Jain temples and a wildlife sanctuary; in 2020 it was announced as one of five iconic archaeological sites for development.

topics.ch: Part I: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
topics.t: A dynamic text: the Mahabharata through the ages
topics.h: A Bengali writer retold one episode from the point of view of a nishada woman who died in the fire meant for the Pandavas. The epic speaks back!
p: The Mahabharata did not stop growing after the Sanskrit versions. Over centuries, versions were written in a variety of languages through an ongoing dialogue between peoples, communities and those who wrote the texts.
Many local stories, which originated in specific regions or circulated among certain people, found their way into the epic. At the same time, the central story was often retold in different ways.
Episodes were depicted in sculpture and painting, and provided themes for a wide range of performing arts: plays, dance and other kinds of narration.

The Bengali writer Mahasweta Devi wrote 'Kunti O Nishadi', a short story in which a nishada woman questions Kunti about the burning of the lac house, in which a nishada woman and her five sons died so that the Pandavas could escape. Such retellings explore voices left out of the original.
This is why the Mahabharata is called a dynamic text: it kept changing in dialogue with changing social practices and new audiences.

ex.q: Give three reasons why the Mahabharata is called a dynamic text.
st: It was written in many regional languages.
Local stories were absorbed and the central story retold differently.
It was expressed in sculpture, painting, theatre and dance.
Modern authors retell it from new perspectives.
ex.a: Because it kept changing through regional versions, art and performance, and retellings that question the original.

topics.rl: From Kerala's Kathakali to Pandavani storytelling in Chhattisgarh by Teejan Bai, Mahabharata episodes are performed across India, each region adding its own flavour.
