In 1699, Guru Gobind Singh laid the foundation of the Khalsa Panth (army of the pure) and defined its five symbols: uncut hair, a dagger, a pair of shorts, a comb and a steel bangle. Under him the community became consolidated as a socio-religious and military force.

ex.q: How did Guru Nanak's message differ from ritual-based religion?
st: He rejected sacrifices, ritual baths, image worship and austerities.
He taught that the Divine has no form or gender.
He proposed remembering and repeating the Divine Name through shabad.
He organised congregational worship (sangat).
ex.a: He replaced rituals with remembrance of the formless Divine through hymns and collective worship.

topics.rl: Guru Nanak's birth anniversary, Gurpurab, is a national holiday in India; the Kartarpur Corridor opened in 2019 lets Indian pilgrims visit Gurdwara Darbar Sahib in Pakistan, where he spent his last years.

topics.ch: Part II: Bhakti-Sufi Traditions: Changes in Religious Beliefs and Devotional Texts
topics.t: Mirabai, the devotee princess
topics.h: A Rajput princess who left the palace to sing for Krishna, guided, some say, by a leather-worker saint: Mirabai broke more than one rule!
p: Mirabai (c. fifteenth–sixteenth centuries) is perhaps the best-known woman poet in the bhakti tradition. Her biography has been reconstructed mainly from bhajans attributed to her, transmitted orally for centuries.
According to these, she was a Rajput princess from Merta in Marwar, married against her wishes to a prince of the Sisodia clan of Mewar, Rajasthan.

She defied her husband and did not submit to the traditional role of wife and mother. Instead she recognised Krishna, the avatar of Vishnu, as her lover. Her in-laws tried to poison her, but she escaped from the palace to live as a wandering singer, composing songs of intense devotion.

According to some traditions, her preceptor was Raidas, a leather worker, which would indicate her defiance of the norms of caste society. After leaving the palace she is said to have worn the white robes of a widow or the saffron robe of a renouncer.

Mirabai did not attract a sect or group of followers, but she has been a source of inspiration for centuries. Her songs are still sung by women and men, especially by those considered 'low caste' in Gujarat and Rajasthan.

ex.q: Summarise the major teachings of Kabir, Guru Nanak and Mirabai.
st: Kabir: formless Ultimate Reality; rejected rituals of Hinduism and Islam.
Guru Nanak: nirguna bhakti; remembering the Divine Name; sangat.
Mirabai: saguna devotion to Krishna; defied family and caste norms.
All three emphasised personal devotion over ritual.
ex.a: Kabir and Nanak taught devotion to a formless God and rejected rituals; Mirabai expressed loving devotion to Krishna and defied social norms.

topics.rl: Mirabai's bhajans like 'Payoji maine Ram ratan dhan payo' are sung across India, and M.S. Subbulakshmi's 1945 film 'Meera' made her songs famous nationwide.

topics.ch: Part II: Bhakti-Sufi Traditions: Changes in Religious Beliefs and Devotional Texts
topics.t: Reconstructing histories of religious traditions
topics.h: A Persian poet sat with Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya and wrote down his conversations. That record, the Fawa'id-al-Fu'ad, is one of our best windows into Sufi life!
p: Historians use many sources to reconstruct religious traditions: sculpture and architecture, stories about religious preceptors, compositions attributed to women and men, and hagiographies written by followers.

Sufi traditions produced special kinds of texts. Malfuzat (literally 'uttered') are conversations of Sufi saints. An early example is the Fawa'id-al-Fu'ad, a collection of conversations of Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya, compiled by Amir Hasan Sijzi Dehlavi, a noted Persian poet.
Maktubat (literally 'writings') are letters written by Sufi masters to their disciples and associates, giving insight into their spiritual experiences and their lives.

Tazkiras (from Arabic, 'to mention, memorialise') are biographical accounts of saints. The first Sufi tazkira written in India was Mir Khwurd Kirmani's Siyar-ul-Auliya (fourteenth century), mainly about Chishti saints. A famous later one is Abdul Haqq Muhaddis Dehlavi's Akhbar-ul-Akhyar (1590).

Challenges: many traditions were transmitted orally and reworked over time, so there are many versions; compositions are in many regional languages; and hagiographies were written by followers who may not have been concerned with exact historical accuracy. Historians need to understand many languages and read sources critically.

ex.q: A historian wants to study Nizamuddin Auliya's ideas. Which sources would she use and what caution would she take?
st: Use the malfuzat, Fawa'id-al-Fu'ad, for his conversations.
Use tazkiras like Siyar-ul-Auliya for his life.
Use poems by disciples like Amir Khusrau.
Remember these were written by devotees, so read critically and compare.
ex.a: Malfuzat, tazkiras and disciples' poetry, read critically since they were written by admirers.

topics.rl: Today, oral history projects in India record the songs of Baul singers in Bengal and Kabirpanthi singers in Malwa before these living traditions change further.

topics.ch: Part II: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
topics.t: The discovery of Hampi
topics.h: A city so grand that a Persian ambassador counted seven lines of walls lay in ruins for over two centuries, until a Company engineer began mapping it in 1800.
p: Vijayanagara, or 'city of victory', was the name of both a city and an empire. The empire was founded in the fourteenth century and at its height stretched from the river Krishna in the north to the extreme south of the peninsula.

In 1565 the city was sacked and soon deserted. It lived on in the memories of people of the Krishna–Tungabhadra doab, who remembered it as Hampi, a name derived from the local mother goddess, Pampadevi.

In 1800 the ruins were brought to light by Colonel Colin Mackenzie, an engineer and antiquarian employed by the English East India Company, who prepared the first survey map of the site. He later became the first Surveyor General of India (1815). His early information came from the memories of priests of the Virupaksha temple and the shrine of Pampadevi.

From 1836 epigraphists began collecting dozens of inscriptions from Hampi and other temples. From 1856 photographers recorded the monuments; Alexander Greenlaw took the first detailed photographs. Historians combined these with travellers' accounts and literature in Telugu, Kannada, Tamil and Sanskrit.

Landmarks: 1800 Mackenzie visits; 1836 inscriptions collected; 1856 Greenlaw's photographs; 1876 J.F. Fleet begins documenting temple inscriptions; 1902 conservation begins under John Marshall; 1986 Hampi declared a World Heritage Site.

ex.q: Why were Greenlaw's photographs valuable to later researchers?
st: They recorded the monuments in 1856.
Many structures decayed or changed later.
So the photos show how buildings looked earlier.
Researchers could compare them with what survives.
ex.a: They preserved a visual record of the monuments as they stood in 1856, useful for study and conservation.

topics.rl: Hampi in Karnataka's Vijayanagara district is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of India's most visited heritage destinations; its stone chariot appears on the ₹50 note.

topics.ch: Part II: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
topics.t: Rayas, rivals and the travellers who saw them
topics.h: An Italian trader, a Persian ambassador, a Russian merchant and three Portuguese visitors all wrote about Vijayanagara. What a guestbook!
p: According to tradition and epigraphic evidence, two brothers, Harihara and Bukka, founded the Vijayanagara empire in 1336. The rulers called themselves rayas.
The empire included people of different languages and religious traditions.

On their northern frontier, the Vijayanagara kings competed with the Sultans of the Deccan and the Gajapati rulers of Orissa for control of fertile river valleys and the resources generated by lucrative overseas trade. These interactions also led to sharing of ideas, especially in architecture.

Foreign visitors left valuable accounts: Niccolo de Conti (an Italian trader), Abdur Razzaq (an ambassador sent by the ruler of Persia) and Afanasii Nikitin (a Russian merchant) in the fifteenth century; and Duarte Barbosa, Domingo Paes and Fernao Nuniz from Portugal in the sixteenth century.

Timeline: 1206 Delhi Sultanate established → 1336 Vijayanagara founded → 1347 Bahmani kingdom established → 1509–29 Krishnadeva Raya rules → 1526 Babur founds the Mughal empire → 1565 battle of Rakshasi-Tangadi.

ex.q: Why did Vijayanagara fight the Deccan Sultans and the Gajapatis?
st: All three wanted fertile river valleys.
They also wanted control of lucrative overseas trade.
So conflict arose on the northern frontier.
Yet contact also led to sharing of architectural ideas.
ex.a: To control fertile river valleys and trade wealth; the contact also led to exchange of ideas.

topics.rl: Karnataka's Hampi Utsav festival, held among the ruins, celebrates the empire's music, dance and history every year.

topics.ch: Part II: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
topics.t: Kings and traders: horses, spices and the Portuguese
topics.h: Warfare in the Deccan depended on cavalry, and the best horses came by sea from Arabia and Central Asia. Horse traders could make or break empires!
p: Warfare in this period depended on effective cavalry, so the import of horses from Arabia and Central Asia was very important for rival kingdoms.
This trade was initially controlled by Arab traders. Local communities of merchants known as kudirai chettis, or horse merchants, also took part.

From 1498 other actors appeared: the Portuguese arrived on the west coast of the subcontinent and tried to set up trading and military stations. Their superior military technology, especially the use of muskets, made them important players in the politics of the time.

Vijayanagara was also noted for its markets dealing in spices, textiles and precious stones. Trade was often a status symbol: the wealthy population demanded high-value exotic goods, especially precious stones and jewellery.
Revenue from trade contributed significantly to the prosperity of the state.

ex.q: Why were horse traders so important to Vijayanagara?
st: Cavalry decided battles.
Good war horses were not bred locally in enough numbers.
They had to be imported from Arabia and Central Asia.
So whoever controlled the horse trade gained military advantage.
ex.a: Because effective cavalry depended on imported horses, making horse traders vital to military power.

topics.rl: Kerala and Karnataka's spice trade continues today; India is the world's largest producer and exporter of spices, with the Spices Board headquartered in Kochi.

topics.ch: Part II: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
topics.t: The apogee: Krishnadeva Raya
topics.h: Krishnadeva Raya not only won wars; he wrote a Telugu book on statecraft advising kings to look after foreign sailors and encourage imports!
p: The first dynasty, the Sangama, ruled till 1485. It was supplanted by the Saluvas, military commanders, who ruled till 1503, and then by the Tuluvas. Krishnadeva Raya belonged to the Tuluva dynasty and ruled from 1509 to 1529.

His rule was marked by expansion and consolidation: he acquired the land between the Tungabhadra and Krishna rivers (the Raichur doab) in 1512, subdued the rulers of Orissa in 1514, and inflicted severe defeats on the Sultan of Bijapur in 1520.
Although the kingdom stayed in constant military preparedness, it flourished under conditions of unparalleled peace and prosperity.

He is credited with building some fine temples and adding impressive gopurams to many important south Indian temples. He also founded a suburban township near Vijayanagara called Nagalapuram, after his mother.

His Telugu work on statecraft, the Amuktamalyada, advised the king to improve harbours and encourage commerce so that horses, elephants, precious gems, sandalwood and pearls were freely imported, and to look after foreign sailors well.

ex.q: Arrange Krishnadeva Raya's military achievements in order.
st: 1512: acquires the Raichur doab.
1514: subdues the rulers of Orissa.
1520: severe defeats on the Sultan of Bijapur.
ex.a: Raichur doab (1512) → Orissa (1514) → Bijapur (1520).

topics.rl: Krishnadeva Raya's court poets, the Ashtadiggajas, including Tenali Rama, are celebrated in Telugu and Kannada folklore and in popular TV cartoons for children.

topics.ch: Part II: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
topics.t: Decline, and the rayas and nayakas
topics.h: In 1565, at Rakshasi-Tangadi, the combined armies of three Sultanates routed Vijayanagara's forces. Within a few years the great city was abandoned.
p: After Krishnadeva Raya's death in 1529, his successors were troubled by rebellious nayakas (military chiefs). By 1542 control shifted to the Aravidu lineage, which remained in power till the end of the seventeenth century.

In 1565, Rama Raya, the chief minister of Vijayanagara, led the army into battle at Rakshasi-Tangadi (also called Talikota), where it was routed by the combined armies of Bijapur, Ahmadnagar and Golconda. The victors sacked the city, which was abandoned within a few years. The focus of the empire shifted east, to Penukonda and later Chandragiri (near Tirupati). Relations between Sultans and rayas were not always hostile; many historians feel Rama Raya's policy of playing off one Sultan against another led them to combine.

Nayakas were military chiefs who usually controlled forts and had armed supporters. They often moved from one area to another, sometimes with peasants looking for fertile land, and usually spoke Telugu or Kannada. Many submitted to the kings but often rebelled and had to be subdued.

The amara-nayaka system was a major political innovation, with many features derived from the iqta system of the Delhi Sultanate. Amara-nayakas were military commanders given territories to govern by the raya. They collected taxes from peasants, craftspersons and traders, kept part of the revenue for personal use and to maintain a stipulated contingent of horses and elephants, and used some for temples and irrigation works.

They sent tribute to the king annually and appeared at court with gifts to show loyalty. Kings sometimes transferred them to assert control. But in the seventeenth century many nayakas set up independent kingdoms, hastening the collapse of the central imperial structure.

ex.q: Explain the relationship between the rayas and the nayakas.
st: Rayas gave amara-nayakas territories to govern.
Nayakas collected revenue and kept horses and elephants for the king.
They sent annual tribute and appeared at court to show loyalty.
But they often rebelled and later set up independent kingdoms.
ex.a: It was a relationship of dependence and tension: nayakas served and paid tribute to the raya but often rebelled and finally broke away.

topics.rl: The Nayaka kingdoms of Madurai, Thanjavur and Ikkeri, which grew out of this system, left monuments like the Meenakshi temple's great gopurams and Madurai's Thirumalai Nayak Palace.

topics.ch: Part II: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
topics.t: Water resources of the capital
topics.h: Vijayanagara stood in one of the driest zones of the peninsula. Yet its people built tanks and canals that still water fields today!
p: The most striking feature of the location is the natural basin formed by the river Tungabhadra, which flows in a north-easterly direction. The surrounding landscape has stunning granite hills that seem to form a girdle around the city.
A number of streams flow down from these rocks to the river. In almost all cases, embankments were built along these streams to create reservoirs of varying sizes.
Since this was one of the driest zones of the peninsula, elaborate arrangements had to be made to store rainwater and conduct it to the city.

The most important tank was built in the early years of the fifteenth century and is now called the Kamalapuram tank. Its water irrigated nearby fields and was also conducted through a channel to the 'royal centre'.

One of the most prominent waterworks is the Hiriya canal, which drew water from a dam across the Tungabhadra and irrigated the cultivated valley that separated the 'sacred centre' from the 'urban core'. It was apparently built by kings of the Sangama dynasty.

ex.q: How were the water requirements of Vijayanagara met?
st: Natural basin of the Tungabhadra provided the river.
Embankments on streams created reservoirs.
Kamalapuram tank stored water for fields and the royal centre.
Hiriya canal brought water from a dam on the Tungabhadra to the valley.
ex.a: Through the river basin, reservoirs created by embankments, the Kamalapuram tank and the Hiriya canal.

topics.rl: The modern Tungabhadra Dam near Hosapete, completed in the 1950s, still irrigates lakhs of acres in Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh, continuing the region's long water story.

topics.ch: Part II: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
topics.t: Fortifications, roads and gateways
topics.h: Abdur Razzaq counted seven lines of walls around Vijayanagara, with fields and gardens between them. Why would anyone build walls around farmland?
p: Abdur Razzaq, an ambassador sent by the ruler of Persia to Calicut (Kozhikode) in the fifteenth century, was greatly impressed by the fortifications and mentioned seven lines of forts. They encircled not only the city but also its agricultural hinterland and forests.

The outermost wall linked the hills around the city. The massive masonry walls were slightly tapered; no mortar was used, and wedge-shaped stone blocks held in place by interlocking. Bastions projected outwards. A second line went round the inner core of the urban complex, and a third surrounded the royal centre.

Agricultural tracts were enclosed within the walls. Abdur Razzaq noted that between the first, second and third walls there were cultivated fields, gardens and houses. Medieval sieges aimed to starve defenders into submission and could last months or years; most rulers built large granaries, but Vijayanagara's rulers adopted the more expensive strategy of protecting the agricultural belt itself.

The fort was entered through well-guarded gates linking the city to major roads. The arch over the gateway and the dome over the gate are typical features introduced by the Turkish Sultans; art historians call this style Indo-Islamic.
Roads generally wound through valleys, avoiding rocky terrain. Some of the most important roads extended from temple gateways and were lined by bazaars.

ex.q: What were the advantages and disadvantages of enclosing farmland within the fortifications?
st: Advantage: during a long siege, the city could still grow food.
Advantage: enemies could not starve the city into submission easily.
Disadvantage: building such vast walls was very expensive.
Disadvantage: long walls needed more soldiers to defend and were harder to maintain.
ex.a: It protected food supply during sieges but was costly to build, maintain and defend.

topics.rl: Tourists at Hampi today still walk through gateways like the Bhima's Gate, while modern cities in India rely on ring roads instead of walls.

topics.ch: Part II: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
topics.t: The urban core: houses, traders and shrines
topics.h: Fragments of fine Chinese porcelain found in one corner of Vijayanagara hint that rich traders once lived there!
p: Beyond the roads, there are few archaeological traces of the houses of ordinary people. Barbosa wrote that ordinary people's houses were thatched but well built and arranged according to occupation in long streets with many open places.
Archaeologists have found fine Chinese porcelain in some areas, including the north-eastern corner of the urban core, and suggest these areas may have been occupied by rich traders.
This area was also a Muslim residential quarter. The tombs and mosques there have distinctive functions, yet their architecture resembles the mandapas found in the temples of Hampi.
Field surveys show that the whole area was dotted with numerous shrines and small temples, pointing to a variety of cults, perhaps supported by different communities.
Wells, rainwater tanks and temple tanks probably served as sources of water for ordinary town dwellers.

ex.q: What can Chinese porcelain finds tell us about Vijayanagara's urban core?
st: Chinese porcelain was a costly import.
Finding it suggests wealthy owners.
So those areas were probably occupied by rich traders.
It also shows links with long-distance trade.
ex.a: That rich traders probably lived there, and that the city was linked to long-distance trade networks.

topics.rl: In many Indian cities today, neighbourhoods are still named after occupations, like Kumharwada (potters) or Sunar Gali (goldsmiths), echoing Barbosa's streets 'arranged according to occupations'.

topics.ch: Part II: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
topics.t: The royal centre and the mahanavami dibba
topics.h: Imagine a stone platform 40 feet high, its base covered in carvings, where the king watched nine nights of festivities. That is the mahanavami dibba!
p: The royal centre was located in the south-western part of the settlement. Although called a royal centre, it included over 60 temples, showing that patronage of temples was important for rulers seeking to legitimise their authority through association with the deities.

About thirty building complexes have been identified as palaces: large structures not associated with ritual functions. Temples were built entirely of masonry, whereas the superstructures of secular buildings were made of perishable materials.

The 'king's palace' is the largest enclosure, though it has not yielded definitive evidence of being a royal residence. It has two impressive platforms, the 'audience hall' and the 'mahanavami dibba'. The mahanavami dibba is a massive platform rising from a base of about 11,000 sq ft to a height of 40 ft, with evidence that it supported a wooden structure. Its base is covered with relief carvings.

Rituals there probably coincided with Mahanavami (literally 'the great ninth day') of the ten-day festival in September–October, known as Dussehra in north India, Durga Puja in Bengal and Navaratri or Mahanavami in peninsular India. Vijayanagara kings displayed their prestige, power and suzerainty on this occasion.

Ceremonies included worship of the image, worship of the state horse, and sacrifice of buffaloes and other animals; dances, wrestling matches, processions of horses, elephants, chariots and soldiers; and ritual presentations by nayakas and subordinate kings. On the last day the king inspected his army and the armies of the nayakas, who brought rich gifts and tribute.

ex.q: What was the significance of the mahanavami dibba?
st: It was a huge, high platform in the royal centre.
It was used for rituals during the Mahanavami festival.
The king displayed his power and received tribute from nayakas there.
So it was a stage for royal authority and loyalty.
ex.a: It was the stage where the king displayed power and received the loyalty and tribute of nayakas during Mahanavami.

topics.rl: Mysuru Dasara in Karnataka, with its grand procession of decorated elephants, continues traditions that go back to Vijayanagara's Mahanavami celebrations.

topics.ch: Part II: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
topics.t: Other buildings of the royal centre
topics.h: The 'Lotus Mahal' got its romantic name from British travellers. Nobody is quite sure what it was used for!
p: One of the most beautiful buildings in the royal centre is the Lotus Mahal, so named by British travellers in the nineteenth century. Historians are not sure what it was used for. One suggestion, found in a map drawn by Mackenzie, is that it may have been a council chamber where the king met his advisers.
Nearby are large structures identified as elephant stables, which shows the importance of elephants in the army and in royal display.

Most temples were located in the sacred centre, but some were in the royal centre. The Hazara Rama temple was probably meant to be used only by the king and his family. The images in its central shrine are missing, but sculpted panels on its walls survive, including scenes from the Ramayana on the inner walls of the shrine.
The royal centre also had palaces with high stone platforms, an 'audience hall' with rows of pillars, water tanks and a stepped tank, supplied with water from channels.
Many structures were destroyed when the city was sacked, but the tradition of building palaces continued under the nayakas, and many of their palaces survive.

ex.q: How do historians try to work out the use of a building like the Lotus Mahal?
st: Examine its design and location in the royal centre.
Check old maps and records, such as Mackenzie's map.
Compare with travellers' descriptions.
Then offer a suggestion, like a council chamber, while admitting uncertainty.
ex.a: By combining its architecture and location with maps and texts, and presenting conclusions as suggestions rather than certainties.

topics.rl: Hampi's elephant stables, with their alternating domed chambers, are a favourite spot for tourists and photographers today.

topics.ch: Part II: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
topics.t: The sacred centre: Virupaksha, Vitthala and gopurams
topics.h: Every royal order of Vijayanagara was signed 'Shri Virupaksha'. The kings claimed to rule on behalf of the god!
p: The 'sacred centre' lay at the rocky northern end of the city on the banks of the Tungabhadra. Local tradition says these hills sheltered the monkey kingdom of Vali and Sugriva in the Ramayana (Kishkindha). Another tradition says Pampadevi, the local mother goddess, did penance here to marry Virupaksha, the guardian deity of the kingdom, recognised as a form of Shiva; their marriage is still celebrated annually in the Virupaksha temple.

The choice of the capital may have been inspired by these shrines. Kings claimed to rule on behalf of Virupaksha, and royal orders were signed 'Shri Virupaksha', usually in Kannada script. Rulers also used the title 'Hindu Suratrana', a Sanskritisation of the Arabic 'Sultan', meaning Hindu Sultan. Temples served as centres of learning and as religious, social, cultural and economic centres.

Vijayanagara architecture introduced structures of immense scale bearing the imprint of imperial authority, best seen in the raya gopuras, royal gateways that often dwarfed the towers of the central shrines and signalled the temple from far away. They reminded people of the king's power to command resources, techniques and skills.

Other features include mandapas (pavilions) and long pillared corridors around shrines. Halls were used for music, dance and drama, for swinging the deities and for celebrating the marriages of deities (sometimes called kalyana mandapas).

The Virupaksha temple was built over centuries; its earliest shrine dates to the ninth–tenth centuries. Krishnadeva Raya built the hall in front of the main shrine to mark his accession and is credited with the eastern gopuram. The Vitthala temple's deity, a form of Vishnu worshipped in Maharashtra, shows how rulers drew on different traditions; it has a shrine designed as a chariot, and chariot streets extended from its gopuram, paved with stone slabs and lined with pillared pavilions where merchants set up shops.

ex.q: What do the gopurams of Vijayanagara temples tell us about royal power?
st: They were enormous and visible from far away.
They often dwarfed the towers of the central shrine.
Building them required huge resources, techniques and skills.
So they reminded people of the king's power and his link with the divine.
ex.a: They symbolised the king's power to command resources and his close association with the gods.

topics.rl: The annual chariot festival (rathotsava) of the Virupaksha temple at Hampi still draws thousands, and the temple remains in active worship.

topics.ch: Part II: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
topics.t: Plotting the city and questions in search of answers
topics.h: Archaeologists divided Hampi into squares, then smaller squares, and recorded thousands of structures, even the bases of long-lost pillars.
p: From the 1980s, a major project documented Vijayanagara's material remains through extensive and intensive surveys over nearly twenty years. Scholars like John M. Fritz, George Michell and M.S. Nagaraja Rao worked at the site for years.

The whole area was divided into squares, each given a letter, and each square was subdivided into smaller squares again and again. This painstaking method recorded thousands of structures, from small shrines and houses to elaborate temples, and traces of roads, paths and bazaars located through pillar bases and platforms.
These field surveys were combined with travellers' accounts, inscriptions and literature to understand buildings, the uses of spaces and the people who built and used them.

Yet buildings cannot tell us everything. They show how space was organised and what functions it served, but not what ordinary men, women and children thought or felt. Many sources record elite perspectives: kings, nobles and travellers who met them.

Activities include reading plans and photographs of buildings, and map work: locating Vijayanagara on the Tungabhadra, and its neighbours such as the Deccan Sultanates (Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda) to the north and the Gajapati kingdom of Orissa to the north-east.

ex.q: Why did researchers divide Hampi into squares and smaller squares?
st: The site is huge, with thousands of structures.
Squares allow systematic recording, so nothing is missed.
Each structure can be located precisely on a grid.
This builds a detailed map of the whole city.
ex.a: To record every structure systematically and precisely across a very large site.

topics.rl: Today, archaeologists in India use GPS, drones and GIS mapping, a digital version of the grid method, at sites like Keeladi in Tamil Nadu and Vadnagar in Gujarat.

topics.ch: Part II: Peasants, Zamindars and the State: Agrarian Society and the Mughal Empire
topics.t: Sources and terms for peasants
topics.h: Peasants left almost no writings of their own. So how do we know what they grew, paid and argued about in Akbar's time?
p: About 85 per cent of the people of India lived in villages in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries; both peasants and landed elites took part in agricultural production.

The main source for the agrarian history of the sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries is the Ain-i Akbari (Ain), written by Akbar's court historian Abu'l Fazl. Other sources include seventeenth- and eighteenth-century revenue records from Gujarat, Maharashtra and Rajasthan, and the extensive records of the East India Company.
Indo-Persian sources of the Mughal period used terms like raiyat (plural riaya) and muzarian for a peasant. Terms like kisan and asami were also used.

Seventeenth-century sources refer to two kinds of peasants. Khud-kashta were residents of the village in which they held their lands. Pahi-kashta were non-resident cultivators who belonged to another village but cultivated lands elsewhere on a contractual basis.
People became pahi-kashta by choice, for example when better revenue terms were offered in a distant village, or by compulsion, for example when forced by economic distress after a famine.

ex.q: A peasant of village A cultivates land in village B on a contract after a famine. What type of peasant is he, and why did he move?
st: He lives in A but cultivates in B.
So he is a non-resident, pahi-kashta cultivator.
He moved because of distress after a famine.
So it was by compulsion, not choice.
ex.a: He is a pahi-kashta peasant who moved out of compulsion.

topics.rl: India's PM-KISAN scheme pays income support to farmers; the word 'kisan' was already used for peasants in Mughal-era sources.

topics.ch: Part II: Peasants, Zamindars and the State: Agrarian Society and the Mughal Empire
topics.t: Peasants, land, irrigation and technology
topics.h: Babur noticed that in Lahore and Sirhind, farmers watered fields with a wheel, while around Agra they used buckets. Irrigation varied from place to place!
p: The average peasant of north India seldom owned more than a pair of bullocks and two ploughs; most had even less. In Gujarat, peasants with about six acres were considered affluent; in Bengal, five acres was the upper limit of an average peasant farm, and ten acres made one rich.
Cultivation was based on individual ownership. Peasant lands were bought and sold in the same way as the lands of other property owners.

The abundance of land, available labour and the mobility of peasants helped agriculture expand. The monsoon remained the backbone of Indian agriculture, but some crops needed extra water, so artificial irrigation was developed. Babur described a wheel (the Persian wheel) used in Lahore, Dipalpur and Sirhind, and buckets used around Agra. The state supported irrigation: new canals were dug and old ones repaired, like the Shah Nahr in Punjab during Shah Jahan's reign.

Peasants used technologies that harnessed cattle energy. The wooden plough was light, easily assembled and had an iron tip or coulter; it did not make deep furrows, which helped preserve moisture during intense heat.
A drill pulled by a pair of giant oxen was used to plant seeds, though broadcasting seed was most common. Hoeing and weeding were done with a narrow iron blade with a small wooden handle.

ex.q: Why was the shallow-furrowing wooden plough well suited to Indian conditions?
st: It was light and easy to assemble.
Its iron tip broke the soil without digging too deep.
Shallow furrows preserved soil moisture in intense heat.
So it suited hot, often dry conditions.
ex.a: Because shallow furrows kept moisture in the soil during intense heat, and the plough was light and easy to use.

topics.rl: Over half of India's farmland still depends on the monsoon; schemes like 'Har Khet Ko Pani' under PMKSY aim to expand irrigation.

topics.ch: Part II: Peasants, Zamindars and the State: Agrarian Society and the Mughal Empire
topics.t: An abundance of crops: from staples to New World arrivals
topics.h: Indian food without chillies, tomatoes or potatoes? Before the sixteenth century, that was reality! These crops came from the Americas.
p: Agriculture was organised around two major seasonal cycles, the kharif (autumn) and the rabi (spring). Most regions, except the driest, produced at least two crops a year; where rainfall or irrigation was assured, even three.
The Ain says the Mughal provinces of Agra produced 39 varieties of crops and Delhi 43 over the two seasons. Bengal produced 50 varieties of rice alone.

Although staple crops for subsistence were the main focus, cultivation was not only for subsistence. Cash crops were called jins-i kamil (literally 'perfect crops'), such as cotton and sugarcane, the jins-i kamil par excellence; oilseeds (like mustard), lentils and indigo were also grown for the market. Cotton grew over central India and the Deccan; Bengal was famed for its sugar.

New crops from the New World arrived: maize (makka) came into India via Africa and Spain and by the seventeenth century was listed as a major crop of western India. Vegetables like tomatoes, potatoes and chillies, and fruits like pineapple and papaya, were also introduced.
Agricultural prosperity supported population growth: India's population is estimated to have increased by about 50 million people over the two hundred years from 1600 to 1800.

ex.q: To what extent was agricultural production in Mughal India only for subsistence?
st: Staple crops like rice, wheat and millets fed families.
But peasants also grew cash crops (jins-i kamil) like cotton and sugarcane for the market.
Revenue was increasingly demanded in cash, encouraging market crops.
So production combined subsistence with commercial farming.
ex.a: It was not purely subsistence: peasants grew staples for themselves and cash crops for the market.

topics.rl: India today is the world's largest producer of chillies and the second-largest of potatoes, crops that arrived from the Americas only about 400–500 years ago.

topics.ch: Part II: Peasants, Zamindars and the State: Agrarian Society and the Mughal Empire
topics.t: The village community and caste
topics.h: A Mughal village had cultivators, a panchayat and a headman. But who stood at the bottom, and could anyone climb up?
p: Peasants held their land in individual ownership but belonged to a collective village community. The community had three constituents: the cultivators, the panchayat, and the village headman (muqaddam or mandal).

Deep inequities based on caste existed. Cultivators were a heterogeneous group, and a large number of landless labourers (mazdur) stood at the bottom. Caste distinctions kept some groups in menial tasks and poverty.
Among Muslim communities too, menials like the halalkhoran (scavengers) were housed outside village boundaries; in Bihar, the mallahzadas (literally 'sons of boatmen') were comparable to slaves.
There was a direct correlation between caste, poverty and social status at the lower strata of society, but not so marked in the middle.

Some castes rose in status: the Ahirs, Gujars and Malis, because cattle rearing and horticulture were profitable. In eastern regions, intermediate pastoral and fishing castes like the Sadgops and Kaivartas acquired the status of peasants.

ex.q: How could a caste like the Ahirs rise in social status?
st: Cattle rearing became profitable.
Profit brought wealth and land.
Wealth helped them gain higher social standing.
So economic change could alter caste status.
ex.a: Because cattle rearing became profitable, their economic gains raised their social status.

topics.rl: Social mobility through economic change continues: dairy cooperatives like Amul in Gujarat helped many pastoral families prosper.

topics.ch: Part II: Peasants, Zamindars and the State: Agrarian Society and the Mughal Empire
topics.t: Panchayats and headmen
topics.h: Low-caste villagers in Rajasthan petitioned their panchayats against unfair taxes and forced labour. Rural people knew how to complain!
p: The village panchayat was an assembly of elders, usually important people of the village with hereditary rights over property. In mixed-caste villages it was usually a heterogeneous body: an oligarchy representing various castes and communities, though village menial-cum-agricultural workers were unlikely to be represented. Its decisions were binding.

The headman, the muqaddam or mandal, was chosen through the consensus of village elders and ratified by the zamindar. He held office as long as he had the elders' confidence. His chief function was supervising the village accounts, assisted by the accountant or patwari.
The panchayat drew funds from contributions to a common pool, used for entertaining revenue officials and for community welfare like tiding over floods, building bunds or digging canals.

A key function was to ensure caste boundaries were maintained; in eastern India marriages were held in the mandal's presence. It could levy fines and inflict punishments like expulsion from the community, a drastic step usually for a limited period.

Each jati also had its own panchayat. In Rajasthan, jati panchayats arbitrated civil disputes, mediated land claims, decided whether marriages followed norms and settled ritual precedence. Archival records from western India contain petitions to panchayats complaining of extortionate taxation or demands for unpaid labour (begar) by 'superior' castes or officials, usually from groups protesting morally illegitimate demands.

ex.q: What were the main functions of a village panchayat?
st: Maintain caste boundaries and supervise conduct.
Levy fines and punish, including expulsion.
Manage common funds for officials and welfare such as bunds and canals.
Settle disputes and hear petitions.
ex.a: It enforced caste norms, punished offenders, managed common funds for welfare, and settled disputes.

topics.rl: Today's gram panchayats are elected under the 73rd Constitutional Amendment (1992), with reserved seats for women, SCs and STs, very different from the elders' oligarchy of Mughal times.

topics.ch: Part II: Peasants, Zamindars and the State: Agrarian Society and the Mughal Empire
topics.t: Village artisans, 'little republics' and the cash nexus
topics.h: British officials called the Indian village a 'little republic'. Historians say: look closer, and you will find inequality, caste and plenty of cash!
p: Villages had many artisans: potters, blacksmiths, carpenters, barbers and even goldsmiths. Villagers paid them for their services in various ways: a share of the harvest, or an allotment of land, perhaps land that was cultivable but lying unused.

In Maharashtra such lands became the artisans' miras or watan, their hereditary holding. In Bengal, zamindars paid blacksmiths, carpenters and goldsmiths a small daily allowance and diet money. This later came to be described as the jajmani system, though the term was not in use in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.
Some nineteenth-century British officials saw the village as a 'little republic', made up of fraternal partners sharing resources and labour collectively.

But this was not a sign of rural egalitarianism. There was individual ownership of assets and deep inequality based on caste and gender. Powerful individuals decided the affairs of the village and exploited weaker sections.
Villages were also connected to wider markets through a cash nexus: cash transactions were already extensive, and in Mughal India even the wages of artisans were often paid in cash.

ex.q: Was the Mughal village a 'little republic'?
st: British officials saw it as self-sufficient and egalitarian.
But land and assets were individually owned.
There were deep inequalities of caste and gender.
Villages were linked to markets through cash.
So it was neither equal nor isolated.
ex.a: No: villages had individual property, caste and gender inequality, and cash links with wider markets.

topics.rl: Many Indian villages still have hereditary artisan families; the PM Vishwakarma scheme (2023) supports traditional artisans like carpenters, blacksmiths and potters.

topics.ch: Part II: Peasants, Zamindars and the State: Agrarian Society and the Mughal Empire
topics.t: Women in agrarian society
topics.h: In eighteenth-century Bengal, one of the biggest zamindaris, Rajshahi, was run by a woman. Rural women did far more than history books often admit!
p: Women and men worked shoulder to shoulder in the fields. Men tilled and ploughed, while women sowed, weeded, threshed and winnowed the harvest.

Biases linked to women's biological functions persisted: in western India, menstruating women were not allowed to touch the plough or the potter's wheel; in Bengal, they could not enter groves where betel leaves (paan) were grown.
Artisanal tasks like spinning yarn, sifting and kneading clay for pottery, and embroidery depended on female labour. The more commercialised a product, the greater the demand on women's labour.

Women were valued as labour and for their reproductive role in a society with high mortality. In many rural communities marriage required payment of bride-price rather than dowry to the bride's family. Remarriage was considered legitimate for both divorced and widowed women. Women petitioned panchayats for justice: wives protested against their husbands' infidelity or neglect of wife and children by the male head of the household.

Among the landed gentry, women had the right to inherit property. In Punjab, women, including widows, actively sold inherited land. Hindu and Muslim women inherited zamindaris, which they could sell or mortgage. Women zamindars were known in eighteenth-century Bengal; Rajshahi had a woman at its helm.

ex.q: Describe the role of women in agricultural production.
st: Women sowed, weeded, threshed and winnowed.
They did spinning, kneading clay and embroidery.
Commercialisation increased demands on their labour.
Yet biases restricted them from touching the plough in some regions.
ex.a: Women were essential workers in farming and crafts, though they faced restrictions and biases.

topics.rl: Women make up a large share of India's agricultural workforce today; schemes like the Mahila Kisan Sashaktikaran Pariyojana aim to recognise and support women farmers.

topics.ch: Part II: Peasants, Zamindars and the State: Agrarian Society and the Mughal Empire
topics.t: Forests and tribes
topics.h: Gum lac from Indian forests was a major export in the seventeenth century. Forests were never 'empty': people, elephants and trade filled them!
p: Beyond settled villages were huge areas of forest or scrubland in eastern India, central India, northern India (including the India–Nepal border), Jharkhand, and the Western Ghats and Deccan plateau. Contemporary sources called forest dwellers jangli.

Being jangli did not mean lacking 'civilisation'; it described people whose livelihood came from gathering forest produce, hunting and shifting agriculture. These activities were seasonal: the Bhils, for example, collected forest produce in spring, fished in summer, cultivated in the monsoon and hunted in autumn and winter.

Outsiders entered forests for many reasons. The state needed elephants for the army, so the peshkash (tribute) from forest people often included elephants. In Mughal ideology, the hunt (shikar) symbolised the state's concern for justice; hunting expeditions let the emperor travel across the empire and personally hear grievances.

Commercial agriculture and trade also reached forests. Honey, beeswax and gum lac were in great demand; gum lac was a major export in the seventeenth century. Elephants were captured and sold. Some tribes, like the Lohanis in Punjab, traded overland between India and Afghanistan.

Tribal chiefs became zamindars, and some even kings, building armies from their lineages. In Assam, the Ahom kings had paiks, people obliged to give military service in exchange for land, and declared the capture of wild elephants a royal monopoly. The Koch kings also emerged from such chiefdoms.

ex.q: Why did the Mughal state take an interest in forests?
st: It needed elephants for its army.
Forest people paid tribute (peshkash), often in elephants.
Hunting expeditions let the emperor tour and hear grievances.
Forest products like gum lac were valuable for trade.
ex.a: For elephants, tribute, trade in forest products and the political symbolism of the royal hunt.

topics.rl: Forest communities today have rights under the Forest Rights Act, 2006, and minor forest produce like honey and lac is bought under schemes like Van Dhan.

topics.ch: Part II: Peasants, Zamindars and the State: Agrarian Society and the Mughal Empire
topics.t: The zamindars
topics.h: Zamindars sat at the narrow top of the rural pyramid. They had forts, troops and land, yet peasants sometimes joined them against the state!
p: Zamindars earned their living from agriculture but did not take part directly in production. They were landed proprietors who enjoyed social and economic privileges due to their superior status in rural society; caste was one factor, and they also performed services (khidmat) for the state.
They held extensive personal lands called milkiyat (property), cultivated for their private use, often with hired or servile labour. They could sell, bequeath or mortgage these lands.

Their power also came from collecting revenue on behalf of the state, for which they were compensated, and from military resources: most had fortresses (qilachas) and armed contingents of cavalry, artillery and infantry. In the rural social pyramid, zamindars formed the very narrow apex.

Zamindari rights originated in conquest (dispossession of weaker people by powerful military chiefs), colonisation of new lands, transfer of rights, orders of the state, or purchase. Zamindars spearheaded the colonisation of agricultural land and helped settle cultivators by providing means of cultivation, including cash loans. Buying and selling of zamindaris increased monetisation of the countryside.

Zamindars could be exploitative, yet their relationship with peasants had an element of reciprocity, paternalism and patronage. Bhakti saints who condemned oppression usually portrayed the revenue official, not the zamindar, as the oppressor. In many seventeenth-century agrarian uprisings, zamindars often received peasant support against the state.

ex.q: What role did zamindars play in Mughal India?
st: Held milkiyat lands and enjoyed privileges.
Collected revenue for the state and were compensated.
Had forts and armed contingents.
Helped expand cultivation and gave loans to peasants.
Could be exploitative but also patrons.
ex.a: They were powerful rural elites who collected revenue, held military power, expanded agriculture and had a mixed relationship with peasants.

topics.rl: The zamindari system was abolished after independence through state laws like the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950.

topics.ch: Part II: Peasants, Zamindars and the State: Agrarian Society and the Mughal Empire
topics.t: The land revenue system
topics.h: Mughal officials sorted land into four classes, from land cultivated every season to land left fallow for five years or more, and taxed each differently.
p: Revenue from land was the economic mainstay of the Mughal empire, so the state created an administrative apparatus to control agricultural production and fix and collect revenue.

The office (daftar) of the diwan was responsible for supervising the fiscal system of the empire. Below him was a hierarchy of revenue officials and record-keepers, including the amil-guzar, the revenue collector.
Revenue collection had two stages: first, assessment (jama), the amount fixed; second, actual collection (hasil), the amount collected.
Akbar decreed that the amil-guzar should fix the revenue and encourage cultivators to pay in cash, while retaining the option of payment in kind.

Under Akbar, land was classified into four types: polaj, land annually cultivated for each crop in succession and never left fallow; parauti, land left out of cultivation for a time to recover its strength; chachar, land lying fallow for three or four years; and banjar, land uncultivated for five years and more. Polaj and parauti were further divided into good, middling and bad; the average produce was calculated, and one-third of it was taken as the royal dues.

ex.q: A polaj field yields 30, 24 and 18 maunds per bigha for good, middling and bad land. What is the royal due per bigha?
st: Add the three: 30 + 24 + 18 = 72.
Average produce = 72 ÷ 3 = 24 maunds.
Royal due = one-third of 24 = 8 maunds.
ex.a: 8 maunds per bigha.

topics.rl: Land records and revenue are still state subjects in India; land is still classified and recorded by patwaris and tehsildars, terms that go back to Mughal times.

topics.ch: Part II: Peasants, Zamindars and the State: Agrarian Society and the Mughal Empire
topics.t: The flow of silver
topics.h: Silver mined in the Americas crossed oceans to pay for Indian cloth and pepper, and ended up as Mughal rupees in a peasant's hand!
p: The Mughal empire was one of the large territorially centralised empires of Asia, along with the Ming (China), Safavid (Iran) and Ottoman (Turkey) empires, which consolidated power and resources in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Their political stability helped create vibrant overland trade networks from China to the Mediterranean.
Voyages of discovery and the opening up of the New World led to a massive expansion of Asia's, and particularly India's, trade with Europe.

This expanding trade brought huge amounts of silver bullion into Asia to pay for goods bought from India. A large part of it gravitated towards India, which was good because India did not have natural resources of silver.

As a result, the period from the sixteenth to the eighteenth centuries saw remarkable stability in the availability of metal currency, particularly the silver rupya, an unprecedented expansion of minting and circulation of money, and the ability of the Mughal state to collect taxes and revenue in cash.
The Italian traveller Giovanni Careri, who passed through India around 1690, gave a vivid account of how silver travelled across the globe to reach India.

ex.q: Why was monetary trade important in the Mughal period?
st: Indian goods were in demand worldwide.
Silver flowed into India to pay for them.
This made a stable silver rupee widely available.
The state could collect revenue in cash, and villages were drawn into markets.
ex.a: It brought silver into India, stabilised the currency, expanded minting and allowed cash revenue and wider market links.

topics.rl: The word 'rupee' comes from the silver rupya; today the RBI issues the Indian rupee, though coins are no longer made of silver.

topics.ch: Part II: Peasants, Zamindars and the State: Agrarian Society and the Mughal Empire
topics.t: The Ain-i Akbari of Abu'l Fazl
topics.h: Abu'l Fazl revised the Ain five times before finishing it in 1598. It counted everything: crops, revenue, castes, even the emperor's household!
p: The Ain-i Akbari was the culmination of a large historical and administrative project of classification undertaken by Abu'l Fazl on Akbar's orders. It was completed in 1598, the forty-second regnal year of the emperor, after five revisions.

The Ain is part of a larger history-writing project commissioned by Akbar, the Akbar Nama, in three books. The first two give a historical narrative; the Ain-i Akbari, the third book, is a compendium of imperial regulations and a gazetteer of the empire.

The Ain itself has five books (daftars). The first, manzil-abadi, concerns the imperial household. The second, sipah-abadi, covers military and civil administration, with notices on mansabdars, learned men, poets and artists. The third, mulk-abadi, deals with the fiscal side of the empire, with rich quantitative information on revenue rates and an 'Account of the Twelve Provinces'.
The fourth and fifth books deal with the religious, literary and cultural traditions of the people of India and include a collection of Akbar's 'auspicious sayings'.

For Abu'l Fazl, gathering detailed information about the empire was part of good, just governance. The Ain provides rich quantitative data on administration, revenue and population, and remains an extraordinary source for the agrarian history of Mughal India.

ex.q: Which book of the Ain-i Akbari would you consult for revenue rates, and why?
st: The Ain has five books.
The third, mulk-abadi, deals with the fiscal side of the empire.
It gives revenue rates and the Account of the Twelve Provinces.
So it is the right book for revenue data.
ex.a: The third book, mulk-abadi, because it deals with fiscal matters and revenue rates.

topics.rl: Modern India's Census and the National Sample Survey collect statistics for governance, an idea Abu'l Fazl would have appreciated.

topics.ch: Part II: Peasants, Zamindars and the State: Agrarian Society and the Mughal Empire
topics.t: Limits of the Ain and the Mughal timeline
topics.h: The Ain has small arithmetic errors, gaps for Bengal and Orissa, and price lists mostly from around Agra. Great source, but handle with care!
p: Historians who have studied the Ain closely note several limitations. Numerous errors in totalling have been detected, but these are minor arithmetic errors that do not seriously affect its overall reliability.

A bigger limitation is the skewed nature of the quantitative data. Data were not collected uniformly from all provinces; for example, detailed information on the caste composition of zamindars was compiled for many subas but not for Bengal and Orissa.

While the fiscal data from the subas are remarkably rich, vital parameters such as prices and wages are not as well documented. The detailed list of prices and wages comes mainly from areas in or around the imperial capital of Agra and is therefore of limited relevance for the rest of the country.
So historians supplement the Ain with other sources, such as revenue records from Gujarat, Maharashtra and Rajasthan, and East India Company records.

Mughal timeline: 1526 Babur defeats Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat; 1530–40 first phase of Humayun's reign; 1540–55 Humayun defeated by Sher Shah and in exile at the Safavid court; 1555–56 Humayun regains lost territories; 1556–1605 Akbar; 1605–27 Jahangir; 1628–58 Shah Jahan; 1658–1707 Aurangzeb.

ex.q: What problems do historians face in using the Ain as a source for agrarian history?
st: Minor errors in totalling.
Data not collected uniformly from all provinces (e.g., no caste data on zamindars for Bengal and Orissa).
Prices and wages mainly from around Agra.
So it must be used with other sources.
ex.a: Its arithmetic errors, uneven provincial coverage and Agra-centred prices and wages limit its use, so historians supplement it.

topics.rl: Indian statisticians today adjust national data for regional differences; a price list from one city alone, like Agra's in the Ain, cannot represent the whole country.

topics.ch: Part III: Colonialism and the Countryside: Exploring Official Archives
topics.t: Colonialism in the countryside and official archives
topics.h: Revenue records, surveys and commission reports were written to serve the Company. Today historians read them to recover the stories of zamindars, tribal peoples and peasants.
p: Colonial rule affected rural society deeply, mainly through new land revenue policies, changes in property rights and the expansion of markets.

This chapter looks at three regions: Bengal and its zamindars under the Permanent Settlement; the Rajmahal hills (in present-day Jharkhand), home of the Paharias and Santhals; and the Bombay Deccan (western Maharashtra), where ryots revolted against moneylenders.

Historians use official sources: revenue records, survey reports, reports of commissions and committees, and travelogues by officials. These were produced by the colonial state for its own purposes: to collect revenue, control territory and justify policy.
Because they reflect official concerns, historians read them critically, asking who wrote them, why, and what they left out, and comparing them with other evidence.
Map work: Bengal (Burdwan), the Rajmahal hills and the Santhal Pargana (Jharkhand), and the Bombay Deccan (Poona and Ahmednagar).

ex.q: Why must historians read colonial revenue reports critically?
st: They were written by colonial officials.
Their purpose was to collect revenue and justify policy.
They may hide the state's own role in problems.
So they must be compared with other sources.
ex.a: Because they reflect the interests and viewpoint of the colonial state and may be biased or incomplete.

topics.rl: The National Archives of India in New Delhi and state archives hold many such colonial records, which researchers still use today.

topics.ch: Part III: Colonialism and the Countryside: Exploring Official Archives
topics.t: An auction in Burdwan and the Permanent Settlement
topics.h: In 1797, estates of the Raja of Burdwan were auctioned for unpaid revenue. Many 'buyers' turned out to be the Raja's own agents!
p: In 1797 an auction was held in Burdwan (present-day Bardhaman). Several mahals (estates) held by the Raja of Burdwan were sold because he had accumulated huge arrears of revenue.

Many of the purchasers were the Raja's own servants and agents who bought the lands on his behalf. These were benami purchases (literally 'anonymous'), made in the name of an insignificant person while the real beneficiary stayed hidden. In this way the Raja kept control of his estates.

The auctions were a result of the Permanent Settlement introduced in Bengal in 1793 by the East India Company under Governor-General Lord Cornwallis. The revenue each zamindar had to pay was fixed permanently, and estates of those who failed to pay were auctioned.

The Company saw rajas and taluqdars as zamindars. A zamindar was not a landowner in the village but a revenue collector of the state; a zamindari could include as many as 400 villages. Zamindars collected rent from ryots and paid fixed revenue to the Company.

Aims: Bengal's economy was in crisis, with recurrent famines and falling output. Officials hoped that fixing revenue permanently would ensure a regular flow of revenue to the Company, encourage investment in land (since landholders would keep any increased profits), and create a class of loyal landholders and 'improving' farmers with capital and enterprise.

ex.q: How did the Raja of Burdwan keep control of his estates despite the auction?
st: His estates were auctioned for arrears.
His own agents bought many of them.
These were benami purchases in other people's names.
So the Raja remained the real controller.
ex.a: Through benami purchases by his agents, so the estates stayed under his control.

topics.rl: The Permanent Settlement was finally ended after independence when West Bengal passed the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, abolishing zamindari.

topics.ch: Part III: Colonialism and the Countryside: Exploring Official Archives
topics.t: Why zamindars defaulted
topics.h: If the revenue did not reach the treasury by sunset on the due date, the zamindari could be auctioned. That was the 'Sunset Law'!
p: Revenue arrears were common, and many zamindaris were auctioned in the decades after the Permanent Settlement. Several reasons explain this.

First, the initial demand was very high. Since the demand was fixed for all time, the Company feared it could never claim a share of increased income later, so it pegged the demand high, arguing the burden would fall as production expanded and prices rose.

Second, this high demand was imposed in the 1790s, when prices of agricultural produce were depressed, making it hard for ryots to pay their dues to the zamindar. Third, the revenue was invariable, regardless of the harvest, and had to be paid punctually; under the Sunset Law, if payment did not come in by sunset of the specified date, the zamindari could be auctioned.

Fourth, the Settlement initially limited the zamindar's power to collect rent and manage the zamindari. Zamindars' troops were disbanded, customs duties abolished, and their cutcheries (courts) brought under the supervision of a Collector appointed by the Company. They lost the power to organise local justice and police; the collectorate became an alternative centre of authority.
Fifth, ryots sometimes delayed payment deliberately, encouraged by rich peasants, and harvests were uneven. Zamindars could take defaulting ryots to court, but justice was slow.

ex.q: Why were so many zamindaris auctioned after the Permanent Settlement?
st: Revenue demand was set very high.
Agricultural prices were low in the 1790s.
The Sunset Law required punctual payment regardless of harvest.
Zamindars' powers over troops and courts were curtailed.
Ryots delayed payment, and courts were slow.
ex.a: Because of high fixed demand, low prices, the rigid Sunset Law, reduced zamindari powers and ryots' resistance.

topics.rl: Modern loans also have strict due dates and penalties; the Sunset Law was an extreme version where one missed sunset could cost an entire estate.

topics.ch: Part III: Colonialism and the Countryside: Exploring Official Archives
topics.t: The rise of the jotedars
topics.h: While zamindars struggled, a group of rich peasants in the villages of north Bengal grew so powerful that they could defy zamindars and even buy their estates!
p: By the end of the eighteenth century, rich peasants were consolidating their position in villages. In parts of Bengal they were called jotedars; elsewhere haoladars, gantidars or mandals. Francis Buchanan's survey of Dinajpur district vividly describes the jotedars.

By the early nineteenth century, jotedars had acquired vast areas of land, sometimes several thousand acres. They controlled local trade and moneylending, exercising immense power over poorer cultivators.
Much of their land was cultivated by sharecroppers (adhiyars or bargadars), who brought their own ploughs, worked the fields and handed over half the produce to the jotedar after the harvest.

Unlike zamindars, who often lived in towns, jotedars lived in the villages, so their power within villages was more effective. They fiercely resisted zamindars' efforts to increase the jama (revenue) of the village, prevented zamindari officials from doing their work, mobilised dependent ryots and deliberately delayed revenue payments.
When zamindars' estates were auctioned for arrears, jotedars were often among the purchasers. They were most powerful in north Bengal.

ex.q: Why were jotedars powerful in rural Bengal?
st: They held vast lands, sometimes thousands of acres.
They controlled local trade and moneylending.
They lived in villages, unlike many zamindars.
Sharecroppers and poor ryots depended on them.
ex.a: Because of their land, control of trade and credit, residence in villages, and the dependence of poorer cultivators.

topics.rl: Operation Barga (1978) in West Bengal registered bargadars (sharecroppers) to protect their rights, a reform rooted in this long history of sharecropping.

topics.ch: Part III: Colonialism and the Countryside: Exploring Official Archives
topics.t: Zamindars resist, and the Fifth Report
topics.h: Over 800 of the Fifth Report's 1,002 pages were appendices: petitions, collectors' reports and tables. It was a monster of a document, and it had an agenda!
p: Zamindars found ways to survive. The Raja of Burdwan first transferred part of his zamindari to his mother, since the Company had decreed that the property of women would not be taken over.

At auctions, zamindars' agents manipulated the proceedings: they outbid genuine buyers and then refused to pay, so the estate had to be resold; this was repeated until the price fell and the zamindar's agent bought it cheaply. Through such fictitious sales and benami purchases, zamindars kept control. Lathyals (lathi-wielding strongmen) sometimes drove off outside buyers, and ryots also resisted outsiders.
By the early nineteenth century the depression in prices ended. Zamindars who had survived the 1790s consolidated their power, and the Company relaxed its rules of revenue payment.

The Fifth Report, submitted to the British Parliament in 1813, was the fifth of a series of reports on the administration and activities of the East India Company in India. It ran to 1,002 pages, of which over 800 were appendices reproducing petitions of zamindars and ryots, reports of collectors, statistical tables and notes on revenue and judicial administration of Bengal and Madras.

In Britain, many groups attacked the Company's monopoly and its officials' corruption, and Parliament passed Acts to regulate Company rule and demanded regular reports. The Fifth Report became the basis of intense debates. Historians note it exaggerated the collapse of traditional zamindari power and the scale on which zamindars were losing land.

ex.q: How did zamindars manage to retain control over their zamindaris?
st: Transferred estates to women, whose property the Company would not take.
Manipulated auctions through agents who outbid and refused to pay.
Made benami purchases.
Used lathyals to keep out outside buyers.
ex.a: Through transfers to women, fictitious sales, benami purchases and force against outsiders.

topics.rl: Parliamentary committees in India today, like the Public Accounts Committee, also scrutinise government spending and administration through detailed reports.

topics.ch: Part III: Colonialism and the Countryside: Exploring Official Archives
topics.t: The hoe: Buchanan and the Paharias
topics.h: Plains zamindars paid tribute to hill chiefs to stop raids, and traders paid tolls to use mountain passes. The Paharias were masters of their hills!
p: Francis Buchanan was a physician in the Bengal Medical Service who undertook detailed surveys for the East India Company. In 1810–11 he travelled through the Rajmahal hills. He looked at the landscape as a Company employee, judging its potential for 'improvement' and commercial value.

The Paharias lived around the Rajmahal hills. They subsisted on forest produce and practised shifting cultivation: they cleared patches by cutting bushes and burning undergrowth, which enriched the soil with potash, and grew pulses and millets, scratching the ground lightly with hoes. After a few years they left the land fallow.

They collected mahua flowers for food, silk cocoons and resin for sale, and wood for charcoal. Their identity was intimately linked with the forest. Their chiefs maintained unity, settled disputes and led the tribe in battles.

The Paharias regularly raided the plains where settled farmers lived. Raids helped them survive in years of scarcity, asserted their power over settled communities, and were a way of negotiating political relations with outsiders.

Plains zamindars purchased peace by paying regular tribute to hill chiefs. Traders paid a small amount for permission to use passes controlled by them; once paid, Paharia chiefs protected the traders' goods.

ex.q: How did the Paharias respond to outsiders before the late eighteenth century?
st: They raided the plains, especially in years of scarcity.
Zamindars paid them tribute for peace.
Traders paid them to use hill passes, and were protected in return.
So they negotiated power with outsiders on their own terms.
ex.a: Through raids and negotiated arrangements: tribute from zamindars and payments from traders in return for peace and protection.

topics.rl: Mahua flowers are still collected by tribal communities in Jharkhand, Odisha and Chhattisgarh, and are an important minor forest produce today.

topics.ch: Part III: Colonialism and the Countryside: Exploring Official Archives
topics.t: The plough: pacification, Santhals and Damin-i-Koh
topics.h: From 40 Santhal villages in 1838 to 1,473 by 1851: the Damin-i-Koh filled with plough farmers, and the Paharias were pushed deeper into the hills.
p: In the last decades of the eighteenth century, settled agriculture expanded aggressively in eastern India. To the British, extending settled agriculture would enlarge land revenue, produce crops for export and create a settled, ordered society. They saw forest people as savage, unruly and difficult to govern.

In the 1770s the British followed a brutal policy of extermination, hunting down and killing Paharias. By the 1780s, Augustus Cleveland, the Collector of Bhagalpur, proposed pacification: Paharia chiefs were given an annual allowance and made responsible for their men's conduct. Many refused; those who accepted lost authority in their community as stipendaries of the government. Many Paharias withdrew deep into the mountains.

Around 1800 the Santhals began coming into the area. They cleared forests, cut timber, ploughed the land and grew rice and cotton. The British saw them as ideal settlers: hardworking and good at reclaiming land. Zamindars also hired them to expand cultivation.

In 1832 a large area was demarcated as the Damin-i-Koh, declared the land of the Santhals. They were to live within it and practise plough agriculture. The land grant required that at least one-tenth of the area be cleared and cultivated within the first ten years. The area was surveyed, mapped and enclosed by boundary pillars.

Santhal settlements grew rapidly: from 40 villages in 1838 to 1,473 villages by 1851, and the population rose from about 3,000 to over 82,000. As Santhals occupied the lower hills, the Paharias had to recede further. This was a conflict between the hoe, symbol of shifting cultivation, and the plough, symbol of settled agriculture.

ex.q: Why is the story of the Rajmahal hills called a conflict between the hoe and the plough?
st: Paharias used the hoe for shifting cultivation.
Santhals used the plough for settled farming.
The British favoured the plough and gave land to Santhals.
As Santhals expanded, Paharias lost land and moved deeper into the hills.
ex.a: Because the plough-using Santhals, backed by the British, expanded at the expense of the hoe-using Paharias.

topics.rl: The Santhal Pargana division of Jharkhand, with towns like Dumka and Sahibganj, grew out of the Damin-i-Koh area.

topics.ch: Part III: Colonialism and the Countryside: Exploring Official Archives
topics.t: The Santhal rebellion and Buchanan's account as a source
topics.h: The Santhals cleared forests to farm, but soon found their land slipping away to taxes, moneylenders and zamindars. In 1855 they rose in revolt, the hul!
p: The Santhals soon found that the land they had brought under cultivation was slipping away. The state levied heavy taxes; moneylenders (dikus) charged high rates of interest and took over land when debts were unpaid; and zamindars asserted control over the Damin area.

By the 1850s the Santhals felt the time had come to rebel against zamindars, moneylenders and the colonial state, to create an ideal world where they would rule themselves. The Santhal rebellion (hul) of 1855–56 was led by figures such as Sidhu and Kanhu.

After the revolt, the Santhal Pargana was created, carved out of the districts of Bhagalpur and Birbhum (about 5,500 square miles). The colonial state hoped that a new territory with some special laws would conciliate the Santhals.
Buchanan's account is a valuable source: it describes landscapes, crops, settlements, forest products and peoples in rich detail.

But it also has limits. Buchanan wrote as a Company employee, interested in resources and 'improvement'; he was critical of forest dwellers' ways of life and saw forests as land to be turned into fields. His account reveals what the Company valued, and conceals how local people themselves saw their world.

ex.q: Why did the Santhals rebel against British rule?
st: Heavy taxes were imposed on their land.
Moneylenders charged high interest and took over land.
Zamindars asserted control over the Damin area.
The colonial state backed this system, so they rose against all three.
ex.a: Because taxes, moneylenders and zamindars, backed by the colonial state, were taking away their land and freedom.

topics.rl: Hul Diwas is observed every year on 30 June in Jharkhand to remember the Santhal rebellion and its leaders.

topics.ch: Part III: Colonialism and the Countryside: Exploring Official Archives
topics.t: Account books come to be burnt: Supa, 1875
topics.h: On 12 May 1875, ryots in Supa village near Poona demanded the moneylenders' account books and set them on fire. Paper had become a symbol of oppression!
p: On 12 May 1875, ryots from surrounding rural areas gathered at Supa, a large village in Poona district (present-day Maharashtra), where many shopkeepers and moneylenders lived.

They attacked the shopkeepers and moneylenders (sahukars), demanding their bahi khatas (account books) and debt bonds. They burnt the khatas, looted grain shops and in some cases set fire to sahukars' houses.

From Poona the revolt spread to Ahmednagar, and over the next two months to many more villages. Everywhere the pattern was similar: sahukars were attacked, account books burnt and debt bonds destroyed.
Terrified sahukars fled their villages, often leaving their property behind. British police posts were set up in villages, and many people were arrested and convicted.
The ryots' anger focused on the account books and bonds because these records were the instruments through which they believed they had been cheated and trapped in debt.

ex.q: Why did the ryots target account books and debt bonds rather than just the moneylenders?
st: The books and bonds recorded their debts.
They believed the entries were manipulated.
Destroying them wiped out the proof of debt.
So the documents themselves were seen as instruments of oppression.
ex.a: Because the books and bonds were the legal proof of debts they felt were unjust, so burning them was an attack on the system of exploitation.

topics.rl: Farm loan waivers announced by many Indian states show that agrarian debt remains a major political issue even today.

topics.ch: Part III: Colonialism and the Countryside: Exploring Official Archives
topics.t: Ryotwari, Ricardo and the debt trap
topics.h: In the Bombay Deccan, the Company dealt directly with each ryot and resurveyed lands every 30 years. Sounds fair? Not when the demand was too high!
p: After the Bengal experience, a different system was introduced in the Bombay Deccan in the 1820s: the ryotwari settlement, made directly with the ryot. The average income from different types of soil was estimated, the ryot's revenue-paying capacity assessed and a proportion fixed as the state's share. Lands were resurveyed every 30 years and revenue rates increased. The demand was not permanent.

Officials were influenced by the economist David Ricardo, who argued that a landowner should have a claim only to the 'average rent' prevailing at a given time. When land yielded more than this, the surplus should be taxed by the state; otherwise cultivators would become rentiers and not invest productively. Many officials thought Bengal's ryots had turned into rentiers, confirming Ricardo's theory.

The first revenue settlement in the Bombay Deccan was so high that in many places peasants deserted their villages and migrated to new regions, especially in areas of poor soil and fluctuating rainfall. When rains failed and harvests were poor, peasants could not pay; collectors, keen to show efficiency, seized property and imposed fines.
In the 1830s, agricultural prices fell sharply and did not recover for about fifteen years, cutting peasants' incomes further. Famine also struck the countryside.

To pay revenue and meet everyday and production needs, ryots borrowed from moneylenders. Once taken, loans were hard to repay; as debts mounted, ryots became dependent on moneylenders. By the 1840s officials found alarming levels of peasant indebtedness everywhere.

ex.q: How did a Deccan ryot fall into a debt trap?
st: Revenue demand was high and had to be paid even in bad years.
Prices fell in the 1830s, reducing income.
The ryot borrowed from the moneylender to pay revenue and buy necessities.
Interest piled up and the loan could not be repaid.
So he became dependent on the moneylender.
ex.a: High revenue and falling prices forced borrowing; mounting interest made repayment impossible, trapping him in debt.

topics.rl: Microfinance and Kisan Credit Cards aim to give Indian farmers cheaper formal credit so they do not fall into the hands of high-interest moneylenders.

topics.ch: Part III: Colonialism and the Countryside: Exploring Official Archives
topics.t: The cotton boom and bust
topics.h: When the American Civil War broke out in 1861, cotton from India suddenly became gold. Then the war ended, and the boom collapsed!
p: Before the 1860s, three-fourths of the raw cotton imports into Britain came from America. British cotton manufacturers, worried about this dependence, formed bodies like the Cotton Supply Association (1857) and the Manchester Cotton Company (1859) to encourage cotton cultivation elsewhere, including India.
When the American Civil War broke out in 1861, raw cotton imports from America fell to less than three per cent of the normal. By 1862 over 90 per cent of cotton imports into Britain came from India.
