In the Bombay Deccan, credit flowed freely: export merchants in Bombay advanced money to urban sahukars, who extended credit to rural moneylenders, who lent to ryots. Ryots expanded cotton cultivation. Rich peasants gained, but most cotton ryots got deeper into debt.

When the Civil War ended in 1865, cotton production in America revived and Indian cotton exports to Britain declined steadily. Export merchants and sahukars were no longer keen to give long-term credit; moneylenders refused loans to ryots.
At the same time, the next revenue settlement increased the demand dramatically, by 50 to 100 per cent. Ryots were squeezed from both sides: no credit and higher revenue.

ex.q: Trace the chain of credit during the cotton boom.
st: Bombay export merchants advanced money to urban sahukars.
Urban sahukars extended credit to rural moneylenders.
Rural moneylenders lent to ryots.
Ryots expanded cotton cultivation.
ex.a: Export merchants → urban sahukars → rural moneylenders → ryots.

topics.rl: Global events still affect Indian farmers: the 2022 war in Ukraine raised world wheat and fertiliser prices, showing how far-off conflicts reach Indian fields.

topics.ch: Part III: Colonialism and the Countryside: Exploring Official Archives
topics.t: The experience of injustice: Limitation Law and petitions
topics.h: A law meant to protect ryots from endless interest ended up trapping them further, because moneylenders made them sign a fresh bond every three years!
p: Ryots were angry when moneylenders refused loans after the cotton boom. They were also angry that moneylenders violated customary norms. One norm was that the interest charged could not be more than the principal; under colonial rule this broke down, and in one case a moneylender charged over ₹2,000 as interest on a loan of ₹100.

In 1859 the British passed a Limitation Law stating that loan bonds signed between moneylenders and ryots would be valid for only three years. The law was meant to check the accumulation of interest over time.

Moneylenders manipulated the law by forcing the ryot to sign a new bond every three years. The unpaid balance, the original loan plus accumulated interest, was entered as the principal of the new bond, and new interest was charged on it.

Ryots' petitions complained that moneylenders refused to give receipts for repayments, entered fictitious figures in bonds, acquired the peasants' harvest at low prices and finally took over their property.
Most ryots were illiterate and did not know what they were signing. Deeds and bonds thus became symbols of a new oppressive system, which explains why, in 1875, ryots burnt them.

ex.q: Explain how moneylenders manipulated the Limitation Law.
st: The law made bonds valid for only three years.
Moneylenders made ryots sign a new bond every three years.
Unpaid loan plus interest became the new principal.
New interest was charged on this bigger sum, so debts grew.
ex.a: By renewing bonds every three years with interest added to the principal, so the law that was meant to limit interest actually increased debts.

topics.rl: Today, laws against usury and state Money-Lenders Acts in Maharashtra and other states cap interest rates and require licences for moneylenders.

topics.ch: Part III: Colonialism and the Countryside: Exploring Official Archives
topics.t: The Deccan Riots Commission and reading official records
topics.h: An official commission studied the riots and concluded: 'Government revenue is not to blame; the moneylenders are.' Would a government ever blame itself?
p: When the revolt spread in the Deccan, the Bombay government was initially unconcerned. But the Government of India, worried by the memory of 1857, pressured it to set up a commission of enquiry. The commission's report, the Deccan Riots Report, was presented to the British Parliament in 1878.

The commission held enquiries in the districts where the riots had spread, recorded statements of ryots, sahukars and eyewitnesses, compiled statistics on revenue rates, prices and interest rates in different regions, and collated reports from district collectors.

The commission was mainly interested in whether the level of government revenue demand caused the revolt. After examining the evidence, it reported that the government demand was not the cause of peasant anger; it blamed the moneylenders.

This shows the colonial government's reluctance to admit that popular discontent was ever caused by its own actions. Official reports are invaluable sources, but they must be read carefully and juxtaposed with evidence from newspapers, unofficial accounts, legal records and, where possible, oral sources.

Timeline: 1765 Company acquires Diwani of Bengal; 1773 Regulating Act; 1793 Permanent Settlement; around 1800 Santhals come to the Rajmahal hills; 1820s ryotwari in the Bombay Deccan; 1855–56 Santhal hul; 1861 cotton boom begins; 1875 Deccan riots; 1878 Deccan Riots Report.

ex.q: Why did the Deccan Riots Commission blame moneylenders rather than revenue demand?
st: The commission was set up by the colonial government.
Admitting that revenue caused the revolt would blame the government itself.
So it concluded that moneylenders were responsible.
Historians therefore read such reports critically alongside other evidence.
ex.a: Because the colonial government was reluctant to admit its own policies caused discontent; this is why such reports must be read critically.

topics.rl: Commissions of inquiry are still set up in India after major events; journalists and researchers routinely compare their findings with other evidence.

topics.ch: Part III: Rebels and the Raj: The 1857 Revolt and its Representations
topics.t: Meerut to Delhi: the revolt begins
topics.h: On the afternoon of 10 May 1857, sepoys at Meerut rose in mutiny. By the next morning they were at the gates of the Red Fort, asking the old Mughal emperor to lead them!
p: On the afternoon of 10 May 1857, a mutiny broke out in the cantonment of Meerut. It started with the sepoys of the native infantry, spread to the cavalry and then to the city. Ordinary people of the town and nearby villages joined the sepoys.
The sepoys captured the bell of arms (the arsenal), attacked white people, and plundered and set fire to their bungalows and records.
Late at night a group of sepoys rode to Delhi, arriving at the gates of the Red Fort early on 11 May. They demanded that the Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah, give them his blessings.
The emperor, old and with only a nominal court, was not happy at first, but eventually agreed to become the nominal leader of the rebellion.

This gave the revolt legitimacy: it could now be carried out in the name of the Mughal emperor, whose name still carried great prestige across north India. When the news spread that Delhi had fallen, mutinies broke out in cantonments across the Ganga valley and to the west of Delhi.

ex.q: Why was the Mughal emperor important to the rebels?
st: The Mughal name carried centuries of prestige.
The emperor's blessing gave the revolt legitimacy.
Rebels could claim to fight for a recognised sovereign, not just as mutineers.
This helped bring together different groups under one symbol.
ex.a: Because the emperor's name gave the revolt legitimacy and a unifying symbol across north India.

topics.rl: Meerut has a Shaheed Smarak (martyrs' memorial) and a freedom struggle museum that recall the events of 10 May 1857.

topics.ch: Part III: Rebels and the Raj: The 1857 Revolt and its Representations
topics.t: How the mutinies began: signals and targets
topics.h: In cantonment after cantonment, the revolt started with a signal: the evening gun or a bugle call. Then the targets were always the same.
p: In every cantonment, sepoys began their action with a signal: the firing of the evening gun or the sounding of the bugle.
They first seized the bell of arms and plundered the treasury.
They then attacked government buildings: the jail, treasury, telegraph office, record room and bungalows, burning all records.

Everything and everybody connected with the white man became a target. Proclamations in Hindi, Urdu and Persian appealed to the population, both Hindus and Muslims, to unite and eliminate the firangis (foreigners).
Ordinary people joined the revolt and attacks spread to others seen as allies of the British, such as moneylenders and the rich in some places.

ex.q: Why did rebels target treasuries, jails, telegraph offices and record rooms?
st: Treasuries and arsenals gave money and weapons.
Jails and courts were symbols of British power.
Telegraph offices were key to British communication.
Records held revenue and debt details used to control people.
ex.a: Because these were the sources of British money, weapons, control and communication, and symbols of their rule.

topics.rl: The British built the Mutiny Memorial on Delhi's Ridge in 1863; in 1972 India renamed it Ajitgarh and added a plaque honouring the Indian fighters of 1857.

topics.ch: Part III: Rebels and the Raj: The 1857 Revolt and its Representations
topics.t: Lines of communication and sepoy panchayats
topics.h: Sepoy panchayats met at night in the Kanpur lines. Far from being random, the revolt showed planning and collective decisions!
p: The sequence of events in different cantonments was similar, suggesting planning and coordination. Sepoys or their emissaries carried messages from one station to another.

A story from Awadh shows this: Captain Hearsey of the Awadh Military Police was protected by his Indian subordinates during the mutiny. The 41st Native Infantry, stationed nearby, insisted that since they had killed all their white officers, the Military Police should also kill Hearsey or hand him over. The Military Police refused.
It was decided that the matter would be resolved by a panchayat composed of native officers drawn from each regiment.
Charles Ball, who wrote one of the earliest histories of the revolt, noted that panchayats were convened nightly in the Kanpur sepoy lines. Decisions were taken collectively.
Sepoys lived together in the lines and shared a lifestyle; many came from the same caste and region. This made it natural for them to come together and decide their own future.

ex.q: How did the rebels communicate and organise?
st: Emissaries carried messages between stations.
Similar patterns in different places suggest coordination.
Sepoy panchayats of native officers took collective decisions.
Shared life in the lines and common backgrounds helped them organise.
ex.a: Through messengers between cantonments and through sepoy panchayats that took collective decisions.

topics.rl: The word 'panchayat' is familiar to every Indian; in 1857 even soldiers used this village institution to make collective decisions.

topics.ch: Part III: Rebels and the Raj: The 1857 Revolt and its Representations
topics.t: Leaders and followers
topics.h: A Peshwa's adopted son, a queen, an elderly zamindar, a begum, a village leader, a wandering maulvi with a drum and a tribal cultivator: 1857 had leaders of every kind!
p: At Kanpur, Nana Sahib, the adopted son of the late Peshwa Baji Rao II, gathered armed forces, expelled the British garrison, proclaimed himself Peshwa and declared that he was a governor under Emperor Bahadur Shah.

At Lucknow, Birjis Qadr, the young son of the deposed Nawab Wajid Ali Shah, was declared the new Nawab; his mother, Begum Hazrat Mahal, took an active part in organising the uprising. At Jhansi, Rani Lakshmibai assumed leadership. In Bihar, Kunwar Singh, a local zamindar of Arrah, led the revolt.

Local leaders emerged too. Shah Mal of Baraut pargana (western Uttar Pradesh) mobilised the headmen and cultivators of 84 villages, moving from village to village at night. His men attacked government buildings, destroyed a bridge and dug up metalled roads; he turned an English officer's bungalow into a 'hall of justice'. He was killed in battle in July 1857.

Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah of Faizabad prophesied the end of British rule and fought the British in Lucknow and Awadh. He came to be known as Danka Shah, the maulvi with the drum. Gonoo, a tribal cultivator of Singhbhum in Chotanagpur, became a rebel leader of the Kol tribals.
Map work: centres of the revolt include Meerut, Delhi, Lucknow, Kanpur, Jhansi, Arrah and Bareilly. From Bareilly, the soldier Bakht Khan led a large force to Delhi.

ex.q: Why did the revolt need both big leaders and local leaders?
st: Big leaders (Nana Sahib, Rani Lakshmibai, Begum Hazrat Mahal) gave legitimacy and command in major centres.
Local leaders (Shah Mal, Gonoo) mobilised villagers and tribals.
Local leaders understood local grievances and terrain.
Together they spread the revolt widely.
ex.a: Big leaders provided legitimacy and command; local leaders mobilised ordinary people, so the revolt spread widely.

topics.rl: Rani Lakshmibai's statue stands in Jhansi, and Begum Hazrat Mahal Park in Lucknow honours her role; Kunwar Singh is remembered across Bihar as 'Veer Kunwar Singh'.

topics.ch: Part III: Rebels and the Raj: The 1857 Revolt and its Representations
topics.t: Rumours and prophecies
topics.h: A low-caste worker at Dum Dum taunted a Brahmin sepoy who refused him water: 'You will soon lose your caste, for you will have to bite cartridges covered with the fat of cows and pigs!' The rumour spread like wildfire.
p: Rumours played a big role. The sepoys at Meerut and elsewhere believed that the cartridges of the new Enfield rifle were greased with the fat of cows and pigs, and that biting them would corrupt their caste and religion.

Captain Wright's report (January 1857) traced one source: at Dum Dum, near Calcutta, a low-caste khalasi asked a Brahmin sepoy for water from his lota; when refused, he said the sepoy would soon lose his caste by biting cartridges greased with cow and pig fat.

Another rumour said the British had mixed the bone dust of cows and pigs into the flour sold in the market. In towns and cantonments people refused to touch the atta. A prophecy said British rule would end on the centenary of the Battle of Plassey, 23 June 1857. Chapatis were also being distributed from village to village.

Rumours spread because they resonated with deeper fears. Since the late 1820s, under Lord William Bentinck, the British had promoted Western education, Western ideas and institutions, and laws abolishing sati (1829) and permitting the remarriage of Hindu widows (1856).

The British also annexed states on the plea of misgovernment and through the Doctrine of Lapse. Many people feared that everything they cherished, including their religion and social customs, was being destroyed and that Christianity would be imposed.

ex.q: Why did people believe the rumours about greased cartridges and bone dust?
st: They fitted fears created by British reforms like the abolition of sati and widow remarriage law.
Annexations through the Doctrine of Lapse showed the British could take away rulers' rights.
Missionary activity raised fears of forced conversion.
So the rumours seemed to confirm what people already feared.
ex.a: Because they matched widespread fears that the British were destroying Indian religion and customs.

topics.rl: Fact-checking units in India today counter fake news on WhatsApp, a reminder that rumours spread fastest when they confirm people's fears.

topics.ch: Part III: Rebels and the Raj: The 1857 Revolt and its Representations
topics.t: Awadh: 'a cherry that will drop into our mouth'
topics.h: In 1851 Lord Dalhousie called Awadh 'a cherry that will drop into our mouth one day'. Five years later the British annexed it, and Awadh became the heart of the revolt.
p: In 1851 Governor-General Lord Dalhousie described the kingdom of Awadh as 'a cherry that will drop into our mouth one day'. Five years later, in 1856, it was formally annexed.

The process had begun earlier: the Subsidiary Alliance was imposed on Awadh in 1801. In 1856, Nawab Wajid Ali Shah was dethroned and exiled to Calcutta on the plea that the region was being misgoverned.

The British wrongly assumed the Nawab was unpopular. He was widely loved, and many followed him all the way to Kanpur singing songs of lament: 'Angrez Bahadur ain, mulk lai linho' (the Englishmen have come and taken the country).

The taluqdars of Awadh, local landholders with forts and armed retainers, were disarmed and their forts destroyed. The Summary Settlement of 1856, based on the assumption that taluqdars were interlopers with no permanent stake in the land, removed them wherever possible and gave the land to the peasants.

Before annexation, taluqdars held 67 per cent of the villages of Awadh; after the Summary Settlement, this fell to 38 per cent. Peasants did not gain much either: revenue was over-assessed and their insecurity grew.

ex.q: How did the annexation of Awadh create widespread resentment?
st: The popular Nawab was dethroned and exiled.
Taluqdars were disarmed and lost their lands.
Peasants faced over-assessed revenue.
So nobles, landholders and peasants all had grievances.
ex.a: It hurt the Nawab's supporters, the taluqdars and the peasants alike, uniting many groups against the British.

topics.rl: Lucknow's culture of music, kathak, poetry and Awadhi cuisine, which flourished under Wajid Ali Shah, is still celebrated; he took this culture with him to Matiaburj in Kolkata.

topics.ch: Part III: Rebels and the Raj: The 1857 Revolt and its Representations
topics.t: Awadh in revolt: courtiers, sepoys and peasants together
topics.h: Awadh was called the 'nursery of the Bengal Army'. When its villages suffered, its sepoys felt it, and the revolt became a people's war.
p: The removal of the Nawab led to the dissolution of the court and its culture. A whole range of people lost their livelihood: musicians, dancers, poets, cooks, retainers and administrative officials.
Taluqdars, deprived of land and power, and peasants, burdened by over-assessed revenue, shared grievances. In many places taluqdars and peasants fought together against the British.

A large number of sepoys of the Bengal Army were recruited from the villages of Awadh, which was called the 'nursery of the Bengal Army'. For decades sepoys had complained about low pay and the difficulty of getting leave.

The sepoys' grievances merged with the grievances of their families and villages. Sepoys were linked to peasants by ties of kinship, so news of distress at home reached the lines, and the anger of the countryside reached the army.
That is why the revolt in Awadh became particularly widespread: it was a popular rebellion in which sepoys, taluqdars, peasants and the dependants of the old court all took part.

ex.q: Why was the revolt particularly widespread in Awadh?
st: The popular Nawab's removal hurt courtiers, artists and officials.
Taluqdars lost lands and forts; peasants faced high revenue.
Many sepoys came from Awadh villages and shared their families' grievances.
So almost every section of society had reasons to rebel.
ex.a: Because grievances of the court's dependants, taluqdars, peasants and sepoys all came together in Awadh.

topics.rl: Lucknow's Residency ruins, with cannon-ball marks still visible, preserve the memory of the long siege during the revolt.

topics.ch: Part III: Rebels and the Raj: The 1857 Revolt and its Representations
topics.t: What the rebels wanted
topics.h: British accounts called the rebels mere mutineers. But their own proclamations tell a different story, of grievances, unity and a different idea of rule.
p: The rebels' own proclamations and messages are key sources for understanding their vision, since most other accounts were written by the British.

The proclamations in the name of Bahadur Shah appealed to all sections regardless of caste and creed, calling people to join the fight under the standards of both Muhammad and Mahavir. Hindu–Muslim unity was striking; British attempts to create divisions, such as spending money in Bareilly to incite Hindus against Muslims, failed.

The proclamations attacked symbols of British rule: land revenue settlements that had dispossessed landholders, foreign commerce that had ruined artisans and weavers, the threat to religion through Christianity, and moneylenders seen as allies of the British.

The Azamgarh Proclamation of 25 August 1857 listed grievances of different groups: zamindars (high revenue assessments), merchants (taxes and Company monopoly of trade), public servants (no high posts and low salaries for Indians), artisans (English goods causing unemployment), and pundits and fakirs (British hostility to Hindu and Muslim religions).

Where British rule collapsed, rebels in Delhi, Lucknow and Kanpur tried to set up an administration modelled on the eighteenth-century Mughal world: they made appointments to administrative and military posts, collected land revenue, paid troops and issued orders to stop looting. These structures were mainly for the needs of war and did not last.

ex.q: Using the Azamgarh Proclamation, show what different groups resented about British rule.
st: Zamindars: high revenue assessments.
Merchants: taxes and Company monopoly of trade.
Public servants: no high posts, low salaries.
Artisans: unemployment from English goods.
Pundits and fakirs: hostility to their religions.
ex.a: Each group had specific economic or religious grievances, which the proclamation brought together against British rule.

topics.rl: The Indian Postal Department issued stamps honouring 1857 leaders, and the 150th anniversary in 2007 was marked as a celebration of the 'First War of Independence'.

topics.ch: Part III: Rebels and the Raj: The 1857 Revolt and its Representations
topics.t: Repression
topics.h: In 1857, laws were passed under which even ordinary Britons could try and punish Indians suspected of rebellion, and death was the only punishment.
p: Before sending troops, the British passed a series of laws. By Acts passed in May and June 1857, the whole of north India was put under martial law, and military officers and even ordinary Britons were given the power to try and punish Indians suspected of rebellion.
The ordinary processes of law and trial were suspended, and it was made clear that rebellion had only one punishment: death.

Reinforcements were brought from Britain. Delhi was recaptured after a two-pronged attack, one from Calcutta and the other from Punjab; the attempt began in June 1857, but the city was captured only in late September.
In the Gangetic plain the British advanced slowly, recapturing territory village by village. Punishments were harsh: rebels were hanged or blown from cannon in public, and villages were burnt.

In Awadh, the British also used diplomacy to break the unity of the rebels. They promised big landholders that their estates would be returned. Rebel landholders who did not submit were dispossessed, while loyal ones were rewarded.

ex.q: How did the British suppress the revolt?
st: Passed laws giving officers and Britons power to try and punish rebels; death the only punishment.
Brought reinforcements and recaptured Delhi in September 1857.
Advanced village by village with harsh punishments: hangings, blowing from cannon, burning villages.
In Awadh, won back taluqdars by promising to restore their estates.
ex.a: Through harsh laws, military force, public terror and a policy of winning back taluqdars.

topics.rl: Jallianwala Bagh (1919) and other later events show that colonial repression continued; memorials across India today recall these moments.

topics.ch: Part III: Rebels and the Raj: The 1857 Revolt and its Representations
topics.t: The revolt in images: celebrating the avengers and the honour of Britain
topics.h: British paintings showed their generals as saviours and English women as innocent victims. Images were weapons too, shaping how people in Britain felt about 1857.
p: Pictures, paintings, cartoons and popular prints produced by the British and by Indians are important sources. They show how the revolt was represented and remembered, and how images shaped public opinion.

British paintings celebrated those who saved the English and repressed the rebels. 'Relief of Lucknow', painted by Thomas Jones Barker in 1859, shows the moment the British commander Colin Campbell arrived at the Lucknow Residency and was greeted by James Outram and Henry Havelock.

During the siege, Henry Lawrence, the Commissioner of Lucknow, had gathered the Christian population in the fortified Residency. Lawrence was killed, but the siege continued; Outram and Havelock cut through the rebel forces to reinforce the garrison, and later Colin Campbell's forces rescued it. In British accounts they became heroes.

Images of English women and children were used to show the 'honour of Britain' under threat. 'In Memoriam' by Joseph Noel Paton shows English women and children huddled together, helpless and innocent, as if awaiting dishonour and death, stirring anger and grief in Britain.
Other images showed English women as heroic defenders. A print of Miss Wheeler at Kanpur shows her defending herself single-handedly against rebels, presented as protecting her honour.

ex.q: What purpose did paintings like 'Relief of Lucknow' and 'In Memoriam' serve in Britain?
st: 'Relief of Lucknow' glorified British commanders as rescuers.
'In Memoriam' showed English women and children as helpless victims.
Both stirred emotions of pride, grief and anger.
They built public support for harsh repression.
ex.a: They glorified British heroes, portrayed the English as victims and stirred public feeling in favour of revenge and repression.

topics.rl: Indian films and TV serials about 1857, like 'Manikarnika' (2019), also use images to shape how audiences feel about history.

topics.ch: Part III: Rebels and the Raj: The 1857 Revolt and its Representations
topics.t: Retribution, terror and 'Clemency Canning'
topics.h: When Lord Canning urged leniency, the British press mocked him as 'Clemency Canning'. The mood in Britain was revenge, not mercy.
p: As news of the revolt reached Britain, there were demands for retribution and revenge. Images expressed this mood.

'Justice', an allegorical image by John Tenniel published in the magazine Punch in September 1857, showed a fierce female figure of Justice with sword and shield, attacking rebels while Indian women and children cowered in fear. It expressed the demand for vengeance.

Terror was displayed openly. Rebels were executed in public, blown from cannons and hanged from gallows, and images of these punishments were widely circulated in popular journals. The aim was to create fear and discourage further rebellion.
Lord Canning, the Governor-General, declared that a soft line and gestures of clemency would help win back the loyalty of the sepoys.

The British press ridiculed him. A cartoon in Punch, 'The Clemency of Canning', showed him as a benign figure patting the head of a sepoy who still held a bloodied sword. He was mocked as 'Clemency Canning', showing there was no time for mercy in British public opinion.

ex.q: What do images like 'Justice' and 'The Clemency of Canning' tell us about British public opinion?
st: 'Justice' showed the demand for vengeance.
Public executions were shown to spread terror.
'The Clemency of Canning' mocked any idea of mercy.
So British opinion was dominated by anger and the desire for revenge.
ex.a: That British public opinion demanded harsh retribution and scorned leniency.

topics.rl: Political cartoons remain powerful in India: R.K. Laxman's 'Common Man' in The Times of India commented on public life for over five decades.

topics.ch: Part III: Rebels and the Raj: The 1857 Revolt and its Representations
topics.t: Nationalist imagery and reading the sources of 1857
topics.h: 'Khoob ladi mardani woh to Jhansi wali rani thi.' Subhadra Kumari Chauhan's poem made generations of Indian children see Rani Lakshmibai as a fearless warrior.
p: In the twentieth century, the nationalist movement drew inspiration from 1857. A whole world of nationalist imagination was woven around the revolt. It was celebrated as the First War of Independence, in which people of all classes came together to fight colonial rule; V.D. Savarkar wrote of it in this way.

Art and literature helped keep the memory alive. Rani Lakshmibai was portrayed as a heroic, masculine figure chasing the enemy, slaying British soldiers and fighting bravely till the last. Popular prints showed her on horseback, sword in one hand, reins in the other.
Children grew up reading Subhadra Kumari Chauhan's poem with the lines 'Khoob ladi mardani woh to Jhansi wali rani thi' (Like a man, she fought valiantly, the Rani of Jhansi).

Historians compare different visual representations: British images glorified rescuers, portrayed English women as victims and demanded revenge; nationalist images glorified rebel leaders and presented the revolt as a war of independence.

Timeline: 1801 Subsidiary Alliance imposed on Awadh; 1856 Awadh annexed; 10 May 1857 mutiny at Meerut; late September 1857 Delhi recaptured; June 1858 Rani Lakshmibai killed in battle; 1858 an Act of the British Parliament ended Company rule and transferred power to the British Crown.

ex.q: What do visual representations tell us about the revolt of 1857?
st: British images showed British heroes, English women as victims and demanded revenge.
Nationalist images showed rebels like Rani Lakshmibai as heroic freedom fighters.
Both used images to shape emotions and memory.
So images tell us about how different people remembered and interpreted 1857.
ex.a: They reveal how British and Indian audiences interpreted the revolt, each through its own concerns.

topics.rl: Rani Lakshmibai's name lives on in the Rani Lakshmi Bai Central Agricultural University in Jhansi and the Rani Jhansi Regiment of Netaji's INA during the Second World War.

topics.ch: Part III: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
topics.t: A leader announces himself
topics.h: In January 1915 a lawyer returned to India after two decades in South Africa. Within a few years, he would change the meaning of Indian nationalism.
p: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi returned to India in January 1915 after two decades in South Africa, where he had gone as a lawyer and become a leader of the Indian community.

It was in South Africa that he first forged the distinctive technique of non-violent protest known as satyagraha, first promoted harmony between religions, and first alerted upper-caste Indians to their discriminatory treatment of low castes and women. The historian Chandran Devanesan remarked that South Africa was 'the making of the Mahatma'.

The India of 1915 was very different from the India of 1893. The Indian National Congress, founded in 1885, now had branches in most major cities and towns. Through the Swadeshi movement of 1905–07 it had broadened its appeal among the middle classes.

That movement produced major leaders: Bal Gangadhar Tilak of Maharashtra, Bipin Chandra Pal of Bengal and Lala Lajpat Rai of Punjab ('Lal, Bal and Pal'), who advocated militant opposition to colonial rule. 'Moderates' like Gopal Krishna Gokhale and Mohammad Ali Jinnah preferred a gradual and persuasive approach.
On the advice of his political mentor Gokhale, Gandhi spent a year travelling around British India, getting to know the land and its peoples.

ex.q: Why did Gokhale advise Gandhi to travel through British India first?
st: Gandhi had been away for two decades.
India and its politics had changed greatly.
Travelling would help him understand the land and its peoples.
This knowledge would help him lead a mass movement.
ex.a: So that Gandhi could understand India and its people before taking a leading role.

topics.rl: The Pravasi Bharatiya Divas, celebrated on 9 January, marks the day Gandhi returned to India from South Africa in 1915.

topics.ch: Part III: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
topics.t: Banaras speech and the first satyagrahas
topics.h: At the opening of Banaras Hindu University in 1916, Gandhi told jewel-laden princes that India's salvation would come through its farmers, not its lawyers, doctors or rich landlords!
p: Gandhi's first major public appearance was at the opening of the Banaras Hindu University (BHU) in February 1916. The invitees included princes and philanthropists whose donations had helped found BHU.

Gandhi charged the Indian elite with a lack of concern for the labouring poor. He said there was no salvation for India unless the wealthy held their riches in trust for their countrymen, and that 'our salvation can only come through the farmers', not through lawyers, doctors or rich landlords.
The speech showed that Indian nationalism was still an elite phenomenon, a creation of lawyers, doctors and landlords, and that Gandhi wanted to make it representative of the whole Indian people.

In December 1916, at the Congress session in Lucknow, a peasant from Champaran in Bihar told Gandhi about the harsh treatment of peasants by British indigo planters. In 1917 Gandhi spent much time in Champaran, seeking security of tenure for the peasants and the freedom to cultivate crops of their choice.

In 1918 he was involved in two campaigns in Gujarat: a labour dispute in Ahmedabad, demanding better working conditions for textile mill workers, and in Kheda, asking the state to remit taxes after the failure of the harvest. These campaigns established Gandhi as a nationalist with deep sympathy for the poor.

ex.q: How did the Champaran, Ahmedabad and Kheda campaigns build Gandhi's reputation?
st: Champaran: for indigo peasants' rights.
Ahmedabad: for mill workers' conditions.
Kheda: for tax remission after crop failure.
Each took up the cause of poor people, showing his concern for them.
ex.a: By championing peasants and workers in all three, they established him as a leader who cared for the poor.

topics.rl: The centenary of the Champaran Satyagraha was celebrated across Bihar in 2017, a hundred years after Gandhi took up the indigo peasants' cause.

topics.ch: Part III: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
topics.t: The Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh
topics.h: Punjab's soldiers had fought for Britain in the First World War. Their reward? A law allowing detention without trial, and then the massacre at Jallianwala Bagh.
p: During the First World War (1914–18), the British had instituted censorship of the press and permitted detention without trial. On the recommendation of a committee chaired by Sir Sidney Rowlatt, these tough measures were continued after the war. This was the Rowlatt Act of 1919.

Gandhi called for a countrywide campaign against the Rowlatt Act. In towns across north and west India, life came to a standstill as shops shut down and schools closed in response to the call for a hartal (bandh).
The protests were particularly intense in Punjab, where many men had served on the British side in the war and expected to be rewarded. Instead they got the Rowlatt Act.

Gandhi was detained while on his way to Punjab, and prominent local Congressmen were arrested. The situation escalated, and in April 1919 at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar, a British Brigadier ordered his troops to open fire on a nationalist meeting. More than four hundred people were killed in this massacre.
It was the Rowlatt satyagraha that made Gandhi a truly national leader.

ex.q: Why were protests against the Rowlatt Act especially intense in Punjab?
st: Many Punjabi men had served in the British army in the First World War.
They expected to be rewarded after the war.
Instead the Rowlatt Act continued repressive measures.
Arrests of leaders and Gandhi's detention escalated the anger.
ex.a: Because people who had served Britain in the war felt betrayed by the Rowlatt Act, and arrests inflamed feelings further.

topics.rl: The Jallianwala Bagh memorial in Amritsar, with bullet marks still visible on its walls, is visited by lakhs every year; 13 April is remembered as the day of the massacre.

topics.ch: Part III: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
topics.t: Non-cooperation and Khilafat
topics.h: 'Non-cooperation became the name of an epoch in the life of India and of Gandhi,' wrote Louis Fischer. Students, lawyers, workers, tribals and peasants all joined in!
p: After Jallianwala Bagh, Gandhi called for a campaign of non-cooperation with British rule, launched in 1920. Indians who wished colonialism to end were asked to stop attending schools, colleges and law courts and not to pay taxes. They were asked to renounce all voluntary association with the British government, including giving up titles. Gandhi said that if non-cooperation was carried out effectively, India would win swaraj within a year.

To broaden the struggle, Gandhi joined hands with the Khilafat Movement, led by Muslim leaders such as Mohammad Ali and Shaukat Ali, which sought to defend the position of the Khalifa (Caliph), the Ottoman Sultan of Turkey, and restore his authority after the First World War. Gandhi hoped this would bring Hindus and Muslims together.

Students stopped going to government schools and colleges. Lawyers refused to attend court. Foreign cloth was boycotted and burnt in bonfires. The working class went on strike in many towns and cities: according to official figures there were 396 strikes involving 6,00,000 workers in 1921.

The countryside was seething: hill tribes in northern Andhra violated forest laws; farmers in Awadh did not pay taxes; peasants in Kumaun refused to carry loads for colonial officials. These protests were sometimes carried out in defiance of the local nationalist leadership.

As the American biographer Louis Fischer wrote, 'Non-cooperation became the name of an epoch in the life of India and of Gandhiji.' It was negative enough to be peaceful but positive enough to be effective.

ex.q: How did the Non-Cooperation Movement become a form of protest that reached many groups?
st: Students boycotted government schools and colleges.
Lawyers boycotted courts; titles were renounced.
Foreign cloth was boycotted; workers went on strike.
Tribals defied forest laws and peasants refused taxes and forced labour.
ex.a: By giving every group a way to withdraw cooperation, from boycotting schools and courts to strikes and defying forest and tax laws.

topics.rl: Jamia Millia Islamia in Delhi and Gujarat Vidyapith in Ahmedabad were founded in 1920 as national institutions during non-cooperation, when students left government colleges.

topics.ch: Part III: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
topics.t: Chauri Chaura and Gandhi's trial
topics.h: After a mob burnt a police station at Chauri Chaura in 1922, Gandhi called off a nationwide movement at its height. Then a British judge told him he was 'a great patriot'!
p: In February 1922, a group of peasants attacked and torched a police station in the hamlet of Chauri Chaura in the United Provinces (now Uttar Pradesh). Several constables perished in the fire.
This act of violence prompted Gandhi to call off the Non-Cooperation Movement altogether. He said that no provocation could justify the brutal murder of men who had been rendered defenceless.
During the movement, thousands of Indians were put in jail. Gandhi himself was arrested in March 1922 and charged with sedition.

The judge who presided over his trial, Justice C.N. Broomfield, made a remarkable speech while sentencing him. He said that Gandhi was in a different category from anyone he had ever tried; that in the eyes of millions he was a great patriot and leader; and that even those who differed with him saw him as a man of high ideals and noble, even saintly, life.
Since Gandhi had violated the law, the Bench was obliged to sentence him, and he was sentenced to six years' imprisonment.

ex.q: Why did Gandhi call off the Non-Cooperation Movement after Chauri Chaura?
st: The movement was based on non-violence.
At Chauri Chaura, a mob killed defenceless policemen.
Gandhi felt no provocation could justify such violence.
He believed the people were not yet ready for non-violent mass struggle, so he called it off.
ex.a: Because the violence at Chauri Chaura went against the principle of non-violence on which the movement was based.

topics.rl: A memorial at Chauri Chaura in Gorakhpur district was built to remember the events of 1922; the centenary was observed in 2021–22.

topics.ch: Part III: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
topics.t: A people's leader
topics.h: In villages of eastern UP, rumours said that anyone who spoke against 'Gandhi baba' would see their house collapse or their crops fail. Peasants saw him as more than a politician!
p: By 1922, Gandhi had transformed Indian nationalism. It was no longer a movement of professionals and intellectuals; hundreds of thousands of peasants, workers and artisans participated. Many venerated him as their 'Mahatma'.

Gandhi dressed like ordinary people, lived like them and spoke their language. Unlike other leaders, he did not stand apart from the common folk but identified with them. He was often seen in a simple dhoti.

He spent part of each day working on the charkha (spinning wheel) and encouraged other nationalists to do the same. Spinning helped him break the traditional boundaries between mental labour and manual labour.

The historian Shahid Amin traced the image of Gandhi among peasants in eastern Uttar Pradesh, as reported in the local press. Rumours spread of his miraculous powers: that he had been sent by the King to redress the grievances of farmers, that he could overrule local officials, and that those who opposed him would suffer misfortunes.
Peasants knew him as 'Gandhi baba', 'Gandhi Maharaj' or simply 'Mahatma'. To them he was a saviour who would rescue them from high taxes and oppressive officials, and restore their dignity.

ex.q: How did Gandhi identify with the common people?
st: He dressed simply, in a dhoti.
He lived like them and spoke their language.
He spun on the charkha daily, valuing manual labour.
He took up peasants' and workers' causes.
ex.a: Through his simple dress and lifestyle, use of their language, manual labour on the charkha and support for their causes.

topics.rl: Khadi Gram Udyog stores across India and the Khadi and Village Industries Commission continue Gandhi's idea of the charkha as a symbol of self-reliance.

topics.ch: Part III: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
topics.t: Constructive programme and the growth of the Congress
topics.h: For Gandhi, freedom was not just about getting the British out. India also had to free itself of untouchability, child marriage and communal hatred.
p: Gandhi believed India would not be fit for swaraj unless it freed itself of social evils such as child marriage and untouchability. He worked to remove untouchability and promoted Hindu–Muslim harmony.

He promoted khadi (hand-spun, hand-woven cloth) as a means of economic self-reliance and as a symbol of the nation. The constructive programme included khadi, village industries, Hindu–Muslim unity and the abolition of untouchability.
Under Gandhi's leadership, new branches of the Congress were set up in various parts of India. A series of Praja Mandals was established to promote the nationalist creed in the princely states.

Gandhi encouraged communication in the mother tongue rather than English. Provincial Congress committees were based on linguistic regions rather than the artificial boundaries of British India. Nationalism thus reached the farthest corners of the country.

The movement also gained support from prosperous peasants and from industrialists, such as G.D. Birla, who supported the national movement. Gandhi had talented followers, including Mahadev Desai, Vallabhbhai Patel, J.B. Kripalani, Subhas Chandra Bose, Abul Kalam Azad, Jawaharlal Nehru, Sarojini Naidu, Govind Ballabh Pant and C. Rajagopalachari.

ex.q: How did the Congress spread to all parts of India under Gandhi?
st: New branches were set up across India.
Praja Mandals spread nationalism in princely states.
Provincial committees were organised on linguistic lines.
Communication in mother tongues reached ordinary people.
ex.a: Through new branches, Praja Mandals, linguistic provincial committees and the use of mother tongues.

topics.rl: The linguistic organisation of Congress committees foreshadowed the States Reorganisation Act of 1956, which reorganised Indian states largely on linguistic lines.

topics.ch: Part III: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
topics.t: Purna Swaraj and the choice of salt
topics.h: Of all things, why salt? Because every household needed it, the British had a monopoly over it, and even the poorest paid a tax on it!
p: In 1928 the Simon Commission, sent by Britain to enquire into conditions in the colony, arrived in India. As it had no Indian members, it was boycotted with the slogan 'Simon go back'.
In December 1929 the Congress held its annual session in Lahore, with Jawaharlal Nehru as president. It declared its commitment to Purna Swaraj, complete independence.

On 26 January 1930, 'Independence Day' was observed: the national flag was hoisted at different venues and patriotic songs were sung. Gandhi gave precise instructions on how the day should be observed.
Soon after, Gandhi announced a march to break the salt law, one of the most widely disliked laws in British India. It gave the state a monopoly over the manufacture and sale of salt.

Salt was used in every Indian household, yet Indians were forbidden from making it even for domestic use and were compelled to buy it at a high price from shops. By targeting the salt monopoly, Gandhi hoped to mobilise a wider discontent against British rule, since the salt tax hurt everyone, rich and poor.

ex.q: Why did the salt law become an important issue?
st: Salt was a basic necessity used in every household.
The British held a monopoly over its manufacture and sale.
Indians could not make salt even for home use and paid a high price.
So breaking the salt law united everyone against an unjust tax.
ex.a: Because the tax on a universal necessity affected every Indian, making it a powerful symbol of unjust British rule.

topics.rl: Republic Day is celebrated on 26 January because the Constitution came into force on that date in 1950, chosen to honour the Purna Swaraj Day of 1930.

topics.ch: Part III: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
topics.t: The Dandi March and Civil Disobedience
topics.h: On 12 March 1930, Gandhi set out from Sabarmati with his followers. About three weeks later, at Dandi, he picked up a fistful of salt, and an empire trembled.
p: Gandhi notified the Viceroy, Lord Irwin, of his plan in advance, but Irwin failed to grasp the significance of the action.

On 12 March 1930 Gandhi began walking from his ashram at Sabarmati towards the ocean. He reached Dandi three weeks later and, on 6 April 1930, made a fistful of salt, thereby breaking the law. Parallel salt marches were held in other parts of the country.

This launched the Civil Disobedience Movement. Peasants breached forest laws; factory workers went on strike; lawyers boycotted British courts; and students refused to attend government-run educational institutions. Over 60,000 Indians were arrested, including Gandhi himself.

The march was significant for three reasons. First, it brought Gandhi to world attention: it was widely covered by the European and American press. Second, it was the first nationalist activity in which women participated in large numbers; the socialist activist Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay had persuaded Gandhi not to restrict the protests to men alone.
Third, the march forced the British to realise that their Raj would not last forever and that they would have to devolve some power to Indians.

ex.q: What was the significance of the Salt March?
st: It brought Gandhi to world attention through European and American press coverage.
Women participated in large numbers for the first time.
It made the British realise they would have to devolve power.
It launched the nationwide Civil Disobedience Movement.
ex.a: It drew world attention, brought women into the movement and forced the British to see that their rule could not last.

topics.rl: The National Salt Satyagraha Memorial at Dandi in Gujarat, opened in 2019, recreates the march with statues of Gandhi and the 80 marchers.

topics.ch: Part III: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
topics.t: Dialogues: Round Tables, the Irwin Pact and the Poona Pact
topics.h: At the Second Round Table Conference in London, Gandhi claimed to speak for all of India. Three groups disagreed: the Muslim League, the princes and Dr B.R. Ambedkar.
p: The British began a series of Round Table Conferences in London. The first, in November 1930, was held without Gandhi, as the Congress boycotted it; it was futile.

Gandhi was released from jail in January 1931 and held long meetings with the Viceroy. These led to the Gandhi–Irwin Pact (March 1931): Civil Disobedience would be called off, all prisoners released and salt manufacture allowed along the coast. Radical nationalists criticised the pact because Gandhi did not get a commitment to political independence.

A Second Round Table Conference was held in London in the latter part of 1931, with Gandhi representing the Congress. His claim that the Congress represented all of India was challenged by the Muslim League (which claimed to stand for the Muslim minority), the princes (who said the Congress had no stake in their territories) and B.R. Ambedkar (who argued that Gandhi and the Congress did not truly represent the lowest castes). The conference was inconclusive, and Gandhi resumed civil disobedience on his return. The new Viceroy, Lord Willingdon, had no sympathy for him.
Ambedkar demanded separate electorates for the depressed classes. Gandhi opposed this, fearing it would permanently divide them from Hindu society, and went on a fast.
The Poona Pact (1932) between Gandhi and Ambedkar resolved the issue: instead of separate electorates, seats were reserved for the depressed classes within the general electorate.

ex.q: Why was Gandhi's claim to represent all of India challenged at the Second Round Table Conference?
st: The Muslim League claimed to represent Muslims.
The princes said the Congress had no stake in their territories.
Ambedkar said the Congress did not represent the lowest castes.
So different groups contested the Congress's claim.
ex.a: Because the Muslim League, the princes and Ambedkar each claimed the Congress did not represent their group.

topics.rl: Reserved seats for Scheduled Castes in Parliament and state assemblies today follow the principle agreed in the Poona Pact: reservation within joint electorates.

topics.ch: Part III: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
topics.t: Provincial ministries, war, Cripps and Quit India
topics.h: 'Do or Die!' In August 1942 Gandhi gave this call, and within hours he and other leaders were in jail. Yet the movement raged on for over a year.
p: The Government of India Act of 1935 promised some form of representative government. In 1937, elections were held on a restricted franchise, and the Congress won a comprehensive victory: eight out of eleven provinces had a Congress 'Prime Minister' working under a British Governor.

In September 1939, two years after the Congress ministries took office, the Second World War broke out. Gandhi and Nehru were critical of Hitler and the Nazis and promised support if the British promised independence after the war. The offer was refused, and in protest the Congress ministries resigned in October 1939.

In 1942 Prime Minister Winston Churchill sent Sir Stafford Cripps to forge a compromise with Gandhi and the Congress. Talks broke down when the Congress insisted that, if it was to help defend India from the Axis powers, the Viceroy must first appoint an Indian as the Defence Member of his Executive Council.

After the failure of the Cripps Mission, Gandhi launched his third major movement, Quit India, in August 1942, with the call 'Do or Die'. Gandhi and other leaders were jailed at once, but younger activists organised strikes and acts of sabotage across the country. Socialist members of the Congress, such as Jayaprakash Narayan, were particularly active in the underground resistance.

In several districts, such as Satara in the west and Medinipur in the east, 'independent' governments were proclaimed. The British responded with great force, yet it took more than a year to suppress the rebellion. Quit India was a genuine mass movement involving hundreds of thousands of ordinary Indians.

ex.q: Why did the Quit India Movement continue even after Gandhi and other leaders were jailed?
st: Younger activists organised strikes and sabotage.
Socialists like Jayaprakash Narayan led underground resistance.
Parallel governments were set up in Satara and Medinipur.
Ordinary people in large numbers joined, making it a mass movement.
ex.a: Because younger and underground leaders and ordinary people carried it on, making it a genuine mass movement.

topics.rl: 9 August is observed as August Kranti Din; the Gowalia Tank Maidan in Mumbai, where the Quit India call was given, is now called August Kranti Maidan.

topics.ch: Part III: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
topics.t: Towards independence: the League, Simla and the Cabinet Mission
topics.h: In the 1946 elections, the Congress swept the general seats while the Muslim League won almost all seats reserved for Muslims. The political polarisation was complete.
p: In 1940 the Muslim League passed a resolution (the Lahore resolution) demanding a measure of autonomy for the Muslim-majority areas of the subcontinent, which came to be seen as a demand for Pakistan. During Quit India, while Congress leaders were in jail, the League worked to extend its influence, especially in Punjab and Sind.

In 1945 a Labour government came to power in Britain, committed to granting independence to India. The Viceroy, Lord Wavell, brought the Congress and the League together for talks, including the Simla conference of 1945, but no agreement was reached.
In early 1946 fresh elections were held to the provincial legislatures. The Congress swept the 'General' category, but in the seats reserved for Muslims the League won an overwhelming majority.

A Cabinet Mission came in the summer of 1946. It failed to get the Congress and the League to agree on a federal system that would keep India together while allowing the provinces a degree of autonomy.

After the talks broke down, Jinnah called for a 'Direct Action Day' on 16 August 1946 to press the League's demand for Pakistan. Bloody riots broke out in Calcutta that day and spread to rural Bengal, Bihar, the United Provinces and Punjab.

ex.q: Why did the Cabinet Mission fail?
st: It proposed a federal system keeping India together with provincial autonomy.
The Congress and the League could not agree on its terms.
Political polarisation after the 1946 elections made compromise harder.
So the talks broke down, followed by Direct Action Day.
ex.a: Because the Congress and the League, deeply polarised after the 1946 elections, could not agree on its federal plan.

topics.rl: Historians in India and Pakistan continue to study the events of 1946–47; the Partition Museum in Amritsar records the experiences of people who lived through them.

topics.ch: Part III: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
topics.t: The last heroic days
topics.h: On 15 August 1947, while Delhi celebrated, Gandhi was in Calcutta, fasting for 24 hours. For him, freedom without peace was incomplete.
p: On 15 August 1947 India became independent, but the joy was mixed with the pain of Partition and communal violence. Gandhi was not in Delhi for the celebrations; he was in Calcutta, where he did not attend any function or hoist a flag, and marked the day with a 24-hour fast.

Gandhi toured riot-torn areas: Noakhali in east Bengal, villages in Bihar, and the riot-torn slums of Calcutta and Delhi, trying to stop the violence and comfort the victims. He worked to ensure that minorities felt safe.
He fasted in Calcutta and in Delhi to restore communal peace. Through his efforts and persuasion, the Congress passed a resolution on the 'rights of minorities', promising to protect them.
On 30 January 1948, Gandhi was shot dead at his daily prayer meeting in Delhi by Nathuram Godse, who had denounced him as an 'appeaser' of Muslims.

His death led to an extraordinary outpouring of grief, with tributes from across the world. Time magazine compared his martyrdom to that of Abraham Lincoln: just as Lincoln had been killed for believing that people were equal regardless of race, Gandhi was killed for believing that friendship between Hindus and Muslims was possible and necessary. Timeline: 1915 return; 1917–18 Champaran, Kheda, Ahmedabad; 1919 Rowlatt satyagraha and Jallianwala Bagh; 1920–22 Non-Cooperation; 1930 Salt March; 1942 Quit India; 1947 independence; 1948 assassination.

ex.q: How did Gandhi spend the last months of his life?
st: He marked Independence Day with a fast in Calcutta.
He toured Noakhali, Bihar, Calcutta and Delhi to stop riots.
He fasted in Calcutta and Delhi to restore peace.
He pressed for protection of minorities' rights.
ex.a: Working for communal harmony: touring riot areas, fasting for peace and protecting minorities.

topics.rl: 30 January is observed in India as Martyrs' Day (Shaheed Diwas), with two minutes of silence at 11 a.m. in memory of Gandhi and other martyrs.

topics.ch: Part III: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
topics.t: Knowing Gandhi: sources and their limits
topics.h: During the Salt March, police reports tried to show that it was failing, while Indian newspapers reported huge crowds. Same event, very different stories!
p: Historians use many sources to study Gandhi and the national movement: the writings and speeches of Gandhi and his contemporaries, including associates and opponents. It is important to distinguish between the public voice (speeches meant for audiences) and private scripts (personal letters and diaries).

Letters give a glimpse of private thoughts: anger, pain, hopes and frustrations. Gandhi regularly published letters others wrote to him in his journal Harijan. Nehru edited a collection of letters written to him during the national movement, A Bunch of Old Letters. But many letters were written knowing they might be published, so even 'private' letters may be shaped for the public.

Autobiographies, like Gandhi's My Experiments with Truth, are retrospective accounts, often written from memory. They tell us what the author remembered, saw as important and how they wanted their life to be viewed; they frame a picture, so we must read them carefully.

Government records are another source. The Home Department prepared fortnightly reports from the early twentieth century, based on police information from localities. These often expressed what higher officials wanted to believe: during the Salt March, they claimed it was not drawing much response, while evidence shows mass participation.

Newspapers, in English and in Indian languages, tracked Gandhi's movements and reported what ordinary people thought. But they were published by people with their own political views: a London newspaper and an Indian nationalist paper might describe the same event very differently. All sources must be read critically and compared.

ex.q: How do private letters and autobiographies differ from official accounts as sources on Gandhi?
st: Letters reveal personal thoughts and feelings, though some were written for publication.
Autobiographies show how the author wanted to be remembered.
Official reports reflect the government's views and interests.
So each has its own bias and must be compared with others.
ex.a: Letters and autobiographies show personal perspectives, while official accounts show the government's view; each must be read critically.

topics.rl: The Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi, published by the Government of India in 100 volumes, are now available online for researchers and students.

topics.ch: Part III: Framing the Constitution: The Beginning of a New Era
topics.t: Framing the Constitution: an introduction
topics.h: India's Constitution was not written in a day. It was argued over, clause by clause, for nearly three years by an Assembly representing a vast and divided country.
p: The Constitution of India came into effect on 26 January 1950. It is among the longest constitutions in the world, reflecting the country's size and diversity.

It was framed between December 1946 and November 1949. Drafts were discussed clause by clause in the Constituent Assembly over eleven sessions, with sittings spread over 165 days; between sessions, committees and sub-committees revised the drafts.
The Constituent Assembly Debates (CAD), the printed record of these discussions, run into eleven bulky volumes and are a major source for historians.

The Constitution was framed against a backdrop of deep diversity and division: a country of many religions, languages, castes and regions, recovering from colonial rule and torn by the violence of Partition. It had to bind together a diverse people and set out a democratic future.

Timeline: 26 July 1945 Labour government in Britain; December 1945–January 1946 general elections in India; 16 May 1946 Cabinet Mission announces its scheme; 16 August 1946 Direct Action Day; 9 December 1946 Constituent Assembly begins; 13 December 1946 Objectives Resolution; 15 August 1947 independence and partition; 26 November 1949 Constitution adopted; 26 January 1950 Constitution comes into effect.

ex.q: Why are the Constituent Assembly Debates an important historical source?
st: They record arguments of members clause by clause.
They show disagreements, compromises and reasons behind provisions.
They reveal the concerns of different groups in a divided society.
So they help us understand why the Constitution looks as it does.
ex.a: Because they record the arguments and compromises behind every provision, revealing how and why the Constitution was framed.

topics.rl: India celebrates Constitution Day (Samvidhan Divas) on 26 November, the day the Constitution was adopted in 1949, and Republic Day on 26 January.

topics.ch: Part III: Framing the Constitution: The Beginning of a New Era
topics.t: A tumultuous time
topics.h: The years before the Constitution saw a navy mutiny, a national army formed abroad, horrific riots and the partition of the country. The framers wrote with these fresh in their minds.
p: The years before the Constitution were tumultuous. The Quit India Movement of 1942 was the last mass movement against British rule. Subhas Chandra Bose had formed the Indian National Army (INA) to fight the British with armed struggle.

In the spring of 1946, ratings of the Royal Indian Navy (RIN) mutinied in Bombay and other cities, in sympathy with the INA and against British rule. There were strikes and protests by workers and peasants across the country.

There was also bitter communal conflict: the Great Calcutta Killings of August 1946 were followed by riots across north and east India, and then by the violence of Partition in 1947, which uprooted millions and killed hundreds of thousands.

Another major problem was the integration of the princely states. During the Raj, roughly one-third of the subcontinent's area was ruled by Nawabs and Maharajas who owed allegiance to the British Crown. At independence their status was uncertain, and some rulers dreamt of independence.
These experiences of violence and fragmentation shaped the framers' concerns: unity, stability, a strong centre and protection for all citizens.

ex.q: How did the tumultuous events of 1946–47 shape the concerns of the framers?
st: Partition violence made unity and order urgent.
Uncertainty over princely states raised fears of fragmentation.
Mass movements and the RIN mutiny showed popular demands for freedom and justice.
So the framers stressed unity, a strong centre and rights for all.
ex.a: They made the framers concerned with national unity, stability and protecting the rights of all citizens.

topics.rl: The Naval Uprising Memorial in Colaba, Mumbai, unveiled in 2001, honours the RIN ratings who mutinied in February 1946.

topics.ch: Part III: Framing the Constitution: The Beginning of a New Era
topics.t: The making of the Constituent Assembly
topics.h: The Constituent Assembly was not elected by every adult Indian. Its members were chosen by provincial legislatures elected on a limited franchise.
p: The members of the Constituent Assembly were not elected on the basis of universal adult franchise. In the winter of 1945–46 provincial elections were held, and the provincial legislatures then chose the representatives to the Constituent Assembly, following the Cabinet Mission plan.

The Muslim League chose to boycott the Constituent Assembly, preferring to press its demand for Pakistan with a separate constitution. The Socialists too were initially unwilling to join, believing the Assembly was a creation of the British.
As a result, the Congress dominated the Assembly: about 82 per cent of its members were also members of the Congress.

But Congress members did not speak in one voice. They differed on critical issues: some were inspired by socialism, others defended landlordism; some were close to communal parties, others were assertively secular. Discussions were therefore lively and real.
The Constituent Assembly had 300 members. Many debates were influenced by public opinion, as arguments in the Assembly were reported in newspapers and discussed widely.

ex.q: Was the Constituent Assembly representative of all Indians? Give reasons.
st: Its members were indirectly elected by provincial legislatures, not by universal franchise.
The Muslim League boycotted it, and Socialists were initially absent.
The Congress dominated it.
But diverse views within the Congress and public opinion brought a range of voices.
ex.a: Not fully, since it was indirectly elected and some groups stayed away, but diverse opinions within it and public debate made it more representative than its composition suggests.

topics.rl: Today Indian legislatures are elected by universal adult franchise; every citizen aged 18 or above can vote, unlike the limited franchise of 1945–46.

topics.ch: Part III: Framing the Constitution: The Beginning of a New Era
topics.t: The dominant voices and public opinion
topics.h: Six members played particularly important roles, but the Constitution was also shaped by a constitutional advisor, a chief draughtsman, and thousands of ordinary citizens who wrote in!
p: Six members of the Constituent Assembly played especially important roles. Three were Congress leaders: Jawaharlal Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel and Rajendra Prasad.

Nehru moved the crucial Objectives Resolution and the resolution proposing the National Flag as a 'horizontal tricolour of saffron, white and dark green in equal proportion', with a wheel in navy blue at the centre. Patel worked mostly behind the scenes, helping draft reports and reconciling opposing points of view. Rajendra Prasad was the President of the Assembly, steering discussions along constructive lines and making sure all members had a chance to speak.

B.R. Ambedkar, the lawyer and economist, served as Chairman of the Drafting Committee and guided the Draft Constitution through the Assembly. Two other lawyers, K.M. Munshi from Gujarat and Alladi Krishnaswamy Aiyar from Madras, gave crucial inputs.

Two civil servants were important too: B.N. Rau, Constitutional Advisor to the Government of India, who prepared background papers on constitutions of other countries; and S.N. Mukherjee, the chief draughtsman, who could put complex proposals into clear legal language.

Public opinion also mattered. Arguments in the Assembly were reported in newspapers, and proposals were publicly debated. The Assembly invited suggestions from the public, and hundreds of responses were received, from linguistic groups, caste associations, religious organisations and others.

ex.q: What roles did the key members and advisors play in framing the Constitution?
st: Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution and the Flag resolution.
Patel worked behind the scenes and reconciled views.
Prasad presided over the Assembly; Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee.
B.N. Rau advised on other constitutions; S.N. Mukherjee drafted the legal language.
ex.a: Leaders gave direction and resolved differences, while lawyers and civil servants turned ideas into precise constitutional text.

topics.rl: The original Constitution was handwritten in calligraphy by Prem Behari Narain Raizada and illustrated by artists of Santiniketan under Nandalal Bose; it is preserved in the Parliament Library.

topics.ch: Part III: Framing the Constitution: The Beginning of a New Era
topics.t: The Objectives Resolution
topics.h: On 13 December 1946, Nehru stood up and moved a resolution that defined what free India would be: an independent sovereign republic guaranteeing justice, liberty and equality.
p: On 13 December 1946, Jawaharlal Nehru introduced the 'Objectives Resolution' in the Constituent Assembly. It was a momentous resolution that outlined the defining ideals of the Constitution and provided the framework within which constitution-making was to proceed.

It proclaimed India to be an 'Independent Sovereign Republic', guaranteed its citizens justice, equality and freedom, and assured that 'adequate safeguards shall be provided for minorities, backward and tribal areas, and Depressed and Other Backward Classes'.

Nehru placed the Indian effort in a long historical tradition of struggles for liberty. He referred to the American and French Revolutions and the making of their constitutions, and to the Soviet Revolution and its emphasis on economic justice.

He stressed that the Indian Constitution would not merely copy others. The objective was to blend liberal ideas of democracy with the socialist idea of economic justice and re-adapt them within the Indian context.
The ideals of the Objectives Resolution later found expression in the Preamble of the Constitution.

ex.q: What ideals were expressed in the Objectives Resolution?
st: India would be an independent sovereign republic.
Citizens would be guaranteed justice, equality and freedom.
Minorities, backward and tribal areas, and depressed classes would receive safeguards.
Liberal democracy would be blended with economic justice in the Indian context.
ex.a: Sovereignty, republicanism, justice, equality, freedom and safeguards for minorities and weaker sections.

topics.rl: The Preamble, which grew out of the Objectives Resolution, is read aloud in many Indian schools and on Constitution Day each year.

topics.ch: Part III: Framing the Constitution: The Beginning of a New Era
topics.t: The will of the people and Somnath Lahiri's critique
topics.h: A Communist member, Somnath Lahiri, warned that the 'dark hand of British imperialism' still hung over the Assembly. Was the Assembly truly free?
p: Nehru argued that the Constitution would be an expression of the will of the people. The Constituent Assembly was expected to express the aspirations of those who had participated in the movement for independence.
Democracy, equality and justice were ideals that had become intimately associated with social struggles in India since the nineteenth century. The Constitution was meant to embody these aspirations.
Not everyone was convinced. Somnath Lahiri, a Communist member, saw the dark hand of British imperialism hanging over the deliberations of the Assembly.

He pointed out that the Constituent Assembly was British-made: it was working according to the Cabinet Mission plan, and British officials could still influence the outcome. He urged members, and Indians in general, to free themselves fully from the influences of imperial rule.

Lahiri's critique reminds historians that the Assembly met before full independence, under conditions set by the departing colonial power, and that members held very different views about its legitimacy.

ex.q: What was Somnath Lahiri's critique of the Constituent Assembly?
st: The Assembly was created under the Cabinet Mission plan.
So it was British-made and could be influenced by the British.
He saw the 'dark hand of British imperialism' over its deliberations.
He urged Indians to free themselves fully from imperial influence.
ex.a: That the Assembly was a British creation under British influence, so Indians needed to free themselves fully from imperialism.

topics.rl: Debate and dissent remain central to Indian democracy; opposition members in Parliament today play a similar role in questioning the government.

topics.ch: Part III: Framing the Constitution: The Beginning of a New Era
topics.t: Defining rights: the debate on separate electorates
topics.h: In August 1947, B. Pocker Bahadur pleaded for separate electorates for Muslims. Many argued fiercely against it, and by 1949 even some Muslim members had changed their minds.
p: How were the rights of individual citizens and of minority groups to be defined? One fiercely debated question was whether separate electorates should continue.

On 27 August 1947, B. Pocker Bahadur from Madras made a powerful plea for continuing separate electorates. He argued that minorities exist in all lands and cannot be wished away; a political system was needed in which minorities could live in harmony with others and have a meaningful say in governance. Separate electorates, he felt, would ensure Muslims a voice.

Most nationalist leaders opposed this. They argued that separate electorates had divided people, been used by the British to divide and rule, and led to Partition. Sardar Patel called separate electorates a 'poison' that had entered the body politic.

G.B. Pant argued that separate electorates were not only harmful for the nation but also for the minorities, as they would permanently isolate minorities and make them vulnerable. He believed citizens should be loyal to the state and not to their community.

By 1949, most Muslim members of the Assembly agreed that separate electorates were against the interests of the minorities. Begum Aizaz Rasul felt they were self-destructive because they isolated minorities from the majority; Muslims should instead take an active part in the democratic process.

ex.q: Why did G.B. Pant argue that separate electorates were harmful to minorities themselves?
st: Separate electorates would permanently isolate minorities.
Isolated minorities would have less influence in the wider political community.
They would become more vulnerable.
Instead, all citizens should be loyal to the state, not just to their community.
ex.a: Because separate electorates would isolate minorities, reduce their influence and make them vulnerable.

topics.rl: India's Constitution guarantees minorities' cultural and educational rights under Articles 29 and 30, while elections are held through joint electorates.

topics.ch: Part III: Framing the Constitution: The Beginning of a New Era
topics.t: 'We will need much more than this Resolution': the poor and the tribes
topics.h: N.G. Ranga said the real minorities were the poor. Jaipal Singh, captain of India's 1928 Olympic gold-winning hockey team, spoke for India's tribes. Both asked for more than words.
p: N.G. Ranga, a socialist who had been a leader of the peasant movement, welcomed the Objectives Resolution but urged that the term 'minorities' be interpreted in economic terms. For him, the real minorities were the poor and the downtrodden.

Ranga argued that legal rights alone would mean nothing to the poor unless they were provided the conditions to make use of them. He said, 'We will need much more than this Resolution'. Ordinary people, including the adivasis, needed protection and support to escape poverty and exploitation.

Jaipal Singh, a tribal leader who had captained India's hockey team at the 1928 Olympics, spoke eloquently on behalf of the tribes. He said tribes were not a numerical minority, but they needed protection.

He explained that tribal people had been dispossessed of the land they had settled, deprived of their forests and pastures, and forced to move. They were looked down upon as primitive and backward by others.

Jaipal Singh pleaded for measures to protect the tribes and to break the physical and emotional distance between tribal and non-tribal society, including reservation of seats in the legislature, so that tribals could have their voices heard.

ex.q: How did N.G. Ranga and Jaipal Singh widen the meaning of minority rights?
st: Ranga said the real minorities were the poor and downtrodden.
He argued that rights needed conditions to be used, not just legal recognition.
Jaipal Singh said tribes needed protection because they had been dispossessed and looked down upon.
He asked for reserved seats so tribals could be heard.
ex.a: Ranga defined minorities economically, and Jaipal Singh stressed tribal dispossession; both demanded real protection beyond legal words.

topics.rl: The Fifth and Sixth Schedules of the Constitution and reserved seats for Scheduled Tribes in Parliament reflect the concerns raised by Jaipal Singh.

topics.ch: Part III: Framing the Constitution: The Beginning of a New Era
topics.t: 'We were suppressed for thousands of years': the depressed castes
topics.h: J. Nagappa told the Assembly: 'We have been suffering, but we are prepared to suffer no more.' The Constitution responded by abolishing untouchability.
p: Members from the depressed castes stressed that their problems could not be solved through protection and safeguards alone. Their disabilities were caused by the social norms and moral values of caste society, which had used their services and labour while keeping them at a social distance.

J. Nagappa from Madras declared, 'We have been suffering, but we are prepared to suffer no more', and pointed out that the depressed castes were not numerically a minority (20 to 25 per cent of the population). K.J. Khanderkar of the Central Provinces said they had been 'suppressed for thousands of years'. Dakshayani Velayudhan, also from Madras, argued that what was needed was not all kinds of safeguards but the immediate removal of social disabilities.
During the national movement, B.R. Ambedkar had demanded separate electorates for the depressed castes, which Gandhi opposed. In the Constituent Assembly, the solution adopted was different.
It was recommended that untouchability be abolished, Hindu temples be thrown open to all castes, and seats in legislatures and jobs in government offices be reserved for the lowest castes.

Many recognised that not all problems could be solved through law; social attitudes had to change. But the Constitution guaranteed fundamental rights to all, abolished untouchability, and provided reservations as a democratic step towards equality.

ex.q: How did different groups define minority rights in the Constituent Assembly?
st: B. Pocker Bahadur: separate electorates for Muslims.
N.G. Ranga: the poor and downtrodden as real minorities.
Jaipal Singh: protection and reserved seats for tribes.
J. Nagappa, K.J. Khanderkar and Dakshayani Velayudhan: an end to caste oppression and removal of social disabilities.
