ex.a: Some defined minorities by religion, others by economic condition, tribal identity or caste, and each sought different protections.

topics.rl: Article 17 abolishes untouchability, and the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 and the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 make its practice punishable.

topics.ch: Part III: Framing the Constitution: The Beginning of a New Era
topics.t: The powers of the state: three lists and K. Santhanam
topics.h: K. Santhanam warned that if the provinces did not get enough money, they would soon be bankrupt. The debate on Centre versus states began on day one!
p: One of the most intensely debated topics was the respective rights of the Central government and the states.

The Draft Constitution provided three lists of subjects: Union, State and Concurrent. Subjects in the Union List were exclusively for the Centre, those in the State List for the states, and those in the Concurrent List were shared by both.

Many more items were placed under exclusive Union control than in other federations, and the Concurrent List was also longer than desired by the provinces. The Union also had control of minerals and key industries.

K. Santhanam from Madras argued that not only the states but also the Centre needed to be strengthened, and that an over-burdened Centre would not function effectively. He argued that the states needed adequate financial resources to carry out their responsibilities.

Santhanam warned that the proposed allocation of revenues would impoverish the provinces, which would soon be bankrupt and unable to undertake development; he predicted that if this was not addressed, the provinces might even rise in revolt against the Centre. Many members from the provinces echoed his fears.

ex.q: What was K. Santhanam's argument about Centre–state relations?
st: An over-burdened Centre would not work effectively.
States needed adequate financial resources for their responsibilities.
The proposed allocation of revenue would make provinces bankrupt.
So states had to be strengthened, especially financially.
ex.a: That states needed adequate finances and powers, as an over-burdened Centre and poor provinces would harm the federation.

topics.rl: The Finance Commission, set up every five years under Article 280, decides how central tax revenues are shared with the states, addressing concerns like Santhanam's.

topics.ch: Part III: Framing the Constitution: The Beginning of a New Era
topics.t: The case for a strong centre
topics.h: Ambedkar declared he wanted 'a strong and united Centre, much stronger than the Centre we had created under the Government of India Act of 1935'. Why?
p: Many members argued for a strong Centre. The violence of Partition and the fear of further fragmentation strengthened this case.
B.R. Ambedkar declared that he wanted 'a strong and united Centre, much stronger than the Centre we had created under the Government of India Act of 1935'.

Jawaharlal Nehru argued that now that Partition was a settled fact, a weak central authority would be injurious to the interests of the country, as it would be incapable of ensuring peace, coordinating vital matters of common concern and speaking effectively for the whole country internationally.

The Constitution gave the Centre significant powers: the Union List was long; Article 356 gave the Centre the power to take over a state's administration on the recommendation of the Governor; emergency provisions strengthened the Centre; and the Governor was appointed by the Centre.

Revenues were distributed so that some taxes (such as customs duties and company taxes) were held by the Centre, others (such as income tax and excise duties) were shared with the states, and some were assigned to the states. The result was a federal structure with a strong unitary bias.

ex.q: What arguments were made for a strong Centre?
st: Partition violence showed the need for peace and order.
A strong Centre could prevent further fragmentation.
It could coordinate matters of common concern.
It could speak effectively for India internationally.
ex.a: That only a strong Centre could ensure peace, prevent fragmentation, coordinate national matters and represent India abroad.

topics.rl: Debates on federalism continue today in discussions on GST, the Finance Commission and the use of Article 356 by the Centre.

topics.ch: Part III: Framing the Constitution: The Beginning of a New Era
topics.t: The language of the nation: Hindustani, Hindi and a compromise
topics.h: R.V. Dhulekar told the Assembly that those who did not know Hindustani were not worthy to be members and had better leave! The House erupted.
p: By the 1930s the Congress had accepted that Hindustani should be the national language. Mahatma Gandhi felt that everyone should speak in a language that common people could easily understand.

Hindustani, a blend of Hindi and Urdu, was a popular language of a large section of people in north India, enriched by the interaction of diverse cultures. Over time, however, as communal conflicts deepened, Hindi and Urdu were drawn apart, with Hindi becoming more Sanskritised and Urdu more Persianised. Gandhi retained his faith in Hindustani.

R.V. Dhulekar, a Congressman from the United Provinces, made an aggressive plea that Hindi be used as the language of constitution-making. When told that not everyone knew the language, he said that those who did not know Hindustani were not worthy to be members of the Assembly and had better leave. This caused an uproar.
The Language Committee of the Assembly produced a compromise formula. Hindi in the Devanagari script would be the official language, but the transition to Hindi would be gradual.

For the first fifteen years, English would continue to be used for all official purposes. Each province was allowed to choose one of the regional languages for official work within the province. The term 'national language' was replaced by 'official language' to avoid controversy.

ex.q: What was the Language Committee's compromise formula?
st: Hindi in Devanagari script would be the official language.
The transition to Hindi would be gradual.
English would continue for official purposes for fifteen years.
Provinces could choose a regional language for their official work.
ex.a: Hindi in Devanagari as official language with a gradual transition, English for fifteen years, and regional languages for provincial work.

topics.rl: The Eighth Schedule of the Constitution today lists 22 languages, reflecting India's commitment to linguistic diversity.

topics.ch: Part III: Framing the Constitution: The Beginning of a New Era
topics.t: The fear of domination and a Constitution of compromise
topics.h: G. Durgabai had worked to spread Hindustani in the south at Gandhi's call. Yet she warned the Assembly that pushing Hindi aggressively would create fear and opposition.
p: Shrimati G. Durgabai from Madras explained her worries about how the language discussion was developing. She said opposition to Hindi in the south was very strong; people felt it was a fight for their existence. She herself had accepted Gandhi's call to propagate Hindustani in the south, but felt that the aggressive push for Hindi had created fear.

T.A. Ramalingam Chettiar from Madras emphasised that whatever was done had to be done with caution. The cause of Hindi would not be served if it was pushed too aggressively. The fears of people, even if unjustified, had to be allayed, or there would be bitter feelings. There should be give and take, and no question of imposition.
The final arrangement allowed regional languages to be used for official work within provinces, and English continued for a transitional period, so that no group felt dominated.

The language debate, like those on rights and federalism, shows that the Constitution was a product of intense debate, disagreement and compromise. Members listened to opposing views, changed their minds, and found solutions acceptable to most.

The Constitution addressed both the past and the present: it responded to the legacy of colonial rule, caste discrimination and separate electorates, and to the present crisis of Partition violence and diversity, by guaranteeing rights, creating a strong Centre and protecting linguistic and cultural diversity.

ex.q: Why was the language issue divisive, and how was it resolved?
st: Many in the north wanted Hindi as the national language.
Members from the south feared domination and saw it as a fight for existence.
Leaders like Durgabai and Ramalingam Chettiar urged caution and no imposition.
The compromise: Hindi as official language with a gradual transition, English for fifteen years, regional languages in provinces.
ex.a: It was divisive because of fears of domination; it was resolved through compromise that respected linguistic diversity.

topics.rl: The Official Languages Act, 1963 ensured that English could continue alongside Hindi for official purposes after the fifteen-year period, continuing the spirit of compromise.

qa.q: Why is the Indus valley civilisation also called the Harappan civilisation?
qa.a: Harappa was the first site of this civilisation to be discovered
qa.e: Archaeologists often name a culture after the first site where it was found. Harappa was the first site discovered.

qa.q: In archaeology, the term 'culture' refers to:
qa.a: A group of objects of a distinctive style found together in a specific area and period
qa.e: An archaeological culture is identified by a set of artefacts of a distinct style that occur together in a region and time.

qa.q: The Mature Harappan civilisation is dated to approximately:
qa.e: NCERT dates the Mature Harappan phase to c. 2600–1900 BCE.

qa.q: Which evidence suggests a break between the Early Harappan and Mature Harappan phases at some sites?
qa.a: Large-scale burning and abandonment of some settlements
qa.e: At some sites, burnt layers and abandonment mark a break before the mature phase began.

qa.q: Which pair of site and present-day location is INCORRECT?
qa.a: Kalibangan – Afghanistan
qa.e: Kalibangan is in Rajasthan. Shortughai is the Harappan site in Afghanistan.

qa.q: Which of these was a Harappan site located in Afghanistan?
qa.a: Shortughai
qa.e: Shortughai in Afghanistan lay near the source of lapis lazuli. Balakot and Nageshwar are coastal sites; Banawali is in Haryana.

qa.q: Which statement about Early Harappan cultures is correct?
qa.a: They existed in the same region before the mature phase and had distinctive pottery
qa.e: Early Harappan cultures preceded the mature phase; their settlements were generally small, with no large buildings.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Archaeologists use the term 'Harappan culture' for many sites spread across a large area.
Reason (R): Objects such as seals, beads, weights and baked bricks of a distinctive style are found together at these sites.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The shared set of distinctive artefacts is exactly why the sites are grouped as one culture, so R explains A.

qa.q: Which specialists study ancient plant remains such as charred grains?
qa.a: Archaeo-botanists
qa.e: Archaeo-botanists study plant remains; archaeo-zoologists study animal bones.

qa.q: Which grain is relatively RARE among Harappan finds?
qa.a: Rice
qa.e: Wheat, barley, lentil, chickpea and sesame are common; rice is rare.

qa.q: Finds of millets come mainly from Harappan sites in which region?
qa.a: Gujarat
qa.e: NCERT notes millets are found from sites in Gujarat.

qa.q: Which animals' bones show that the Harappans kept domesticated animals?
qa.a: Cattle, sheep, goat, buffalo and pig
qa.e: Bones of cattle, sheep, goat, buffalo and pig indicate domestication.

qa.q: Why are historians unsure about how Harappans got meat of wild animals like deer and boar?
qa.a: It is unclear whether they hunted themselves or obtained meat from hunting communities
qa.e: Wild animal bones are found, but the evidence cannot show who did the hunting.

qa.q: Which of these was NOT among the grains and pulses commonly found at Harappan sites?
qa.a: Maize
qa.e: Maize is a New World crop that reached India much later. Lentil, sesame and barley are Harappan finds.

qa.q: A case: At a Harappan site, an excavator finds charred barley, fish bones and deer bones in one house. What is the BEST inference?
qa.a: The household's food came from varied sources, including farming, fishing and possibly hunting
qa.e: Mixed remains point to a varied diet drawn from different producers.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Rice was the most common grain at Harappan sites.
Reason (R): Charred grains and seeds help archaeologists reconstruct the Harappan diet.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: Rice finds are relatively rare; wheat and barley are common.

qa.q: Where was evidence of a ploughed field found?
qa.a: Kalibangan
qa.e: Kalibangan in Rajasthan has a ploughed field from Early Harappan levels.

qa.q: Traces of canals have been found at which Harappan site?
qa.a: Shortughai
qa.e: Canal traces come from Shortughai in Afghanistan; none in Punjab or Sindh.

qa.q: The Kalibangan field had two sets of furrows at right angles. What does this suggest?
qa.a: Two different crops were grown together
qa.e: Criss-cross furrows suggest two crops grown together in one field.

qa.q: Terracotta models of the plough have been found at:
qa.a: Cholistan and Banawali
qa.e: NCERT mentions terracotta plough models from Cholistan and Banawali.

qa.q: Which site is known for water reservoirs used to store water?
qa.a: Dholavira
qa.e: Dholavira in Gujarat had water reservoirs.

qa.q: Why was irrigation probably needed by Harappan farmers?
qa.a: Most Harappan sites are located in semi-arid lands
qa.e: Semi-arid conditions meant rainfall alone was not reliable.

qa.q: What is the BEST statement about Harappan harvesting tools?
qa.a: They may have used stone blades in wooden handles or metal tools, but this is uncertain
qa.e: Archaeologists are unsure; both stone blades and metal tools are possibilities.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Oxen were probably used for ploughing in Harappan times.
Reason (R): The bull appears on seals and in terracotta sculpture.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Familiarity with the bull, shown on seals and terracotta, is the basis for the inference about oxen ploughing.

qa.q: Mohenjodaro was divided into:
qa.a: A smaller, higher Citadel and a larger, lower Lower Town
qa.e: The Citadel was smaller but higher; the Lower Town was larger but lower.

qa.q: Why does building on platforms suggest that Mohenjodaro was planned?
qa.a: The platforms had to be laid first, so the settlement was planned before construction
qa.e: Platforms acted as foundations; laying them first means the layout was decided in advance.

qa.q: A Harappan brick is 12 cm high. What is its length according to the standard ratio?
qa.a: 48 cm
qa.e: Length = 4 × height = 4 × 12 = 48 cm.

qa.q: A Harappan brick has a length of 28 cm. What is its breadth?
qa.a: 14 cm
qa.e: Breadth is half the length (4:2), so 28 ÷ 2 = 14 cm.

qa.q: Which feature of Harappan drains made cleaning possible?
qa.a: Long channels had sumps at intervals
qa.e: Sumps at intervals allowed drains to be cleaned.

qa.q: Which statement about Harappan drainage is correct?
qa.a: It seems drains were laid out first and houses built along them
qa.e: Planning drains first is suggested; drains are also found in smaller towns like Lothal.

qa.q: Reading a site plan of Mohenjodaro, where would you look for the Great Bath?
qa.a: In the Citadel
qa.e: The Great Bath and the warehouse are in the Citadel.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Harappan bricks of the same ratio were used at sites far apart.
Reason (R): Brick sizes depended on each family's choice.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true: the 4:2:1 ratio is found across settlements. R is false: standardisation points to common planning, not family choice.

qa.q: What suggests that Harappan house-builders cared about privacy?
qa.a: No ground-level windows facing streets, and entrances not giving a direct view inside
qa.e: Blank ground-floor walls and indirect entrances kept interiors private.

qa.q: About how many wells were there at Mohenjodaro, according to archaeologists?
qa.e: NCERT notes Mohenjodaro had about 700 wells.

qa.q: What was used to make the Great Bath watertight?
qa.a: Bricks set on edge with a mortar of gypsum
qa.e: The tank was made watertight by bricks set on edge and gypsum mortar.

qa.q: Why do only the lower portions of the Mohenjodaro warehouse survive?
qa.a: The lower parts were brick; the upper parts were of wood and decayed
qa.e: Brick survives better than wood, which decayed long ago.

qa.q: The Great Bath had steps leading into it on which sides?
qa.a: North and south
qa.e: Two flights of steps on the north and south led into the tank.

qa.q: What was probably the main use of the courtyard in a Harappan house?
qa.a: Cooking and weaving, especially in hot and dry weather
qa.e: Archaeologists suggest courtyards were used for cooking and weaving.

qa.q: A case: Across a lane to the north of the Great Bath was a smaller building with eight bathrooms, four on each side of a corridor. What does this suggest?
qa.a: Bathing was organised and may have had a special purpose linked to the Great Bath
qa.e: Its closeness to the Great Bath and its many bathrooms suggest organised, possibly ritual, bathing.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The Great Bath is believed to have been used for some kind of special ritual bath.
Reason (R): It was a distinctive structure located in the Citadel along with other special public buildings.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Its uniqueness and location in the Citadel are the grounds for the ritual interpretation, so R explains A.

qa.q: Archaeologists classify an artefact as a 'luxury' when it is:
qa.a: Rare and made from costly, non-local materials or with complicated technology
qa.e: Luxuries are rare objects of costly or non-local material or difficult technology.

qa.q: Which of these is a utilitarian object?
qa.a: Quern
qa.e: A quern for grinding grain is a daily-use object; the others are rare or costly.

qa.q: Where are expensive faience vessels mainly found?
qa.a: In large settlements like Mohenjodaro and Harappa
qa.e: They are found in large cities and not in small settlements like Kalibangan.

qa.q: What does the presence of pottery and ornaments in some graves possibly indicate?
qa.a: A belief that these could be used in the afterlife
qa.e: Grave goods may reflect beliefs about life after death.

qa.q: What is the overall conclusion about burials as evidence of inequality among Harappans?
qa.a: Differences existed but were not sharp, as precious things were rarely buried
qa.e: Variation exists (brick-lined pits, some goods) but Harappans did not bury great riches.

qa.q: Gold among Harappans was:
qa.a: Rare and found in hoards, so it was precious
qa.e: Gold was rare and, like today, valued; it is found mostly in hoards.

qa.q: In a burial at Harappa, a man was found with an ornament of three shell rings, a jasper bead and hundreds of micro beads. What does this tell us?
qa.a: Ornaments were buried with men as well as women
qa.e: This burial shows men too were buried with jewellery.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Faience pots are considered luxury items.
Reason (R): Faience was difficult to make, and such pots are found mainly in large cities.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Difficult technology and limited distribution are exactly why faience pots are classed as luxuries.

qa.q: Chanhudaro is known as a settlement:
qa.a: Almost exclusively devoted to craft production
qa.e: Chanhudaro was a small site focused on crafts such as bead-making and seal-making.

qa.q: How was the red colour of carnelian beads obtained?
qa.a: By firing the yellowish raw material and beads at various stages
qa.e: Heating changes the yellowish stone to red.

qa.q: Which of these is the BEST evidence that an object was made at a site?
qa.a: Waste material and unfinished objects
qa.e: Waste and unfinished items show manufacture took place there.

qa.q: Which crafts were practised at Chanhudaro?
qa.a: Bead-making, shell-cutting, metal-working, seal-making and weight-making
qa.e: NCERT lists all five crafts at Chanhudaro.

qa.q: Which material was NOT used to make Harappan beads?
qa.a: Glass
qa.e: Harappans used faience, a glass-like paste, but not true glass. Carnelian and steatite were major bead materials.

qa.q: Specialised drills for bead-making have been found at:
qa.a: Chanhudaro, Lothal and Dholavira
qa.e: Drills come from Chanhudaro, Lothal and, more recently, Dholavira.

qa.q: What is the correct sequence for shaping a stone bead?
qa.a: Chip into rough shape → flake into final form → grind, polish and drill
qa.e: Rough chipping comes first, then fine flaking, then finishing.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Archaeologists use waste material to identify craft production centres.
Reason (R): Waste shows that raw material was worked at that place.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Leftover waste is direct evidence of work done on site, so R explains A.

qa.q: The Khetri region of Rajasthan was an important source of:
qa.a: Copper
qa.e: Expeditions went to Khetri for copper.

qa.q: Harappans obtained gold mainly through expeditions to:
qa.a: South India
qa.e: NCERT mentions expeditions to South India for gold.

qa.q: Which culture in the Khetri area had distinctive non-Harappan pottery and an unusual wealth of copper objects?
qa.a: Ganeshwar-Jodhpura culture
qa.e: The Ganeshwar-Jodhpura culture may have supplied copper to Harappans.

qa.q: Which pair of settlement and raw material is correctly matched?
qa.a: Shortughai – lapis lazuli
qa.e: Shortughai was near lapis lazuli. Nageshwar and Balakot were shell centres; Khetri gave copper.

qa.q: Lothal was located near sources of:
qa.a: Carnelian, steatite and metal
qa.e: Lothal was near carnelian (Bharuch), steatite and metal sources.

qa.q: Which objects were made at Nageshwar and Balakot?
qa.a: Shell bangles, ladles and inlay
qa.e: These coastal sites specialised in shell objects.

qa.q: What does a terracotta toy model of a bullock cart suggest?
qa.a: Bullock carts were an important means of overland transport
qa.e: Such models, plus the needs of trade, suggest overland transport by bullock carts.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Harappans set up a settlement at Shortughai.
Reason (R): Shortughai lay near the copper mines of Khetri.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: Shortughai, in Afghanistan, was near lapis lazuli sources; Khetri copper is in Rajasthan.

qa.q: Chemical analysis showing traces of nickel in both Omani copper and Harappan artefacts suggests:
qa.a: Harappan copper may have come from Oman
qa.e: A shared trace element points to a common source for the copper.

qa.q: In Mesopotamian texts, 'Magan' is perhaps:
qa.a: Oman
qa.e: Magan is perhaps Oman; Dilmun is probably Bahrain; Meluhha possibly the Harappan region.

qa.q: Which products of Meluhha are mentioned in Mesopotamian texts?
qa.a: Carnelian, lapis lazuli, copper, gold and varieties of wood
qa.e: These goods match Harappan resources.

qa.q: Some scholars identify the 'haja-bird' of Meluhha mentioned in a Mesopotamian myth with the:
qa.a: Peacock
qa.e: The haja-bird has been suggested to be the peacock.

qa.q: Which evidence points to sea trade between the Harappans and the Gulf region?
qa.a: Persian Gulf seals and depictions of ships and boats on seals
qa.e: Gulf seals and ship depictions suggest sea routes.

qa.q: Mesopotamian texts mentioning Dilmun, Magan and Meluhha date roughly from:
qa.a: The mid-third millennium BCE
qa.e: These texts date from about the mid-third millennium BCE, the time of Mature Harappan cities.

qa.q: Dilmun is probably the island of:
qa.a: Bahrain
qa.e: Dilmun is probably Bahrain in the Persian Gulf.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Meluhha is possibly the Harappan region.
Reason (R): Meluhha is described as a land of seafarers and as the source of carnelian, lapis lazuli and timber.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The described goods and seafaring match the Harappan region; this is the basis of the identification.

qa.q: What was the main purpose of Harappan seals and sealings?
qa.a: To facilitate long-distance communication and secure goods
qa.e: Sealings on sacks showed the goods were untouched and identified the sender.

qa.q: Harappan seals were usually made of:
qa.a: Steatite
qa.e: The typical Harappan seal is made of steatite.

qa.q: Why do scholars think the Harappan script was NOT alphabetic?
qa.a: It has too many signs, between 375 and 400
qa.e: An alphabet has a small number of signs; 375–400 is far too many.

qa.q: How do we know the Harappan script was written from right to left?
qa.a: Some seals show wider spacing on the right and cramped signs on the left
qa.e: The writer began on the right with room to spare and ran out of space on the left.

qa.q: Harappan weights in the lower range followed which series?
qa.e: Lower denominations were binary, doubling each time; higher ones were decimal.

qa.q: A Harappan weight series doubles each time: 1, 2, 4, 8, … What is the weight just after 32?
qa.e: Doubling 32 gives 64.

qa.q: Which statement about Harappan weights is INCORRECT?
qa.a: They carried inscribed numbers on every face
qa.e: Harappan weights had no markings.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The Harappan script has been deciphered with the help of a bilingual inscription.
Reason (R): The Harappan script was written from right to left.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: The script is still undeciphered; its right-to-left direction is known from the spacing of signs.

qa.q: Why was a Harappan stone statue labelled 'priest-king'?
qa.a: Archaeologists were familiar with Mesopotamian history and its priest-kings
qa.e: The label came from comparison with Mesopotamia, not from Harappan evidence.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT cited as evidence of complex decision-making among Harappans?
qa.a: Coins issued by a Harappan king
qa.e: There were no Harappan coins. The others show coordinated decisions.

qa.q: Why is the single-state theory considered the most plausible?
qa.a: It is unlikely that entire communities collectively made and implemented such complex decisions
qa.e: The uniformity and planning point to some central authority.

qa.q: The 'palace' at Mohenjodaro is doubtful mainly because:
qa.a: No spectacular finds were associated with it
qa.e: A building labelled a palace yielded no spectacular finds.

qa.q: Which theory suggests there was one ruler for Mohenjodaro, another for Harappa, and so on?
qa.a: Several rulers
qa.e: This is the 'several rulers' theory.

qa.q: Standard-ratio bricks were found across Harappan sites even though they were not produced in a single centre. This suggests:
qa.a: A common authority enforcing standards
qa.e: Uniform standards from many production places suggest coordinated control.

qa.q: Why can't historians say whether Harappan ritual specialists held political power?
qa.a: Harappan ritual practices are not yet understood
qa.e: Without understanding the rituals, we cannot know whether those performing them also ruled.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The label 'priest-king' does not prove that Harappan priests were also rulers.
Reason (R): The label was borrowed from Mesopotamian history, and Harappan ritual practices are not yet understood.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Because the label comes from Mesopotamia and Harappan rituals are not understood, the statue cannot prove priestly rule. R explains A.

qa.q: By about which date had most Mature Harappan sites in regions like Cholistan been abandoned?
qa.a: c. 1800 BCE
qa.e: Most mature sites were abandoned by c. 1800 BCE.

qa.q: Which regions saw an expansion of new settlements as Harappan cities declined?
qa.a: Gujarat, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh
qa.e: Population expanded into Gujarat, Haryana and western UP.

qa.q: Which of these did NOT disappear in the Late Harappan phase?
qa.a: Agriculture and a rural way of life
qa.e: Life became rural; seals, writing and weights vanished.

qa.q: Which is NOT among the suggested causes for the Harappan decline?
qa.a: Invasion by the Mughals
qa.e: The Mughals came over 3,000 years later. The others are suggested causes.

qa.q: Why do some historians prefer the 'collapse of a unifying element' explanation?
qa.a: Seals, script, distinctive beads and pottery disappeared everywhere, not only at some sites
qa.e: A civilisation-wide loss of standard items suggests the loss of a central authority, perhaps the state.

qa.q: 'Late Harappan' or 'successor' cultures are characterised by:
qa.a: A rural way of life without writing, seals and long-distance trade
qa.e: Successor cultures were rural and lost these distinctive features.

qa.q: A case: At a site occupied after 1900 BCE, excavators find no seals, no standard weights and poorly built houses. Which phase does this most likely belong to?
qa.a: Late Harappan
qa.e: Loss of seals and weights and poorer construction mark Late Harappan levels.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Climatic change cannot by itself explain the end of the entire Harappan civilisation.
Reason (R): Such causes may account for the decline of some settlements but not the collapse of the whole civilisation.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Local causes do not explain a civilisation-wide collapse; R explains A.

qa.q: Who was the first Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India?
qa.a: Alexander Cunningham
qa.e: Cunningham was the first DG of the ASI.

qa.q: Cunningham used the accounts of which travellers to locate early settlements?
qa.a: Chinese Buddhist pilgrims
qa.e: He relied on Chinese Buddhist pilgrims who visited between the 4th and 7th centuries CE.

qa.q: Why did Cunningham fail to recognise the importance of Harappa?
qa.a: Harappan objects did not fit his framework of Early Historic Indian history
qa.e: He tried to place Harappan finds in the Early Historic period he knew, and could not.

qa.q: In which year did John Marshall announce the discovery of a new civilisation in the Indus valley?
qa.e: Marshall made the announcement in 1924.

qa.q: Who found seals at Mohenjodaro similar to those at Harappa?
qa.a: R.D. Banerji
qa.e: R.D. Banerji found seals at Mohenjodaro; Daya Ram Sahni found them at Harappa.

qa.q: What was the main problem with Marshall's excavation method?
qa.a: He dug in uniform horizontal units and ignored stratigraphy
qa.e: Ignoring layers meant artefacts from different periods were grouped together.

qa.q: Which archaeologist began excavations at Dholavira in 1990?
qa.a: R.S. Bisht
qa.e: R.S. Bisht began excavating Dholavira in 1990.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): John Marshall announced the discovery of a new civilisation in 1924.
Reason (R): Marshall carefully followed the stratigraphy of the mound.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: Marshall ignored stratigraphy; it was Wheeler who followed it.

qa.q: After Partition, why did Indian archaeologists explore regions like Kutch, Punjab and Haryana?
qa.a: The major sites Harappa and Mohenjodaro were now in Pakistan
qa.e: With the main sites in Pakistan, Indian archaeologists searched for sites within India.

qa.q: Which identification has been criticised because it depends on later religious traditions?
qa.a: The 'proto-Shiva' seal
qa.e: The proto-Shiva label uses later ideas of Shiva to interpret a Harappan image.

qa.q: Why are some terracotta female figurines called 'mother goddesses'?
qa.a: They are heavily jewelled with elaborate head-dresses and are thought to be objects of worship
qa.e: The label is an interpretation based on their appearance; it is not proven.

qa.q: What is the main difficulty in classifying Harappan artefacts by function?
qa.a: Archaeologists must infer use indirectly, by comparison with present-day objects or from context
qa.e: Function is usually inferred indirectly, which creates uncertainty.

qa.q: Fire altars that may suggest ritual practice have been reported at:
qa.a: Kalibangan and Lothal
qa.e: NCERT mentions fire altars at Kalibangan and Lothal.

qa.q: Which new technique has helped answer questions about Harappan diet and environment?
qa.a: Studies of plant and animal remains
qa.e: Archaeo-botany and archaeo-zoology reveal diet and environment.

qa.q: A case: An excavation report says a stone object was found inside a house next to a hearth, worn smooth on one face. What should an archaeologist do first?
qa.a: Use the context and wear pattern, and compare with known objects like querns, before deciding its function
qa.e: Context and comparison guide interpretation; jumping to a ritual label is unsafe.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Using later texts to interpret Harappan religion has limits.
Reason (R): The Rigveda's Rudra is not depicted as Pashupati or a yogi, unlike the 'proto-Shiva' seal.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The mismatch between the earlier text and the seal shows why projecting later traditions backwards is risky.

qa.q: In which year did James Prinsep decipher Asokan Brahmi?
qa.e: Prinsep achieved the decipherment in 1838.

qa.q: Which two scripts did James Prinsep decipher?
qa.a: Brahmi and Kharosthi
qa.e: Prinsep deciphered Brahmi and Kharosthi, the scripts of the earliest inscriptions and coins.

qa.q: What does the title 'Piyadassi' mean?
qa.a: Pleasant to behold
qa.e: Piyadassi means 'pleasant to behold'; Devanampiya means 'beloved of the gods'.

qa.q: 'Devanampiya', used for Asoka, means:
qa.a: Beloved of the gods
qa.e: Devanampiya is 'beloved of the gods'.

qa.q: Which is the BEST definition of an inscription?
qa.a: Writing engraved on hard surfaces like stone, metal or pottery
qa.e: Inscriptions are engraved on durable surfaces, unlike manuscripts.

qa.q: James Prinsep worked as:
qa.a: An officer in the mint of the East India Company
qa.e: Prinsep was a mint officer, which explains his interest in coins.

qa.q: Why was the decipherment of Brahmi so important for historians?
qa.a: It allowed rulers named in inscriptions and coins to be linked with dynasties in texts, giving an outline of political history
qa.e: Readable inscriptions gave a new direction to political history.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Inscriptions are useful permanent records for historians.
Reason (R): Inscriptions record only what was important to ordinary farmers.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: inscriptions mostly record the views and deeds of those who commissioned them, not farmers' lives.

qa.q: How many mahajanapadas are mentioned in early Buddhist and Jaina texts?
qa.e: The texts list sixteen mahajanapadas, though names vary between lists.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT listed among the frequently mentioned mahajanapadas?
qa.a: Kalinga
qa.e: Vajji, Magadha, Koshala, Kuru, Panchala, Gandhara and Avanti occur often; Kalinga is famous from Asoka's war, not this core list.

qa.q: Ganas or sanghas were:
qa.a: Oligarchies where power was shared by a number of men
qa.e: In ganas or sanghas, many men, called rajas, shared power.

qa.q: Which development is NOT associated with the sixth century BCE turning point?
qa.a: Construction of Harappan cities
qa.e: Harappan cities belong to c. 2600–1900 BCE. Iron, coins and new philosophies mark the sixth century BCE.

qa.q: According to the Dharmasutras, rulers were ideally:
qa.a: Kshatriyas
qa.e: The Dharmasutras said rulers should ideally be Kshatriyas.

qa.q: From whom were rulers advised to collect taxes and tribute?
qa.a: Cultivators, traders and artisans
qa.e: Dharmasutras advised collecting taxes and tribute from cultivators, traders and artisans.

qa.q: In the Vajji sangha, the rajas probably:
qa.a: Controlled resources such as land collectively
qa.e: The rajas of the Vajji sangha probably controlled land collectively.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Mahajanapadas maintained fortified capitals, armies and bureaucracies.
Reason (R): They required resources, which were collected as taxes and tribute.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Fortified cities and armies needed resources, which explains the tax and tribute system; R explains A.

qa.q: In which present-day state was Magadha located?
qa.a: Bihar
qa.e: Magadha lay in present-day Bihar.

qa.q: Which is NOT a factor modern historians give for Magadha's power?
qa.a: Control of Roman trade ports
qa.e: Agriculture, iron, elephants and the Ganga are the factors. Roman trade belongs to a later period.

qa.q: Rajagaha is the Prakrit name for:
qa.a: Rajgir
qa.e: Rajagaha is present-day Rajgir in Bihar.

qa.q: In which century did Magadha's capital shift to Pataliputra?
qa.a: Fourth century BCE
qa.e: The capital shifted to Pataliputra in the fourth century BCE.

qa.q: Early Buddhist and Jaina writers explained Magadha's rise mainly through:
qa.a: The policies of ambitious individuals such as Bimbisara, Ajatasattu and Mahapadma Nanda
qa.e: These writers credited ambitious and ruthless rulers.

qa.q: Why were elephants important for Magadha?
qa.a: They were an important part of the army
qa.e: Forest elephants strengthened Magadha's army.

qa.q: Iron mines that benefited Magadha were located in present-day:
qa.a: Jharkhand
qa.e: Accessible iron mines in present-day Jharkhand supplied tools and weapons.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Pataliputra became a more suitable capital than Rajagaha for an expanding Magadha.
Reason (R): Pataliputra was a fortified settlement surrounded by hills.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true: Pataliputra commanded routes along the Ganga. R is false: Rajagaha, not Pataliputra, was among hills.

qa.q: Who founded the Mauryan empire around 321 BCE?
qa.a: Chandragupta Maurya
qa.e: Chandragupta Maurya founded the empire c. 321 BCE.

qa.q: Megasthenes was:
qa.a: A Greek ambassador to the court of Chandragupta Maurya
qa.e: Megasthenes came as a Greek ambassador.

qa.q: Parts of the Arthashastra were probably composed by:
qa.a: Kautilya or Chanakya
qa.e: Kautilya or Chanakya, traditionally Chandragupta's minister.

qa.q: Asoka conquered Kalinga, which is present-day:
qa.a: Coastal Odisha
qa.e: Kalinga corresponds to coastal Odisha.

qa.q: Asoka was Chandragupta Maurya's:
qa.a: Grandson
qa.e: Asoka was the grandson of Chandragupta.

qa.q: The Mauryan empire under Chandragupta extended in the north-west as far as:
qa.a: Afghanistan and Baluchistan
qa.e: It reached Afghanistan and Baluchistan.

qa.q: Which source is often regarded as among the MOST valuable for the Mauryas?
qa.a: The inscriptions of Asoka on rocks and pillars
qa.e: Asokan inscriptions are first-hand records issued by the ruler.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Megasthenes' account survives complete in its original form.
Reason (R): Megasthenes was a Greek ambassador at the court of Chandragupta Maurya.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: His account survives only in fragments.

qa.q: Which was the capital of the Mauryan empire?
qa.a: Pataliputra
qa.e: Pataliputra was the capital; the other three were provincial centres.

qa.q: Which is NOT one of the five major Mauryan political centres?
qa.a: Mathura
qa.e: The five were Pataliputra, Taxila, Ujjayini, Tosali and Suvarnagiri.

qa.q: Suvarnagiri was probably important because it was near:
qa.a: The gold mines of Karnataka
qa.e: Suvarnagiri means 'golden mountain' and was near Karnataka's gold mines.

qa.q: How many subcommittees did Megasthenes describe for military coordination?
qa.e: There were six subcommittees.

qa.q: Which subcommittee arranged bullock carts, food for soldiers and fodder for animals?
qa.a: Transport and provisions
qa.e: The second subcommittee handled transport and provisions.

qa.q: Where was Mauryan administrative control strongest?
qa.a: Around the capital and the provincial centres
qa.e: Control was strongest near the capital and provincial centres; it was not uniform.

qa.q: Taxila and Ujjayini were important mainly because they:
qa.a: Lay on important long-distance trade routes
qa.e: Both were on major trade routes.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Suvarnagiri was an important Mauryan provincial centre.
Reason (R): Suvarnagiri was the capital of the Mauryan empire.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: Pataliputra was the capital; Suvarnagiri was a provincial centre near the gold mines of Karnataka.

qa.q: According to Asoka's edict, about how many people were killed in the Kalinga war?
qa.e: About 1,00,000 were killed and 1,50,000 deported, according to Rock Edict XIII.

qa.q: Which of these was a principle of Asoka's dhamma?
qa.a: Treating slaves and servants kindly
qa.e: Kindness to slaves and servants was part of dhamma.

qa.q: Who were the dhamma mahamatta?
qa.a: Special officers appointed to spread dhamma
qa.e: Asoka appointed them to teach and spread dhamma.

qa.q: Asoka's dhamma included respect for:
qa.a: Religions and traditions other than one's own
qa.e: Tolerance of other religions and traditions was central.

qa.q: Which is a limitation of the Mauryan empire noted by historians?
qa.a: It lasted only about 150 years and control was uneven
qa.e: Its duration was short and its control was strongest only near centres.

qa.q: In which year of his reign did Asoka conquer Kalinga, according to his edict?
qa.e: The edict says Kalinga was conquered when Asoka had ruled for eight years.

qa.q: Why did 19th-century historians see the Mauryan empire as a high point?
qa.a: Its stone sculpture and inscriptions seemed remarkable for the time
qa.e: The sculpture and inscriptions impressed them.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Asoka propagated dhamma among his subjects.
Reason (R): He believed dhamma would ensure the well-being of people in this world and the next.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: His belief in dhamma's value for people's well-being explains why he spread it.

qa.q: Which Tamil texts describe chiefs and how they acquired and distributed resources?
qa.a: Sangam texts
qa.e: Sangam poems describe the chiefs of Tamilakam.

qa.q: Which statement about chiefs is correct?
qa.a: They received gifts from subordinates and generally had no regular officials or army
qa.e: Chiefs relied on gifts and kin and usually lacked officials and armies.

qa.q: The Kushana title 'devaputra' means:
qa.a: Son of god
qa.e: Devaputra means 'son of god'.

qa.q: Colossal statues of Kushana rulers were found in a shrine at:
qa.a: Mat near Mathura
qa.e: They were found at Mat near Mathura in Uttar Pradesh.

qa.q: The Kushana title 'devaputra' may have been inspired by:
qa.a: Chinese rulers who called themselves sons of heaven
qa.e: Historians suggest a Chinese inspiration.

qa.q: Which dynasty ruled over parts of western and central India?
qa.a: Satavahanas
qa.e: The Satavahanas ruled parts of western and central India.

qa.q: Which was NOT among the chiefdoms of Tamilakam?
qa.a: Kushanas
qa.e: The Kushanas ruled from Central Asia to north-west India.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Kushana rulers adopted the title devaputra.
Reason (R): Tamil chiefs received gifts rather than collecting regular taxes.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but the practice of Tamil chiefs has nothing to do with the Kushana title.

qa.q: Who composed the Prayaga Prashasti?
qa.a: Harishena
qa.e: Harishena, court poet of Samudragupta, composed it.

qa.q: The Prayaga Prashasti praises which ruler?
qa.a: Samudragupta
qa.e: It praises Samudragupta, arguably the most powerful Gupta ruler.

qa.q: Samantas were:
qa.a: Men who maintained themselves through local resources and offered homage and military support to rulers
qa.e: Samantas were subordinate powers who supported the ruler.

qa.q: Why must historians read prashastis carefully?
qa.a: They are poetic praise meant to glorify the king and may not be literally true
qa.e: Prashastis exaggerate; facts must be cross-checked.

qa.q: The Prayaga Prashasti was composed in which language?
qa.a: Sanskrit
qa.e: It was composed in Sanskrit.

qa.q: Which statement about the relationship between samantas and kings is correct?
qa.a: Powerful samantas could become kings, and weak kings could become subordinate
qa.e: The balance of power could shift either way.

qa.q: The Prayaga Prashasti is also known as the:
qa.a: Allahabad Pillar Inscription
qa.e: Prayaga is the old name of Allahabad (Prayagraj).

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Prashastis are an important source for Gupta history.
Reason (R): Prashastis give a balanced account of a king's failures as well as successes.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: prashastis praise the king and rarely mention failures.

qa.q: The Jatakas were written in which language?
qa.a: Pali
qa.e: The Jatakas were written in Pali around the middle of the first millennium CE.

qa.q: What does the Gandatindu Jataka describe?
qa.a: The suffering of the subjects of a wicked king
qa.e: It narrates how all kinds of subjects suffered under a wicked king.

qa.q: Paddy transplantation means:
qa.a: Raising saplings in a nursery and then planting them in waterlogged fields
qa.e: Seedlings are raised and transplanted, which increases yields.

qa.q: In which regions did the iron ploughshare NOT become common until the twentieth century?
qa.a: Semi-arid parts of Punjab and Rajasthan
qa.e: In these semi-arid areas, the iron ploughshare arrived only in the twentieth century.

qa.q: Why did people adopt new strategies to increase agricultural production?
qa.a: Partly to meet the growing demand for taxes
qa.e: Growing tax demands encouraged more production.

qa.q: Which statement about irrigation in this period is correct?
qa.a: Wells and tanks were used, and canals less commonly; communities and individuals both organised works
qa.e: Wells, tanks and some canals were built by communities and individuals.

qa.q: A case: In a story, villagers abandon their homes and move to the forest after the king raises taxes. What does this suggest?
qa.a: Heavy taxation caused tension between kings and subjects, and flight was one form of resistance
qa.e: Flight to the forest shows resistance to oppressive taxes.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Paddy transplantation increased production in the Ganga valley.
Reason (R): Paddy transplantation required very little labour.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true: yields rose sharply. R is false: transplantation is very labour-intensive, back-breaking work.

qa.q: In Tamil Sangam texts, 'uzhavar' refers to:
qa.a: Ploughmen
qa.e: Uzhavar were ploughmen; vellalar were landowners; adimai were slaves.

qa.q: Which term in Pali texts referred to the owner, master or head of a household?
qa.a: Gahapati
qa.e: The gahapati was the head of a household.

qa.q: Agrahara land was:
qa.a: Land granted to Brahmanas, usually exempt from land revenue
qa.e: Agraharas were granted to Brahmanas, usually free of revenue.

qa.q: Prabhavati Gupta was the daughter of:
qa.a: Chandragupta II
qa.e: She was the daughter of Chandragupta II, one of the most important Gupta rulers.

qa.q: Prabhavati Gupta married into which family?
qa.a: Vakataka
qa.e: She married into the Vakatakas, an important power in the Deccan.

qa.q: Most land grant inscriptions were recorded on:
qa.a: Copper plates
qa.e: Some were on stone, but most were on copper plates.

qa.q: Which view sees land grants as a sign of weakening royal power?
qa.a: Kings were losing control over samantas and tried to win allies by granting land
qa.e: This interpretation sees grants as concessions by weakened kings.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Agraharas were usually exempt from land revenue.
Reason (R): Most land grants were recorded on copper plates.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but the material of the record does not explain the revenue exemption.

qa.q: Northern Black Polished Ware (NBPW) refers to:
qa.a: Fine pottery bowls and dishes with a glossy finish
qa.e: NBPW is a fine glossy pottery, probably used by the rich.

qa.q: Shrenis were:
qa.a: Guilds of craft producers and merchants
qa.e: Shrenis procured raw material, regulated production and marketed goods.

qa.q: Which town was near the coast, from where sea routes began?
qa.a: Puhar
qa.e: Puhar was a coastal town.

qa.q: Donative inscriptions from about the second century BCE record:
qa.a: Gifts made to religious institutions by people of many occupations
qa.e: They record gifts by washing folk, weavers, goldsmiths, merchants and others.

qa.q: Which commodity was in especially high demand in the Roman Empire?
qa.a: Pepper
qa.e: Spices, especially pepper, were in demand in Rome.

qa.q: Which of these was NOT a function of the shrenis?
qa.a: Issuing land grants to Brahmanas
qa.e: Land grants were made by rulers, not guilds.

qa.q: Ujjayini developed mainly because it lay:
qa.a: Along land routes
qa.e: Ujjayini lay along important land routes.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Donative inscriptions are valuable for the social history of early cities.
Reason (R): They name many ordinary occupations such as weavers, potters and washing folk.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: By naming ordinary donors and their occupations, they reveal urban society, so R explains A.

qa.q: Which rulers issued the first coins bearing the names and images of rulers?
qa.a: Indo-Greeks
qa.e: The Indo-Greeks were the first to put rulers' names and images on coins.

qa.q: The first gold coins in the subcontinent were issued by:
qa.a: The Kushanas
qa.e: The Kushanas issued the first gold coins c. first century CE.

qa.q: Kushana gold coins were virtually identical in weight to those of:
qa.a: Roman emperors and Parthian rulers of Iran
qa.e: This shows links with wider trade networks.

qa.q: Punch-marked coins were made mainly of:
qa.a: Silver and copper
qa.e: Punch-marked coins were of silver and copper.

qa.q: The Yaudheyas, who issued several thousand copper coins, belonged to which region?
qa.a: Punjab and Haryana
qa.e: The Yaudheyas were a tribal republic of Punjab and Haryana.

qa.q: Roman coin hoards found in south India suggest:
qa.a: Trade links between south India and the Roman world
qa.e: Hoards point to active trade with Rome.

qa.q: Which is one explanation offered for the decline in gold coin finds from the sixth century CE?
qa.a: Decline of long-distance trade after the collapse of the Western Roman Empire
qa.e: Some historians link it to declining long-distance trade; others debate this.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The Mauryas issued the first gold coins in the subcontinent.
Reason (R): Punch-marked coins were made of silver and copper.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: The Kushanas issued the first gold coins, c. first century CE.

qa.q: How did scholars decipher Brahmi?
qa.a: By working backwards from Bengali and Devanagari manuscripts, comparing letters with older specimens
qa.e: Brahmi was traced back from later scripts; Kharosthi was read with bilingual coins.

qa.q: Kharosthi was deciphered with the help of:
qa.a: Indo-Greek coins with legends in Greek and Kharosthi
qa.e: Bilingual Indo-Greek coins provided the key.

qa.q: The earliest inscriptions in India were mostly in which language?
qa.a: Prakrit
qa.e: Early scholars assumed Sanskrit, but the earliest inscriptions were in Prakrit.

qa.q: In which year was the Asiatic Society (Bengal) founded?
qa.e: It was founded in 1784.

qa.q: Who published 'Indian Epigraphy' and 'Indian Epigraphical Glossary' in 1965–66?
qa.a: D.C. Sircar
qa.e: D.C. Sircar published these works.

qa.q: Why do epigraphists add words in brackets when translating an inscription?
qa.a: To make the meaning clear where words are implied or missing
qa.e: Bracketed words clarify meaning, but they are interpretations by scholars.

qa.q: In which year was the first issue of Epigraphia Indica published?
qa.e: Epigraphia Indica began in 1888.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Bilingual coins made it possible to decipher Kharosthi.
Reason (R): Scholars could read the Greek legend and match it to the Kharosthi legend of the same name.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Matching a known Greek name with its Kharosthi version revealed the sign values; R explains A.

qa.q: Which of these is a technical limitation of inscriptional evidence?
qa.a: Letters may be faintly engraved or missing
qa.e: Faint or missing letters make reconstruction uncertain.

qa.q: Why do inscriptions tell us little about the joys and sorrows of daily life?
qa.a: They mostly record what those who commissioned them considered important
qa.e: Inscriptions reflect the concerns of their patrons, usually rulers and elites.

qa.q: Which statement about the number of inscriptions is correct?
qa.a: Several thousand have been found, but not all are deciphered, published or translated
qa.e: Many are still unpublished, and many more have been lost.

qa.q: Alexander of Macedon invaded the north-west in about:
qa.e: Alexander's invasion was c. 327–325 BCE.

qa.q: Approximately when did the Mauryan empire end?
qa.a: c. 185 BCE
qa.e: The Mauryan empire ended around 185 BCE.

qa.q: To reconstruct the lives of ordinary people, historians should:
qa.a: Combine inscriptions, texts like Jatakas, coins and archaeological evidence
qa.e: Ordinary lives are best reconstructed by combining sources.

qa.q: A case: An inscription has a gap where three letters are missing, and the epigraphist fills them with a likely word in brackets. What should a reader remember?
qa.a: The bracketed word is the scholar's reconstruction, not certain
qa.e: Reconstructions are informed guesses and may be uncertain.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Historians cannot rely on inscriptions alone to understand early Indian society.
Reason (R): Inscriptions mostly reflect the perspective of those who commissioned them and leave out much of daily life.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Because of these gaps and biases, other sources are needed; R explains A.

qa.q: Who led the project to prepare the Critical Edition of the Mahabharata that began in 1919?
qa.a: V.S. Sukthankar
qa.e: The noted Sanskritist V.S. Sukthankar led the project.

qa.q: How many years did the Critical Edition project take to complete?
qa.e: It took 47 years.

qa.q: The Critical Edition was prepared by:
qa.a: Comparing Sanskrit manuscripts from across the country and selecting verses common to most
qa.e: Scholars compared many manuscripts and selected common verses.

qa.q: What did the regional variations in Mahabharata manuscripts reveal?
qa.a: Complex processes of transmission of the text over time and space
qa.e: Variations show how the text was transmitted and reshaped.

qa.q: Why are texts like the Dharmasutras described as 'normative'?
qa.a: They lay down norms of how society ought to be
qa.e: Normative texts prescribe ideals; actual practice could differ.

qa.q: Historians use the Mahabharata mainly as a source for the social history of which period?
qa.a: c. 600 BCE–600 CE
qa.e: The chapter studies c. 600 BCE–600 CE.

qa.q: The published Critical Edition runs into over how many pages?
qa.e: It runs to over 13,000 pages in several volumes.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Historians must read Dharmashastras with caution when reconstructing social life.
Reason (R): These texts were normative and were composed largely from a Brahmanical perspective.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Because the texts prescribe ideals from one perspective, historians must check them against other evidence.

qa.q: In Sanskrit texts, 'jnati' refers to:
qa.a: The larger network of kinfolk
qa.e: Kula is family, jnati is the larger kin network, vamsha is lineage.

qa.q: Patriliny means:
qa.a: Descent traced from father to son, grandson and so on
qa.e: Patriliny traces descent through the male line.

qa.q: The conflict between the Kauravas and the Pandavas was mainly over:
qa.a: Land and power
qa.e: It was a feud within one family over land and power.

qa.q: To which lineage did the Kauravas and Pandavas belong?
qa.a: Kuru
qa.e: Both belonged to the Kuru lineage.

qa.q: Under patriliny, who could claim the resources of a father after his death?
qa.a: His sons
qa.e: Sons inherited under the patrilineal ideal.

qa.q: Which is an exception to patrilineal succession mentioned for early India?
qa.a: Prabhavati Gupta exercising power
qa.e: Women like Prabhavati Gupta wielding power were very exceptional.

qa.q: If a king had no sons, who might succeed him according to the variations noted by historians?
qa.a: Brothers or other kinsmen
qa.e: Sometimes brothers or other kinsmen succeeded.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Under patriliny, daughters normally inherited the throne.
Reason (R): Patriliny traces descent from father to son, grandson and so on.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: Under patriliny, sons inherited; women ruling was very exceptional.

qa.q: Marriage outside a kin group is called:
qa.a: Exogamy
qa.e: Exo- means outside; exogamy is marriage outside the unit.

qa.q: Polyandry refers to:
qa.a: A woman having several husbands
qa.e: Polyandry: one woman, several husbands. Polygyny: one man, several wives.

qa.q: How many forms of marriage does the Manusmriti recognise?
qa.e: It recognises eight forms, of which the first four were considered good.

qa.q: Of the forms of marriage recognised in the Manusmriti:
qa.a: The first four were considered good, while the remaining were condemned
qa.e: The text approves the first four and condemns the rest.

qa.q: Why do historians think the condemned forms of marriage were mentioned at all?
qa.a: They may have been practised by those who did not accept Brahmanical norms
qa.e: Mentioning them suggests they existed in practice among some groups.

qa.q: Kanyadana was regarded as:
qa.a: An important religious duty of the father
qa.e: The gift of a daughter in marriage was seen as a father's religious duty.

qa.q: The Manusmriti was compiled between approximately:
qa.a: c. 200 BCE and 200 CE
qa.e: It was compiled between c. 200 BCE and 200 CE.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Daughters were married into families outside their kin under the patrilineal system.
Reason (R): Under patriliny, daughters had no claims to the resources of the household.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Since daughters did not inherit, they were married out of the kin group; R explains A.

qa.q: According to Brahmanical practice, a woman on marriage was expected to:
qa.a: Give up her father's gotra and adopt her husband's
qa.e: The Brahmanical rule was to adopt the husband's gotra.

qa.q: What do names like 'Gotami' and 'Vasithi' of Satavahana queens indicate?
qa.a: They retained names derived from their father's gotra
qa.e: These names come from their fathers' gotras, unlike the Brahmanical rule.

qa.q: 'Gotami-puta' is an example of a:
qa.a: Metronymic
qa.e: It means 'son of Gotami', a name derived from the mother.

qa.q: Although Satavahana rulers used metronymics, succession to their throne was generally:
qa.a: Patrilineal
qa.e: Despite metronymics, the throne usually passed through the male line.

qa.q: Some Satavahana wives belonged to the same gotra as their husbands. This suggests:
qa.a: Endogamy, contrary to the Brahmanical ideal
qa.e: Marrying within the gotra shows endogamy, possibly from southern kinship practices.

qa.q: Gandhari's advice to Duryodhana was to:
qa.a: Make peace with the Pandavas
qa.e: She urged peace; he refused and lost the war.

qa.q: From about when did Brahmanas begin classifying people into gotras?
qa.a: c. 1000 BCE
qa.e: The practice is dated from c. 1000 BCE onwards.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Satavahana metronymics suggest mothers were important.
Reason (R): Succession to the Satavahana throne was generally matrilineal.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: succession was generally patrilineal despite metronymics.

qa.q: According to the Dharmasutras, which occupation was prescribed for Vaishyas?
qa.a: Agriculture, pastoralism and trade
qa.e: Vaishyas were assigned agriculture, pastoralism and trade, along with studying Vedas and making gifts.

qa.q: Which hymn of the Rigveda was cited to claim a divine origin for the varna order?
qa.a: Purusha Sukta
qa.e: The Purusha Sukta describes the varnas emerging from Purusha's body.

qa.q: Which was NOT a strategy used by Brahmanas to enforce the varna order?
qa.a: Abolishing all differences of birth
qa.e: Abolishing differences is the opposite of enforcing them.

qa.q: Administering justice was prescribed in the Dharmasutras as a duty of:
qa.a: Kshatriyas
qa.e: Kshatriyas were to wage war, protect people and administer justice.

qa.q: According to the norms, the only occupation prescribed for Shudras was:
qa.a: Serving the three higher varnas
qa.e: The Dharmasutras assigned Shudras only service to the higher varnas.

qa.q: Why do historians treat the varna duties of the Dharmasutras with caution?
qa.a: They are norms that may not reflect actual practice
qa.e: Prescriptive texts state ideals; practice could differ.

qa.q: Which of these duties was common to Brahmanas, Kshatriyas and Vaishyas in the Dharmasutras?
qa.a: Studying the Vedas
qa.e: All three were to study the Vedas; only Brahmanas were to receive gifts.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Brahmanas presented the varna order as divinely ordained.
Reason (R): Citing the Purusha Sukta made the order seem natural and difficult to question.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: A claim of divine origin gives authority; R explains why the strategy was used.

qa.q: Which dynasties, the immediate successors of the Mauryas, were Brahmanas?
qa.a: Shungas and Kanvas
qa.e: The Shungas and Kanvas were Brahmanas.

qa.q: How did Brahmanical texts describe the origin of the Mauryas?
qa.a: As 'low' origin
qa.e: Brahmanical texts called them of 'low' origin; later Buddhist texts called them Kshatriyas.

qa.q: Who was the best-known Shaka ruler, recorded as rebuilding the Sudarshana lake?
qa.a: Rudradaman
qa.e: Rudradaman (c. second century CE) rebuilt the Sudarshana lake.

qa.q: 'Mlechchha' was a term used by Brahmanas for:
qa.a: Outsiders considered barbarians
qa.e: The Shakas and others outside the Sanskritic order were called mlechchhas.

qa.q: Gotami-puta Siri-Satakani claimed to be:
qa.a: A unique Brahmana and destroyer of the pride of Kshatriyas
qa.e: He called himself 'eka bamhana', a unique Brahmana.

qa.q: What contradiction is seen in Gotami-puta Siri-Satakani's actions?
qa.a: He claimed to prevent intermarriage among varnas but made a marriage alliance with the Shakas
qa.e: His alliance with Rudradaman's kin contradicted his claim.

qa.q: What does the history of non-Kshatriya kings suggest about political power?
qa.a: It was open to anyone who could muster support and resources
qa.e: Many rulers were not Kshatriyas, showing power did not depend on birth.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): One of the earliest Sanskrit inscriptions was issued by a Shaka ruler.
Reason (R): The Shakas were regarded as mlechchhas by Brahmanas.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true: Rudradaman's Sanskrit inscription is early, and Brahmanas did call Shakas mlechchhas. But being called mlechchhas does not explain why Rudradaman used Sanskrit.

qa.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes jati from varna?
qa.a: There were four varnas, but no fixed number of jatis
qa.e: In Brahmanical theory both were birth-based, but jatis had no fixed number.

qa.q: The Mandasor inscription records the history of a guild of:
qa.a: Silk weavers
qa.e: It records a guild of silk weavers.

qa.q: From where did the silk weavers of the Mandasor inscription migrate?
qa.a: Lata (Gujarat)
qa.e: They came from Lata in Gujarat.

qa.q: What was the old name of Mandasor according to the inscription?
qa.a: Dashapura
qa.e: Mandasor was then known as Dashapura.

qa.q: Why did the weavers migrate, according to the inscription?
qa.a: They had heard of the greatness of the local king and wanted to settle in his kingdom
qa.e: The inscription says they were drawn by the king's reputation.

qa.q: Which god's temple did the silk weavers build?
qa.a: Sun god
qa.e: They built a temple dedicated to the sun god.

qa.q: Jatis sharing a common occupation were sometimes organised into:
qa.a: Shrenis or guilds
qa.e: Guilds were called shrenis.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The Mandasor silk weavers migrated from Lata to Dashapura.
Reason (R): In Brahmanical theory there were only four jatis.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: There were four varnas but no fixed number of jatis.

qa.q: To which community did Ekalavya belong?
qa.a: Nishada (forest-dwelling)
qa.e: Ekalavya was a forest-dwelling nishada.

qa.q: What fee did Drona demand from Ekalavya?
qa.a: His right thumb
qa.e: Drona demanded the right thumb, which reduced Ekalavya's skill.

qa.q: Which Chinese pilgrim wrote that 'untouchables' had to sound a clapper in the streets?
qa.a: Fa Xian
qa.e: Fa Xian (c. fifth century CE) recorded this.

qa.q: Xuan Zang (c. seventh century) observed that:
qa.a: Executioners and scavengers were forced to live outside the city
qa.e: He recorded that such groups lived outside the city.

qa.q: According to the Manusmriti, chandalas were to:
qa.a: Live outside the village and use discarded utensils
qa.e: The Manusmriti prescribed exclusion for chandalas.

qa.q: People who spoke non-Sanskritic languages were labelled by Brahmanical texts as:
qa.a: Mlechchhas
qa.e: Mlechchha was used for outsiders, including speakers of non-Sanskritic languages.

qa.q: Bhima's marriage to Hidimba in the Mahabharata illustrates:
qa.a: Contact between the epic's heroes and forest communities outside the Brahmanical order
qa.e: It shows interaction with forest communities, described in Brahmanical terms.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Certain activities were classified as 'polluting' in Brahmanical texts.
Reason (R): This classification was used to place some social groups at the very bottom of the hierarchy.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Defining activities as polluting justified the subordination of those who performed them; R explains A.

qa.q: Compare the Ekalavya story with the episode of Bhima's marriage to Hidimba. Which statement is the BEST comparison?
qa.a: The Ekalavya story shows a forest dweller excluded from elite learning, while the Hidimba episode shows contact and alliance with a forest community
qa.e: Drona denies Ekalavya his teaching and takes his thumb, which reflects exclusion. Bhima marries Hidimba and they have a son, Ghatotkacha, which shows interaction with forest people, though told in Brahmanical terms.

qa.q: What was 'stridhana'?
qa.a: Gifts a woman received at marriage, which she could retain
qa.e: Stridhana, 'a woman's wealth', was mainly marriage gifts.

qa.q: According to the Manusmriti, the paternal estate was to be divided:
qa.a: Equally among sons, with a special share for the eldest
qa.e: Sons divided it equally, with a special share for the eldest.

qa.q: How many means of acquiring wealth does the Manusmriti list for men?
qa.e: Seven for men; six for women.

qa.q: How many means of acquiring wealth does the Manusmriti list for women?
qa.e: It lists six, all essentially gifts.

qa.q: Who had a claim on a woman's stridhana after her death?
qa.a: Her children
qa.e: Stridhana passed to her children; the husband had no claim.

qa.q: Which is NOT one of the means of acquiring wealth for men in the Manusmriti?
qa.a: Gifts from a brother at marriage
qa.e: Gifts from a brother are listed among women's means.

qa.q: A case: A historian reads in the Manusmriti that women should not hoard family property without permission, and also reads Prabhavati Gupta's land grant. What is the best conclusion?
qa.a: Norms restricted women's control of property, but some elite women did hold land
qa.e: Combining a normative text with an inscription shows both the rule and the exceptions.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Social differences between men and women were sharpened in early India.
Reason (R): Land, cattle and money were generally controlled by men.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Male control of key resources deepened gender inequality; R explains A.

qa.q: What does 'mahasammata' mean?
qa.a: The great elect
qa.e: Mahasammata means the great elect, the ruler chosen by the people.

qa.q: In the Sutta Pitaka myth, why did people choose a ruler?
qa.a: To censure and punish wrongdoers as greed and deceit grew
qa.e: They chose him to restore order and punish wrongdoing, in return for rice.

qa.q: The Buddhist idea of kingship as based on human choice is often described as a:
qa.a: Social contract
qa.e: Kingship based on agreement and exchange resembles a social contract.

qa.q: Which statement reflects the Buddhist view of social differences?
qa.a: They existed but were not natural or inflexible, and birth did not justify status
qa.e: Buddhists recognised differences but rejected birth-based claims.

qa.q: In the Majjhima Nikaya story, Kachchana tells King Avantiputra that:
qa.a: A rich Shudra could have members of other varnas as his servants
qa.e: The point is that wealth, not birth, decided who served whom.

qa.q: Tamil Sangam poems praised chiefs mainly for:
qa.a: Their generosity in distributing wealth
qa.e: Chiefs' generosity to bards and poets was celebrated.

qa.q: According to Brahmanical texts, which varnas were in theory the wealthiest?
qa.a: Brahmanas and Kshatriyas
qa.e: The texts linked wealth with the higher varnas, though reality varied.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Tamil Sangam poems praised chiefs for their generosity.
Reason (R): A Sutta Pitaka myth describes people choosing a ruler called mahasammata.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but the Buddhist myth does not explain the Tamil ideal of generosity.

qa.q: The Mahabharata is described as 'itihasa', which means:
qa.a: Thus it was
qa.e: Itihasa means 'thus it was', a kind of history.

qa.q: Who probably composed the original story of the Mahabharata, according to historians?
qa.a: Sutas, charioteer-bards
qa.e: Sutas accompanied warriors and composed poems celebrating them.

qa.q: The Mahabharata is traditionally attributed to:
qa.a: Vyasa
qa.e: Tradition attributes it to the sage Vyasa.

qa.q: The Mahabharata grew to about how many verses?
qa.e: From perhaps less than 10,000 it grew to about 1,00,000 verses.

qa.q: Didactic sections of the Mahabharata contain:
qa.a: Prescriptions about social norms
qa.e: Didactic sections lay down norms; narrative sections tell stories.

qa.q: Between c. 200 BCE and 200 CE, which change took place in the Mahabharata?
qa.a: Krishna came to be identified with Vishnu
qa.e: Vishnu worship grew and Krishna was identified with Vishnu.

qa.q: Why was the Sanskrit of the Mahabharata probably widely understood?
qa.a: It was far simpler than the Sanskrit of the Vedas and prashastis
qa.e: Its simpler Sanskrit made it accessible.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The Mahabharata contains layers from different periods.
Reason (R): Large didactic sections resembling the Manusmriti were added between c. 200 and 400 CE.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Later additions like the didactic sections are an example of layering, so R explains A.

qa.q: Who excavated the village of Hastinapura in 1951–52?
qa.a: B.B. Lal
qa.e: The archaeologist B.B. Lal excavated it.

qa.q: Hastinapura, excavated by B.B. Lal, is in which district?
qa.a: Meerut, Uttar Pradesh
qa.e: It is in Meerut district of UP.

qa.q: How many occupational levels did B.B. Lal find at Hastinapura?
qa.e: He found evidence of five levels.

qa.q: Which features were found in the third phase at Hastinapura?
qa.a: Houses of mud-brick and burnt brick, soakage jars and brick drains
qa.e: The third phase (c. sixth to third centuries BCE) had these features.

qa.q: 'Searching for convergence' in this context means:
qa.a: Checking whether archaeological evidence matches textual descriptions
qa.e: Historians compare the text with archaeological findings.

qa.q: Which is NOT one of the explanations historians offer for Draupadi's polyandry?
qa.a: It was the most common form of marriage among Brahmanas
qa.e: Polyandry fell out of favour among Brahmanas, so it was not common among them.

qa.q: A case: A student argues that because a village called Hastinapura has ancient remains, the Mahabharata war definitely happened there. What is the best response?
qa.a: A shared name and broad date are not proof; the link is uncertain
qa.e: Convergence must be shown by evidence, not by a name alone.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): B.B. Lal's excavation proved that Hastinapura was the capital of the Kauravas.
Reason (R): Lal found evidence of five occupational levels at Hastinapura.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: The identification remains uncertain; the five levels are a genuine finding.

qa.q: Which writer composed the story 'Kunti O Nishadi'?
qa.a: Mahasweta Devi
qa.e: Mahasweta Devi, a Bengali writer, wrote it.

qa.q: In 'Kunti O Nishadi', the nishada woman questions Kunti about:
qa.a: The burning of the lac house
qa.e: She asks about the nishada woman and five sons who died in the lac house fire.

qa.q: Why is the Mahabharata called a dynamic text?
qa.a: It kept changing through regional versions, retellings and art forms
qa.e: Ongoing retellings in many languages and forms made it dynamic.

qa.q: How did local stories relate to the Mahabharata?
qa.a: Many local stories found their way into the epic
qa.e: Regional tales were absorbed into the epic.

qa.q: Which form was NOT used to express Mahabharata episodes in the past?
qa.a: Television serials in the ancient period
qa.e: Television is modern; ancient expressions included sculpture, painting and performance.

qa.q: The process by which the Mahabharata was retold in many languages is best described as:
qa.a: An ongoing dialogue between peoples, communities and those who wrote the texts
qa.e: Different communities shaped and reshaped the epic.

qa.q: What does a retelling like 'Kunti O Nishadi' do for historians and readers?
qa.a: It brings out voices left out of the original narrative
qa.e: Retellings highlight marginalised perspectives.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Episodes from the Mahabharata appear in sculpture, painting and performing arts.
Reason (R): The Mahabharata was composed only for Brahmanas and was kept secret from others.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true: the epic's episodes inspired sculpture, painting, plays and dance. R is false: its simple Sanskrit and many retellings show it reached wide audiences.

qa.q: Which rulers funded the preservation of Sanchi in the nineteenth century?
qa.a: Shahjehan Begum and Sultan Jehan Begum of Bhopal
qa.e: The Begums of Bhopal provided money for preservation.

qa.q: To whom did John Marshall dedicate his volumes on Sanchi?
qa.a: Sultan Jehan Begum
qa.e: He dedicated them to Sultan Jehan Begum, who funded his work.

qa.q: Which gateway of Sanchi did the French want to take to France?
qa.a: Eastern gateway
qa.e: They sought permission to take the eastern gateway.

qa.q: How was the dispute over removing Sanchi's gateway resolved?
qa.a: Plaster-cast copies were made and the originals stayed at the site
qa.e: Both the French and English accepted plaster-cast copies.

qa.q: In which year was Sanchi declared a World Heritage Site?
qa.e: Sanchi became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1989.

qa.q: Sanchi is located in which present-day state?
qa.a: Madhya Pradesh
qa.e: Sanchi is near Bhopal in Madhya Pradesh.

qa.q: Which of these did Sultan Jehan Begum fund?
qa.a: The museum at Sanchi, the guesthouse where Marshall lived, and the publication of his volumes
qa.e: She supported the museum, guesthouse and publication.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Sanchi is one of the most valuable sources for the history of early Buddhism.
Reason (R): Its stupa, gateways and sculptures survive in a well-preserved state at the original site.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Because it survives so well in situ, Sanchi gives rich evidence about early Buddhism; R explains A.

qa.q: Which Rigvedic deity was the god of fire?
qa.a: Agni
qa.e: Agni is the god of fire; Indra is a warrior deity; Soma is a plant and drink.

qa.q: Rajasuya and ashvamedha were:
qa.a: Elaborate sacrifices performed by chiefs and kings with Brahmana priests
qa.e: Kings performed these grand sacrifices, depending on Brahmana priests.

qa.q: The kutagarashala was:
qa.a: A hut with a pointed roof where thinkers debated
qa.e: Literally a hut with a pointed roof, it was a place for debate.

qa.q: Makkhali Gosala is best described as a:
qa.a: Fatalist
qa.e: He held that everything was predetermined.

qa.q: Ajita Kesakambalin argued that:
qa.a: A person is made of four elements and nothing survives death
qa.e: As a materialist, he denied any life after death.

qa.q: To which king did Makkhali Gosala and Ajita Kesakambalin explain their views, according to the Buddhist text?
qa.a: Ajatasattu of Magadha
qa.e: The dialogue is set at the court of King Ajatasattu.

qa.q: Which concepts are associated with the Upanishads?
qa.a: Atman, brahman, karma and rebirth
qa.e: Upanishadic thinkers explored the atman, the brahman, karma and rebirth.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The Upanishads differ from the views of materialists like Ajita Kesakambalin.
Reason (R): Upanishadic thinkers held that the atman exists and actions shape rebirth, while materialists denied life after death.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The opposing views on the soul and afterlife explain the difference; R explains A.

qa.q: How many tirthankaras preceded Mahavira, according to Jaina tradition?
qa.e: Mahavira was the 24th, preceded by 23 tirthankaras.

qa.q: The term 'tirthankara' literally means:
qa.a: Those who guide men and women across the river of existence
qa.e: Tirthankaras guide people across the river of existence.

qa.q: Which idea is most central to Jaina philosophy?
qa.a: The entire world is animated, and ahimsa must be practised towards all living beings
qa.e: Jainas see life everywhere and hold ahimsa central.

qa.q: According to Jainism, freedom from the cycle of karma is possible through:
qa.a: Asceticism and penance after renouncing the world
qa.e: Renunciation, asceticism and penance were required.

qa.q: Which is NOT one of the five Jaina vows?
qa.a: Abstain from eating rice
qa.e: The five vows are about killing, stealing, lying, celibacy and property.

qa.q: In which languages did Jaina scholars produce literature?
qa.a: Prakrit, Sanskrit and Tamil
qa.e: Jaina literature exists in Prakrit, Sanskrit and Tamil.

qa.q: Vardhamana Mahavira was the:
qa.a: 24th tirthankara
qa.e: Mahavira is the 24th tirthankara; the philosophy existed before him.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Mahavira was the first tirthankara.
Reason (R): Jainas believe that even stones, rocks and water have life.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: Mahavira was the 24th tirthankara; the belief that the world is animated is central to Jainism.

qa.q: Siddhartha was the son of a chief of which clan?
qa.a: Sakya
qa.e: He was the son of a Sakya chief.

qa.q: Which sights led Siddhartha to leave the palace?
qa.a: An old man, a sick man and a corpse, and then a peaceful mendicant
qa.e: These sights showed him the reality of decay and death.
